This surah is Meccan, except for three verses: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And indeed, they were about to tempt you away﴾ [al-Isra 17:73]. It was revealed when the delegation of Thaqif came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and when the Jews said, "This is not the land of the prophets." His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And say, "My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance and cause me to exit a sound exit"﴾ [al-Isra 17:80]. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, your Lord encompasses the people﴾ [al-Isra 17:60], and the verse. Muqatil said: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it﴾ [al-Isra 17:107], and the verse. Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) said concerning Bani Isra'il, al-Kahf and [Maryam]: "They are among the first of the old treasures, and they are from my ancient possessions," meaning from his earliest acquisitions.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, whose surroundings We have blessed, in order to show him of Our signs. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ (1)

In it there are eight [sic, as in all the manuscripts; it is noted that the issues are six] issues.

The first: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Subhana﴾ ("Subhana," "glory be to") is a noun placed in the position of a verbal noun (masdar). It is ghayr mutamakkin (indeclinable in the full sense), because it does not take the various case endings (i'rab), the definite article "al-" does not enter it, no verb is derived from it, and it is not declined because it has two extra letters at its end. You say: "sabbahtu tasbihan wa subhanan," like "kaffartu al-yamin takfiran wa kufranan." Its meaning is the declaring of Allah, exalted is He, free from every deficiency and the clearing of Him of all imperfection. It is therefore a great remembrance of Allah, exalted is He, which is not fitting for anyone else. As for the saying of the poet:

I say, when his boasting came to me: "Glory be to whoever is of 'Alqama, the boaster!"

[The verse is by al-A'sha. He says this about 'Ilba ibn 'Ulatha al-Ja'fari in his rivalry with 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl, and al-A'sha had preferred 'Amir and disavowed 'Alqama and his boasting over 'Amir (Hin al-Shantamari).]

It is mentioned by way of rarity. Talha ibn 'Ubayd Allah al-Fayyad, one of the Ten (promised Paradise), narrated that he said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "What is the meaning of Subhana Allah?" He said: "The declaring of Allah free from every evil." According to the school of Sibawayh, the governing element (al-'amil) is the verb whose meaning it carries, not its wording, since no verb has come from its wording; this is like "qa'ada al-qurfusa'" (he sat in the crouching position) and "ishtamala al-samma'" (he wrapped himself in the wrap). [Al-qurfusa': the sitting posture of one who clasps his hands around his knees. Al-samma': a type of wrapping; it is to cover your body with your garment, like the wrapper of the Bedouins with their cloaks: one brings it from his right side over his left hand and left shoulder, then brings it back from his left side over his right hand and right shoulder, covering both together.] So the estimate according to him is: "I declare Allah free, a declaring," so "Subhana Allah" has taken the place of your saying "tanzihan" (a declaring).

The second: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Asra bi-'abdihi﴾ ("asra," "took by night"). "Asra" has two dialectal forms: sara and asra, like saqa and asqa, as has been mentioned before. [See vol. 1, p. 417.] He said:

The starry Jawza' ... a driving wind in it, its cold, frozen, flowed over him by night.

[The verse is by al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani, from his poem that begins: "O abode of Maya in al-'Aliya."]

And another said:

Greet al-Nadira, lady of the curtain; she travelled to me by night, though she had not been traveling.

[The verse is by Hassan ibn Thabit.]

So he combined the two dialects in the two verses. And al-isra' is travel by night. It is said: "sariytu masra and suran, and asraytu israa'an." The poet said:

And a night, dewy, I travelled through, and its journey did not weary me, nor did the sleeping of Layth [(the lion, or a man)].

It is said: asra means he travelled from the beginning of the night, and sara means he travelled from its end, and the first is better known.

The third: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿bi-'abdihi﴾ ("with His servant"). The scholars said: "If the Prophet (ﷺ) had a name more noble than this, He would have named him by it in that exalted state." And concerning its meaning they recited:

O people, my heart is with Zahra'; the hearer and the seer recognize it.
Do not call me except "O slave of her," for it is the most noble of my names.

This has been mentioned before. [See vol. 1, p. 232.] Al-Qushayri said: When Allah, exalted is He, raised him to His exalted presence and lifted him above the upper stars, He bound him to the name of servanthood out of humility for the community.

The fourth: The Isra' is established in all the books of hadith, and it was narrated from the Companions in every region of Islam, so it is mutawatir (mass-transmitted) in this respect. Al-Naqqash mentioned that twenty Companions transmitted it. It is reported in the Sahih from Anas ibn Malik that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I was brought the Buraq, a white animal [tall], above the donkey and below the mule, placing its hoof at the limit of its gaze." He said: "I mounted it until I came to Bayt al-Maqdis." He said: "I tied it to the ring to which the prophets tie." He said: "Then I entered the mosque and prayed two rak'as in it, then I went out, and Jibril (peace be upon him) came to me with a vessel of wine and a vessel of milk, and I chose the milk. Jibril said: 'You have chosen the natural disposition (al-fitra).'" He said: "Then he ascended with us to the heaven..." and he mentioned the hadith.

Among what is not in the two Sahihs is what al-Ajurri and al-Samarqandi narrated. Al-Ajurri said, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, concerning His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, whose surroundings We have blessed﴾: Abu Sa'id said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) told us about the night he was taken on the Isra'. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I was brought an animal, the most like of animals to a mule, with two ears that flap, and it is the Buraq, which the prophets used to ride before. I mounted it, and it set off, its forelegs reaching the limit of its sight. I heard a call from my right: 'O Muhammad, wait for me so I may ask you,' but I went on and did not turn to it. Then I heard a call from my left: 'O Muhammad, wait,' and I went on and did not turn to it. Then a woman met me, adorned with all the adornments of the world, raising her hands, saying: 'Wait for me so I may ask you,' and I went on and did not turn. Then I came to Bayt al-Maqdis al-Aqsa, and I dismounted from the animal and tied it to the ring in which the prophets used to tie. Then I entered the mosque and prayed in it. Jibril (peace be upon him) said to me: 'What did you hear, O Muhammad?' I said: 'A call from my right: O Muhammad, wait for me so I may ask you, and I went on and did not turn.' He said: 'That was the caller of the Jews. Had you stopped, your community would have become Jewish.' He said: 'Then I heard a call from my left: wait for me so I may ask you, and I went on and did not turn to it.' He said: 'That was the caller of the Christians. Indeed, had you stopped, your community would have become Christian.' He said: 'Then a woman met me, adorned with all the adornments of the world, raising her hands, saying: wait. I went on and did not turn to her.' He said: 'That was the world. Had you stopped, you would have chosen the world over the Hereafter.' He said: 'Then I was brought two vessels, one containing milk and the other containing wine. It was said to me: take and drink whichever you wish. I took the milk and drank it. Jibril said to me: You have found the natural disposition. Had you taken the wine, your community would have gone astray.' Then he brought the mi'raj (ascension) in which the spirits of the children of Adam ascend, and it was the most beautiful thing I had seen. [Or: Have you not seen how the dying person fixes his gaze upon it?] So we ascended until we came to the gate of the lowest heaven. Jibril asked for it to be opened, and it was said: 'Who is this?' He said: 'Jibril.' They said: 'And who is with you?' He said: 'Muhammad.' They said: 'Has he been sent for?' He said: 'Yes.' So they opened for me and greeted me. And there was an angel guarding the heaven, called Isma'il, with seventy thousand angels, with each angel a hundred thousand. [He said: 'And none knows the hosts of your Lord except Him.'] ..." and he mentioned the hadith until he said: "Then we went on to the fifth heaven, and there I met Harun ibn 'Imran, the beloved among his people, and around him was a great following of his community." The Prophet (ﷺ) described him and said: "He had a long beard that nearly reached his navel." Then we went on to the sixth heaven, and there I met Musa, and he greeted me and welcomed me." The Prophet (ﷺ) described him and said: "A man with abundant hair; if he had worn two shirts, his hair would have come out through them..." [the hadith].

Al-Bazzar narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was brought a horse and was mounted on it; each step of it reached the limit of his sight... and he mentioned the hadith.

It has come in the description of the Buraq from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "While I was sleeping in al-Hijr, someone came to me and moved me with his foot. I followed the figure, and it was Jibril (peace be upon him), standing at the door of the mosque, with him an animal smaller than a mule and larger than a donkey, its face a human face, its hooves like hooves of a beast, its tail like the tail of an ox, and its mane like the mane of a horse. When Jibril (peace be upon him) brought it near me, it shied and shook its mane. Jibril (peace be upon him) stroked it and said: 'O Burqa, do not shy from Muhammad, for by Allah, no angel brought near and no sent prophet more excellent than Muhammad (ﷺ) has ever ridden you, and none is more honored by Allah than him.' It said: 'I know that he is so, and that he is the owner of intercession, and I love to be among those whom he intercedes for.' I said: 'You are among my intercession, if Allah, exalted is He, wills...'" [the hadith].

Abu Sa'id 'Abd al-Malik ibn Muhammad al-Naysaburi mentioned, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) passed Idris (peace be upon him) in the fourth heaven, he said: "Welcome, righteous brother and righteous prophet, whom we were promised to see, and we did not see him until tonight." He said: "There was Maryam bint 'Imran, who had seventy palaces of pearls, and for the mother of Musa ibn 'Imran there were seventy palaces of red coral, crowned with pearls, its doors and couches of a single vein. When he ascended the ladder to the fifth heaven, and the glorification of its inhabitants was: 'Glory be to Him who combined snow and fire.' Whoever says it once, has the like of their reward. Jibril (peace be upon him) asked for the gate to be opened, and it was opened for him, and there he found an elderly man such as no one had ever seen more handsome, large of eyes, whose beard..."

Near his navel, it was as if it had a streak (shamtah) [[al-shamt: hair that is of two colours, black and white.]], and around him there were people sitting, and he was relating to them. I said, "O Jibril, who is this?" He said, "Harun, the beloved among his people..." and he mentioned the hadith.

This is a brief summary of the hadiths of the Isra' (Night Journey) that lie outside the two Sahihs, which Abu al-Rabi' Sulayman ibn Sabu' has reported in full in his book Shifa' al-Sudur. There is no disagreement among the scholars and the group of biographers (ahl al-siyar) that the prayer was prescribed for the Prophet ﷺ in Makkah at the time of the Isra', when he was taken up to the heavens. They differed about the date of the Isra', the form of the prayer, and whether the Isra' was with his spirit or with his body. These are three questions related to the verse, and they are matters that one should understand and investigate, and they are more important than listing those hadiths. I shall mention, with God's help, what I have come across of the statements of the scholars and the differences of the jurists regarding them.

As for the first question, namely whether the Isra' was with his spirit or with his body, the early and later scholars differed. One group held that it was a journey of the spirit only, that his person did not leave his bed, and that it was a dream in which he saw the realities, and the dreams of the prophets are true. Mu'awiyah and A'ishah held this view, and it is reported from al-Hasan and Ibn Ishaq. Another group said: the Isra' was with the body, awake, to Bayt al-Maqdis, and to the heavens with the spirit. They argued with the words of God, Exalted: ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque﴾, making the Farthest Mosque the limit of the journey. They said: had the journey been with his body beyond the Farthest Mosque, He would have mentioned it, for that would have been more eloquent in praise. Most of the early Muslims and the community held that it was a journey with the body and while awake, and that he rode the Buraq in Makkah, reached Bayt al-Maqdis and prayed in it, and then was taken up bodily. The reports we have pointed to and the verse indicate this. There is nothing impossible in a journey with the body in the waking state, and one does not turn from the apparent and literal meaning to interpretation except when there is an impossibility. Had it been a dream, He would have said "with the spirit of His servant" and not "with His servant." His words, ﴿The eye did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾ [[See vol. 17, p. 92.]], indicate this. Had it been a dream, there would have been no sign or miracle in it, and Umm Hani would not have said to him, "Do not tell the people, lest they call you a liar," and Abu Bakr would not have been the one most worthy of affirming it, and the Quraysh would not have been able to mock and deny him. The Quraysh denied what he reported, so much so that some people who had believed apostatised. Had it been by dream, it would not have been regarded as strange. The polytheists said to him, "If you are truthful, tell us about our caravan, did you meet it?" He said, "At such and such a place I passed by it, and so-and-so was startled." It was said to him, "What did you see, so-and-so?" He said, "I saw nothing, except that the camels had bolted." They said, "Then tell us when the caravan will come to us." He said, "It will come to you on such and such a day." They said, "At what hour?" He said, "I do not know. Will the rising of the sun from here be faster, or the arrival of the caravan from here?" A man said, "That is the day; this is the sun that has risen." Another said, "This is your caravan that has come." They also asked the Prophet ﷺ about the description of Bayt al-Maqdis, and he described it to them, though he had not seen it before that. The Sahih reports from Abu Hurayrah who said: the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "I saw myself in al-Hijr while the Quraysh were asking me about my night journey, and they asked me about things of Bayt al-Maqdis which I had not known well [[i.e. I had not recognised them properly; one says athbatahu and thabatahu when one knows a thing thoroughly.]], so I was distressed with a distress I had never felt like it before. Then God raised it for me so that I could look at it, and whatever they asked me about, I informed them of it..." and the hadith continues.

The statement of A'ishah and Mu'awiyah, "It was only the soul of the Messenger of God ﷺ that was taken on the Isra'," has been objected to on the grounds that she was a child and did not witness it, and she did not narrate it from the Prophet ﷺ. As for Mu'awiyah, he was a disbeliever at that time, not a witness to the event, and he did not narrate from the Prophet ﷺ. Whoever wishes more than what we have mentioned, let him consult the book Ash-Shifa' of Qadi 'Iyad, and he will find therein a cure (shifa').

A'ishah has also been supported by His words, ﴿And We did not make the vision which We showed you except as a trial for people﴾ [[See p. 282 of this volume.]], where He called it a "vision" (ru'yā). But this is refuted by His words, ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night﴾, and one does not say "isra'" for a sleep. Moreover, the word ru'yā may be used for a sight seen with the eye, as will be explained in this surah. In the established reports there is a clear indication that the Isra' was with the body. When a report speaks of something that is possible for the intellect within the power of God, there is no way to deny it, especially in a time of breaking customary norms. The Prophet ﷺ had ascents (ma'arij), so it is not far-fetched that some of them were by vision. On this is interpreted his saying ﴿peace be upon him﴾ in the Sahih: "While I was at the House, between sleeping and waking..." the hadith. And it is possible that the Isra' is to be referred to a sleep. And God knows best.

**The second question** [[In some copies: the fifth and sixth questions instead of the second and third, so that the numbering matches the author's statement at the start: eight questions.]] concerns the date of the *isra'* (the Night Journey). The scholars also differed on this. Reports from Ibn Shihab (al-Zuhri) differ. Musa ibn 'Uqba reported from him that the Prophet was taken by night to Bayt al-Maqdis a year before he migrated to Madina. Yunus reported from him, on the authority of 'Urwa, on the authority of 'A'isha, who said: "Khadija died before prayer was made obligatory." Ibn Shihab said: "That was seven years after the Prophet's (ﷺ) mission began." It is also reported from al-Waqqasi that he said: "He was taken by night five years after his mission began." Ibn Shihab said: "Fasting was made obligatory in Madina before Badr, zakat and the Hajj were made obligatory in Madina, and wine was prohibited after Uhud."

Ibn Ishaq said: "He was taken by night from the Masjid al-Haram to the Masjid al-Aqsa, which is Bayt al-Maqdis, and Islam had already spread among the tribes in Makka." Yunus ibn Bukayr reported from him: "Khadija prayed with the Prophet (ﷺ)." This will come later.

Abu 'Umar (Ibn 'Abd al-Barr) said: "This shows that the *isra'* took place some years before the Hijra, because Khadija died five years before the Hijra. It is also said three years, and it is said four years." Ibn Ishaq's statement contradicts that of Ibn Shihab, although Ibn Shihab's own reports have been differently transmitted, as already mentioned.

Al-Harbi said: "He was taken by night on the twenty-seventh of Rabi' al-Akhir, one year before the Hijra."

Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn al-Qasim al-Dhahabi said in his *Tarikh* (history): "He was taken from Makka to Bayt al-Maqdis, and ascended to the heavens, eighteen months after his mission began."

Abu 'Umar said: "I know of no one among the people of the *sirah* (prophetic biography) who said what al-Dhahabi related. He did not attribute this view to anyone among those to whom this knowledge is attributed, nor did he trace it back to anyone whose reports may be relied upon against them."

**The third question** [[In some copies: the fifth and sixth questions instead of the second and third, so that the numbering matches the author's statement at the start: eight questions.]] concerns the obligation of prayer and its form when it was made obligatory. There is no disagreement among the scholars and the transmitters of the *sirah* that prayer was made obligatory in Makka on the night of the *isra'*, when he was taken up to the heavens, and this is stated explicitly in the *Sahih* and elsewhere. They differed only over its form when it was made obligatory.

It is reported from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that it was first made obligatory as two rak'as each, and then it was increased for residents, so it was completed as four, while the prayer of travel was left at two rak'as. This was the view of al-Sha'bi, Maymun ibn Mihran and Muhammad ibn Ishaq. Al-Sha'bi said: "except the Maghrib."

Yunus ibn Bukayr said: Ibn Ishaq also said: "When prayer was made obligatory for him, that is during the *isra'*, Jibril (peace be upon him) came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and struck the ground with his heel in a part of the valley, and a spring of water gushed forth. Jibril performed ablution while Muhammad watched, peace be upon them both. He washed his face, rinsed his mouth and nose, wiped his head, his ears and his feet up to the ankles, and sprinkled his private parts. Then he stood to pray two rak'as with four prostrations. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned, his eyes refreshed, his soul at ease, and that which he loved from the command of Allah, the Exalted, had come to him. He took Khadija by the hand and brought her to the spring, performed ablution as Jibril had done, then bowed two rak'as with four prostrations, he and Khadija together. After that, he and Khadija prayed alike."

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it was made obligatory as four rak'as for residence and two for travel. Nafi' ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan al-Basri also said this, and it was the view of Ibn Jurayj. Something agreeing with this is also reported from the Prophet (ﷺ).

There is no disagreement that Jibril (peace be upon him) descended on the morning after the night of the *isra'* at the time of midday, and taught the Prophet (ﷺ) the prayer and its times.

Yunus ibn Bukayr reported from Salim, the client of Abu al-Muhajir, who said: "I heard Maymun ibn Mihran say: The first prayer was two rak'as. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed four, and this became the sunna. The prayer for the traveller was retained, and it is complete." Abu 'Umar said: "This chain of transmission is not one on which reliance may be placed. His statement, 'and this became the sunna,' is an objectionable statement. Likewise, al-Sha'bi's exception of the Maghrib alone, without mentioning the Subh (dawn prayer), is a statement with no meaning." The Muslims have agreed that the obligatory prayer for residents is four rak'as, except the Maghrib and the Subh. They know of nothing else, in practice or in widely transmitted reports, and disagreement about what its original obligatory form was does not harm them.

**The fifth question** [[In some copies: this is the seventh question.]] has already been discussed in *al-Ma'ida*, and praise be to Allah. It was also mentioned in *Al 'Imran* [[vol. 4, p. 137.]] that the first mosque set up on earth was the Masjid al-Haram, then the Masjid al-Aqsa, and that between them were forty years, according to the hadith of Abu Dharr. The building of the Masjid al-Aqsa by Sulayman (peace be upon him) and his prayer for it come from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr. The way to reconcile these reports is to be considered there, so there is no point in repeating it.

Here we mention the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Journeys are not undertaken except to three mosques: the Masjid al-Haram, this mosque of mine, and the mosque of Iliya' or Bayt al-Maqdis." Malik transmitted it on the authority of Abu Hurayra. It indicates the virtue of these three mosques over all other mosques. For this reason the scholars said: whoever vows to pray in a mosque which cannot be reached except by a journey and a mount should not do so, but should pray in his own mosque, except in the three mosques mentioned, for whoever vows to pray in them should go there. Malik and a group of scholars said, concerning one who vows to undertake a *ribat* (frontier garrison duty) on a border he guards, that he is obliged to fulfil it wherever the *ribat* is, because it is obedience to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Abu al-Bakhtari added to this hadith "the mosque of the troops," but it is not authentic, it is fabricated, and this was mentioned in the introduction to the book.

**The sixth question** [[In some copies: the eighth question.]] concerns the words of the Exalted: ﴿to the farthest mosque﴾. It was called *al-Aqsa* (the farthest) because of the distance between it and the Masjid al-Haram, and it was the farthest mosque from the people of Makka on earth that is honoured by visitation. Then He said: ﴿whose surroundings We have blessed﴾. It was said: with fruits and flowing rivers. It was also said: with the prophets and righteous people buried around it, and for this reason it was made sacred.

Mu'adh ibn Jabal transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah the Exalted says: O Sham, you are My chosen land of My lands, and I bring to you My chosen ones from among My servants." (Its original form is *Sam*, and then it was Arabicised.)

﴿that We might show him of Our signs﴾. This is from the style of shifting address. The signs are the wonders Allah showed him, which he related to the people. His journey from Makka to the Masjid al-Aqsa in a single night, though it is a month's journey, his ascent to the heavens, and his description of the prophets one by one, are all as established in the *Sahih* of Muslim and elsewhere.

﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾. This has already been discussed [[see vol. 5, p. 258.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 2:

﴿And We gave Moses the Book and made it a guidance for the Children of Israel, [saying], "Do not take other than Me as a trustee."﴾ (17:2)

That is: We honoured Muhammad (ﷺ) with the Night Journey (al-Mi'raj), and We honoured Moses with the Book, which is the Torah. "And We made it" means: that Book. It was also said that it refers to Moses.

It was also said that the meaning of the speech is: "Glory be to the One who took His servant by night and gave Moses the Book," and so it shifts from the third person (al-ghaybah) to speaking about Himself (al-ikhbar 'an nafsihi), exalted is He. It was also said: the meaning of "Glory be to the One who took His servant by night" is "We took him by night" (asrayna). This is supported by what follows it, His saying: ﴿So that We might show him of Our signs﴾ (17:1). So "And We gave Moses the Book" is understood according to this meaning.

(Do not take) — Abu 'Amr read "yattakhidhu" with the letter ya' (third person). The rest read it with ta' (second person). Thus it is an instance of tilwin al-khitab (shifting of address).

"Wakilan" means: a partner (shariken), according to Mujahid. It was also said: a guardian (kafilan) over their affairs, as related by al-Farra'. It was also said: a lord upon whom they rely in their affairs, as said by al-Kalbi. Al-Farra' said: sufficient (kafiyan). The implied sense is: "We charged him in the Book, 'Do not take other than Me as a trustee.'" It was also said: the implied sense is "lest you take."

Al-wakil: the one to whom the matter is entrusted.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 3:

﴿Descendants of those whom We carried with Noah. Indeed, he was a grateful servant.﴾ (17:3)

It means: "O descendants of those whom We carried," in the form of a vocative address. This is the view of Mujahid, and Ibn Abi Najih narrated it from him. By "the descendants" is meant everyone to whom the Qur'an is addressed as proof, who are all those on the earth; this was mentioned by al-Mahdawi. Al-Mawardi said: it means Musa and his people from the Children of Israel, and the meaning is: "O descendants of those whom We carried with Noah, do not associate partners with Me." He mentioned Noah so as to remind them of the blessing of being saved from the drowning granted to their forefathers.

Sufyan narrated from Humayd, from Mujahid, that he recited "dhurriyyata" with a fatha on the dhal and a shaddah on the ra' and the ya'. This reading was narrated by Amir ibn al-Wahid [[So in the copies of the original; we have not found it in the standard sources. In the anomalous readings (shawadh): "dhurriyyah" with kasra is the original.]] from Zayd ibn Thabit. It was also narrated from Zayd ibn Thabit as well: "dhurriyyah" [[So in the copies of the original; we have not found it in the standard sources. In the anomalous readings (shawadh): "dhurriyyah" with kasra is the original.]] with a kasra on the dhal and a shaddah on the ra', and the ya' [[From j.]]

Then He explained that Noah was a grateful servant who thanked Allah for His blessings and saw no good except as coming from Him. Qatadah said: whenever he put on a garment, he would say, "In the name of Allah," and when he took it off, he would say, "Praise be to Allah." Ma'mar narrated this from him. Ma'mar also narrated from Mansur, from Ibrahim, who said: his thanks when he ate was to say, "In the name of Allah," and when he finished eating, to say, "Praise be to Allah." Salman al-Farisi said: it was because he used to praise Allah for his food. Imran ibn Sulaym said: Allah named Noah a grateful servant because whenever he ate he would say, "Praise be to Allah who fed me, and had He willed, He would have left me hungry"; and whenever he drank he would say, "Praise be to Allah who gave me drink, and had He willed, He would have left me thirsty"; and whenever he dressed he would say, "Praise be to Allah who clothed me, and had He willed, He would have left me naked"; and whenever he put on his sandals he would say, "Praise be to Allah who shod me, and had He willed, He would have left me barefoot"; and whenever he relieved himself he would say, "Praise be to Allah who expelled the harm from me, and had He willed, He would have kept it within me."

The purpose of the verse is: you are descendants of Noah, and he was a grateful servant; so you are more worthy of following his example rather than your ignorant forefathers. It was also said: the meaning is that Musa was a grateful servant, since Allah made him a descendant of Noah. It was also said: it is permissible for "dhurriyyata" to be a second object of "tattakhidhu," and His saying "wakilan" is intended as a collective, so this is valid in both readings, namely the ya' and the ta' in "tattakhidhu." It is also permissible in both readings for "dhurriyyata" to be a substitute for His saying "wakilan," since it carries the sense of a plural, as if He said: "Do not take the descendants of those whom We carried with Noah." It is permissible to put it in the accusative by supposing "a'nee" and "amdahu" (I mean and I praise), since the Arabs sometimes use the accusative for praise and blame. It is permissible to put it in the nominative as a substitute for the pronoun in "tattakhidhu" in the reading of whoever reads with the ya'; this is not good for whoever reads with the ta', because the addressed party is not replaced by the absent party. It is permissible to put it in the genitive as a substitute for "Bani Isra'il" in both readings. As for "an" in His saying "alla tattakhidhu," in the reading of whoever reads with the ya' it is in the place of the accusative, with the preposition omitted; the estimate is: "We guided them so that they would not take." In the reading with the ta', it may be an added particle, with the saying implied as mentioned before. It may also be an explanatory particle meaning "i.e.," having no place in grammatical construction, and "la" would then be a prohibition, so that the statement shifts from informing to prohibiting.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 4:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Book﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Abu al-'Aliyah read "fi al-kutub" (in the Books), in the plural form. The singular may be used while its meaning is plural, so the two readings have one meaning. The meaning of "qadayna" (We decreed) is "We informed and notified," as Ibn 'Abbas said. Qatadah said: "We judged." The root of al-qada' (decree) is the firm establishment of a thing and the completion of it. It was also said: "qadayna" means "We revealed," and for this reason He said: "to the Children of Israel." According to Qatadah's view, "ila" (to) carries the meaning of "'ala" (upon), i.e., We decreed upon them and judged. Ibn 'Abbas also said this. The intended meaning of "al-Kitab" (the Book) is the Preserved Tablet.

(Surely you will cause corruption) Ibn 'Abbas read "latufsidunna," and 'Isa al-Thaqafi read "latufsidunna." The meaning in the two readings is close, because when they cause corruption, they are corrupted. The intended meaning of "al-fasad" (corruption) is opposing the rulings of the Torah.

(on the earth) He means the land of Syria, Bayt al-Maqdis, and what surrounds it.

(twice, and you will surely become haughty) The lam in "latufsidunna" and "lata'lunna" is the lam of an implied oath, as previously mentioned.

(with a great haughtiness) He means arrogance, transgression, tyranny, domineering, dominance, and aggression.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 5:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when the promise of the first of them came﴾, meaning the first of the two times of their corruption.

(﴿We sent against you servants of Ours, possessed of great might﴾) They are the people of Babylon, and over them was Bukht Nassar (Nebuchadnezzar) in the first time, when they denied Irmiya (Jeremiah), wounded him and imprisoned him. This was said by Ibn Abbas and others. Qatada said: He sent Jalut (Goliath) against them and he killed them, so he and his people are "possessed of great might." Mujahid said: A army from Persia came to them to spy on their affairs, and with them was Bukht Nassar, who memorised their talk from among his companions. Then they returned to Persia, and there was no fighting. This was in the first time, so there was among them a raiding through the homes without killing. This was mentioned by al-Qushayri Abu Nasr. Al-Mahdawi mentioned from Mujahid that Bukht Nassar came to them and the Children of Israel defeated him, then he came to them a second time and killed them and utterly destroyed them. Ibn Abi Najih narrated it from Mujahid, and al-Nahhas mentioned it. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said in a lengthy report [[See the book Qisas al-Anbiya', known as al-Ara'is, p. 259, Bulaq edition, and Tarikh al-Tabari vol. 2 part 1 p. 638 onward, European edition.]]: The one defeated was Sanharib (Sennacherib), king of Babylon. He came with six hundred thousand banners, under each banner a hundred thousand horsemen, and he camped around Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and Allah defeated him and caused all of them to die except Sanharib and five of his scribes. The king of the Children of Israel, whose name was Siddiqa, sent to pursue Sanharib, and he was captured with the five, one of whom was Bukht Nassar. He cast chains (al-jawami') around their necks, and he took them around Bayt al-Maqdis and Iliya' for seventy days, providing them each day with two loaves of barley for each man. Then he released them and they returned to Babylon. Then Sanharib died after seven years, and Bukht Nassar succeeded him, and the corruption among the Children of Israel grew great. They made lawful the forbidden things and killed their prophet Sha'ya (Isaiah). So Bukht Nassar came to them, and he and his soldiers entered Bayt al-Maqdis and killed the Children of Israel until he annihilated them. Ibn Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud said: The first corruption was the killing of Zakariyya (Zechariah). Ibn Ishaq said: Their corruption in the first time was the killing of Sha'ya, the prophet of Allah, in the tree. That was because when their king Siddiqa died, their affair fell into disorder, they competed for the kingdom, and some of them killed others, while they did not listen to their prophet. So Allah, exalted is He, said to him: "Stand among your people and convey what I reveal to you by your tongue." When he finished what Allah had revealed to him, they rushed at him to kill him, so he fled and a tree split open for him and he entered it. Satan overtook him and took a fringe of his garment and showed it to them, so they placed the saw in the middle of the tree and sawed it until they cut it through, and they cut him in its middle. Ibn Ishaq mentioned that some scholars told him that Zakariyya died a natural death and was not killed, and that the one killed was Sha'ya. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying, may He be exalted: "We sent against you servants of Ours, possessed of great might, and they roamed through the homes," said: He is Sanharib, from the people of Nineveh in Mosul, king of Babylon. This contradicts what Ibn Ishaq said, and Allah knows best. It was also said: They were the Amalaqa (Amalekites), who were disbelievers; this was said by al-Hasan. The meaning of "jasu" (roamed): they spread corruption and killed. Likewise "jasu," "hasu" and "dasu" (all meaning trampled or roamed), as said by Ibn Aziz, and this is the view of al-Qutabi. Ibn Abbas recited "hasu" with an unpointed ha. Abu Zayd said: al-hawas, al-jawas, al-awas and al-hawas are wandering at night. Al-Jawhari said: al-jawsu is the verbal noun of your saying "they roamed through the homes," meaning they penetrated them and sought what was in them, as a man roams (yajus) for news, meaning he seeks it; likewise al-ijtiyas. Al-jawasan (with vowelling) is wandering at night, and this is the view of Abu Ubayda. Al-Tabari said: They went about among the homes seeking them and killing them, going and coming, so he combined the sayings of the lexicographers. Ibn Abbas said: They walked and moved back and forth between the houses and dwellings. Al-Farra' said: They killed you between your houses, and he recited for Hassan:

And among us is the one who met with the sword of Muhammad, and so it roamed among the enemies across the ranks of the armies.

Qutrub said: They descended, he said:

So we roamed their homes by force, and we returned with their masters bound.

(﴿And it was a promise fulfilled﴾) meaning a decree that is certain to happen, with no failure in it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 6:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then We gave you back your turn of victory over them﴾, meaning the dominion (al-dawla) and the return (al-raj'a), and that was when you repented and obeyed. Then it was said: that was by Dawud (David) killing Jalut (Goliath), or by someone else's killing of him, according to the disagreement over who killed them.

(And We aided you with wealth and sons) until your affair returned to what it was.

(And We made you more numerous in manpower (nafir)) meaning more numerous in number and in men than your enemy. The nafir is the group of people who go forth with a man from his clan. It is said: nafir and nafir (nafir and nafir), like qadir and qadir. It is also permissible that nafir be the plural of nafr, like kalib (dogs) and ma'iz (goats) and abid (slaves). The poet said:

Honour to Qahtan for their father, and to Himyar, honour to a people who are a nafir.

The meaning: after this first event they became more united and their conditions more righteous, as a reward from God Exalted for their return to obedience.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 7 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If you do good, you do good for your own souls﴾, meaning the benefit of your good deeds returns to you.

﴿And if you do evil, it is against them﴾, meaning it is upon them, as in the phrase "salamun laka," meaning "salamun 'alayka" (peace be upon you). The poet said:

*So he fell prone upon his hands and his mouth*

meaning upon his hands and upon his mouth. [[This is the second half of a line by Rabi'a ibn Mukaddam. Its first half is:
"And he struck with the long spear, an humiliation"
Before this line is:
"So he turned the mount of the howdah toward him, deliberately, so that some of what was not known would be known"
And after it:
"And he gave another after it, a fierce one, wide-mouthed, gaping like the jaw of a hyena"
These verses were composed on the day of al-Zaʽina. See al-Qali's Amali, vol. 2, p. 270, Dar al-Kutub edition.]]

Al-Tabari said: the lam here carries the meaning of ila (to), meaning "and if you do evil, then toward it," i.e., the evil returns to it, as in His saying: ﴿because your Lord has inspired it (la-ha)﴾, meaning "to it." [[See vol. 20, p. 149.]]

It was also said: "for it is the recompense and the punishment." Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: "for it there is a Lord who forgives the evil."

Then it may be that this is an address to the Children of Israel at the beginning of their history: you did evil, so killing, captivity and destruction befell you; then you did good, so sovereignty, elevation and the restoration of your affairs returned to you.

It may also be that the Children of Israel were addressed with this at the time of Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning: you have recognized that your ancestors deserved punishment for their disobedience, so be wary of the like of it. Or, in this sense, it may be an address to the polytheists of Quraysh.

﴿So when the promise of the Hereafter comes﴾, that is, the time of your corruption. They killed Yahya ibn Zakariya (peace be upon them both) on the second occasion. He was killed by a king of the Children of Israel called Lakhit, as stated by al-Qutabi (Ibn Qutayba). Al-Tabari said: his name was Hirdus, as mentioned in the History, and the one who prompted his killing was a woman named Azbil.

Al-Suddi said: the king of the Children of Israel used to honor Yahya ibn Zakariya and consult him on matters. The king consulted him about marrying the daughter of one of his wives, and he forbade him from her, saying: "She is not lawful for you." So her mother held a grudge against Yahya (peace be upon him). Then she dressed her daughter in thin red garments, perfumed her, and sent her to the king while he was at his drinking. She instructed her to present herself to him, and if he wanted her, to refuse until he gave her whatever she asked. When he agreed, she asked that the head of Yahya ibn Zakariya be brought to her on a golden basin. She did this, until the head of Yahya ibn Zakariya was brought, and the head was speaking until it was placed before him, saying: "She is not lawful for you, she is not lawful for you." In the morning his blood was boiling, so he threw dust upon it, and it boiled above the dust. He kept throwing dust upon it until it reached the walls of the city, and it was still boiling. This was recorded by al-Tha'labi and others.

Ibn 'Asakir the hafiz mentioned in his History, from al-Husayn ibn 'Ali, who said: one of these kings died and left his wife and his daughter, and his brother inherited his kingdom. The brother wished to marry his brother's wife, so he consulted Yahya ibn Zakariya about it. In that era the kings acted according to the commands of the prophets. Yahya said to him: "Do not marry her, for she is a harlot." The woman learned that he had mentioned her and had turned him away from her, so she said: "From where did this come?" until it reached her that it came from Yahya. She said: "Yahya will either be killed or will be driven out of his kingdom." So she went to her daughter, prepared her, and then said: "Go to your uncle in front of the assembly, for when he sees you he will call you and seat you in his lap, and he will say: 'Ask me for whatever you wish, for you will not ask me for anything except that I give it to you.' When he says that to you, say: 'I ask for nothing but the head of Yahya.'" He said: the kings, when one of them spoke something before the assembly and did not carry it out, would be stripped of his kingdom. So she did this. He said: then death began to come to him from the killing of Yahya, and death began to come to him from the loss of his kingdom. He chose his kingdom and killed him. He said: then the earth swallowed up her mother.

Ibn Jud'an said: I narrated this story to Ibn al-Musayyib, and he said: "Shall I not tell you how the killing of Zakariya took place?" I said: "No." [He said:] When Zakariya's son was killed, Zakariya fled from them, and they pursued him until he came upon a tree with a trunk, and the tree called to him, and it split open and enclosed him, leaving a fringe of his garment outside which the winds blew about. They went to the tree and found no trace of him after that, but they looked at that fringe. So they called for a saw and cut the tree, and they cut him with it.

I say: this appears in the Great History of al-Tabari. [[See vol. 3, part 1, p. 713, European edition.]] Abu al-Sa'ib narrated to me, who said: Abu Mu'awiya narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from al-Minhal, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Jesus son of Mary sent Yahya ibn Zakariya with twelve of the disciples to teach the people. He said: among the things they forbade was marrying the daughter of a brother. He said: the king of them had a niece who pleased him... and he related the report in its meaning.

And from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Yahya ibn Zakariya was sent with twelve of the disciples to teach the people, and among what they taught them was forbidding them to marry the daughter of a sister. The king of them had a niece who pleased him, and he wished to marry her, and she had a need that she asked of him every day. When her mother learned that they had been forbidden to marry the daughter of a sister, she said to her: "When you go in to the king and he says, 'Do you have a need?' say: 'My need is that you slaughter Yahya ibn Zakariya.'" He said: "Ask me for something other than this!" She said: "I ask you for nothing but this." When she refused him, he called for a basin, and he called for him and slaughtered him. A drop of his blood fell upon the surface of the earth and continued to boil until Allah sent Bukhtnasar against them. It was cast into his heart that he should kill upon that blood from among them until that blood was still. So he killed upon it seventy thousand of them, and in another narration seventy-five thousand. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: this is the blood-price of every prophet.

And from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Allah revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ): "I have killed seventy thousand for the sake of Yahya ibn Zakariya, and I will kill seventy thousand and seventy thousand for the sake of the son of your daughter."

And from Sumayr ibn 'Atiyya, who said: seventy prophets were killed upon the rock that is in Bayt al-Maqdis, among them Yahya ibn Zakariya.

And from Zayd ibn Waqid, who said: I saw the head of Yahya (peace be upon him) when they wanted to build the Mosque of Damascus. It was brought out from beneath one of the pillars of the dome that is next to the mihrab, on the side facing east, and the skin and hair were in their original state, unchanged.

And from Qurra ibn Khalid, who said: the sky did not weep over anyone except Yahya ibn Zakariya and al-Husayn ibn 'Ali, and its redness is its weeping.

And from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, who said: a son of Adam is at his most desolate in three situations: the day he is born, when he comes out into a house of sorrow; the night he spends with the dead, neighboring people he has never seen the like of; and the day he is raised, when he witnesses a scene he has never seen the like of. Allah, the Exalted, said to Yahya concerning these three situations: ﴿And peace be upon him the day he was born, and the day he dies, and the day he is raised alive﴾. [[See vol. 11, p. 88 onward.]] All of this is from the aforementioned History.

It is disputed who was the one sent against them at the second occurrence. It was said: Bukhtnasar. This was stated by al-Qushayri Abu Nasr, who mentioned no one else. Al-Suhayli said: this is not sound, because the killing of Yahya took place after the raising of Jesus, whereas Bukhtnasar was long before Jesus son of Mary (peace be upon them both), and before Alexander. Between Alexander and Jesus there were about three hundred years. Rather, the second occurrence intended is when they killed Sha'ya (Isaiah). At that time Bukhtnasar was alive, and he was the one who killed them, destroyed Bayt al-Maqdis, pursued them to Egypt, and expelled them from it.

Al-Tha'labi said: whoever narrates that Bukhtnasar was the one who attacked the Children of Israel when they killed Yahya ibn Zakariya has erred, according to the scholars of biographies and reports, for they unanimously agree that Bukhtnasar only attacked the Children of Israel when they killed Sha'ya, and in the time of Irmiya (Jeremiah). They said: from the time of Irmiya and the destruction of Bayt al-Maqdis by Bukhtnasar until the birth of Yahya ibn Zakariya (peace be upon them both) was four hundred and sixty-one years. They count from the time of the destruction of Bayt al-Maqdis until its rebuilding in the time of Kusak [[In al-Tabari's History: "Kirsh," and we have not been able to verify the correct form.]] as seventy years; then from its rebuilding until Alexander's conquest of Bayt al-Maqdis as eighty-eight years; then from the kingdom of Alexander until the birth of Yahya as three hundred and sixty-three years. [[In al-Tabari: "three hundred and three years." See p. 718 of the first part.]]

I say: al-Tabari mentioned all of this in the History, may Allah have mercy on him.

Al-Tha'labi said: the correct account in this matter is what Muhammad ibn Ishaq mentioned, who said: when Allah raised Jesus from among them and they killed Yahya (and some people say: when they killed Zakariya), Allah sent against them a king from the kings of Babylon called Khardus [[In manuscript "j": Jirdush. It is perhaps a scribal error.]]. He marched against them with the people of Babylon and prevailed over them in Syria. Then he said to the commander of his armies: "I had sworn by my god that if Allah granted me victory over Bayt al-Maqdis, I would kill them until their blood flowed in the middle of my army." He ordered that they be killed until that was achieved. The commander entered Bayt al-Maqdis and found blood boiling in it. He asked them, and they said: "It is the blood of an offering we offered, and it has not been accepted from us for eighty years." [[In al-Tabari's History, p. 721: "for eight hundred years."]] He said: "You have not told me the truth." So he slaughtered upon that blood seven hundred and seventy men from among their leaders, but it did not subside. Then he brought seven hundred boys from among their youths, and they were slaughtered upon the blood, but it did not subside. [[An addition from al-Tabari's History.]] Then he commanded that seven thousand of their captives and their wives be brought, and he slaughtered them upon the blood, but it did not cool. He said: "O Children of Israel, tell me the truth before I leave none of you, neither male nor female, who blows upon a fire, except that I kill him." When they saw the severity, they said: "This is the blood of a prophet from among us, who used to forbid us from many things that anger Allah, and so we killed him. This is his blood. His name was Yahya ibn Zakariya; he never disobeyed Allah for the blink of an eye, nor did he intend to commit disobedience." He said: "Now you have told me the truth," and he fell down in prostration. Then he said: "For the like of this you shall be avenged upon." He ordered the doors to be closed, and said: "Remove from here whoever is of Khardus's army," and he was alone with the Children of Israel and said: "O prophet of Allah, O Yahya ibn Zakariya, my Lord and your Lord knows what has befallen your people because of you. Be still, by Allah's permission, before I leave none of them alive." So the blood of Yahya ibn Zakariya became still by the permission of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and he lifted the killing from them, and said: "My Lord, I believe in what the Children of Israel believe in, and I confirm it." Then Allah, the Exalted, revealed to one of the chiefs of the prophets: "This commander is a believer and truthful." Then he said: "The enemy of Allah, Khardus, ordered me to kill among you until your blood flows in the middle of his army, and I will not disobey him." So he commanded them, and they dug a trench. He ordered their property of camels, horses, mules, donkeys, cattle and sheep to be brought, and they slaughtered them until the blood flowed to the army. He ordered that the slain who had been killed before that be thrown upon the slaughtered livestock. Then he departed from them toward Babylon, and he had almost annihilated the Children of Israel.

"I said: There has come in this regard a raised (marfu') hadith, lengthy, from the hadith of Hudhayfah, and we have written it in (Kitab al-Tadhkirah) in fragmented chapters in the reports about the Mahdi, from which we mention here what clarifies the meaning of the verse and explains it so that no further explanation is needed with it. Hudhayfah said: I said, O Messenger of Allah, indeed Bayt al-Maqdis was great with Allah, of immense worth and great rank. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'It is one of the most noble houses, which Allah built for Sulayman ibn Dawud, peace be upon them both, of gold, silver, pearls, rubies and emeralds.' That is because when Sulayman ibn Dawud built it, Allah subjected the jinn to him, and they brought him gold and silver from the mines, and they brought him jewels, rubies and emeralds, and Allah the Exalted subjected the jinn to him until they built it from these kinds. Hudhayfah said: I said, O Messenger of Allah, and how were these things taken from Bayt al-Maqdis? The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'When the Children of Israel disobeyed Allah and killed the prophets, Allah empowered over them Bukht Nassar (Nebuchadnezzar), and he was a Magian, and his rule lasted seven hundred years, and this is His saying: "So when the promise of the first of them came, We sent against you servants of Ours of great might, and they ranged through the homes; and it was a promise fulfilled" [17:5]. So they entered Bayt al-Maqdis, killed the men, took the women and children captive, seized the wealth and all that was in Bayt al-Maqdis of these kinds, and they carried it away on seventy thousand and one hundred thousand carts, until they deposited it in the land of Babel. They then kept the Children of Israel in servitude and subjugation, with disgrace, punishment and torment, for one hundred years. Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, had mercy on them and revealed to a king of the kings of Persia that he should march against the Magians in the land of Babel and rescue those of the Children of Israel who were in their hands. That king marched against them until he entered the land of Babel, rescued those of the Children of Israel who remained from the hands of the Magians, and recovered that ornamentation which had been in Bayt al-Maqdis, and Allah returned it to them as it was the first time. He said to them: "O Children of Israel, if you return to sins, We will return against you with captivity and killing." This is His saying: "Perhaps your Lord will have mercy upon you; but if you return, We will return" [17:8]. When the Children of Israel returned to Bayt al-Maqdis, they went back to sins, so Allah empowered over them the king of the Romans, Caesar, and this is His saying: "So when the promise of the Hereafter came, to sadden your faces and to enter the Masjid as they entered it the first time, and to destroy what they had conquered with complete destruction" [17:7]. So he attacked them by land and sea, took them captive, killed them, seized their wealth and women, and took the ornaments of all of Bayt al-Maqdis and carried it on seventy thousand and one hundred thousand carts, until he deposited it in the church of Gold, where it is now, until the Mahdi takes it and returns it to Bayt al-Maqdis, and it is on one thousand and seven hundred ships which will be anchored at Yafa [[As in al-Tabari and al-Durr al-Manthur. In (A, J, W, W, Y): "ya" instead of "yafa". This is a mistake of the copyists.]] until they are transported to Bayt al-Maqdis, and by it Allah will gather the first and the last..." And he mentioned the hadith.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿So when the promise of the Hereafter came﴾ meaning of the two times. The response of "idha" is omitted, its estimate being "We sent them," indicated by the first "We sent."

(to sadden your faces) meaning by captivity and killing, so the effect of grief appears on your faces. So "li-yasu'u" is connected to an omitted element, meaning: We sent servants to do to you what saddens your faces. It was said: the meaning of "faces" is the nobles, meaning to humiliate them. Al-Kisa'i read "linasu'a" with a nun and an opened hamza, a verb of a speaker referring to himself in the plural of majesty, in consideration of His saying: "and We decreed, and We sent, and We returned." This is similarly reported from Ali. Confirming it is Ubayy's reading "linasu'anna" with the nun and the emphatic particle. Abu Bakr, al-A'mash, Ibn Thabbab, Hamzah and Ibn 'Amir read "liyasu'a" with the ya' in the singular and an opened hamza, and it has two possibilities: first, "liyasu'a Allahu wujuhakum" (that Allah may sadden your faces); second, "liyasu'a al-wa'du wujuhakum" (that the promise may sadden your faces). The rest read "liyasu'u" with the ya' and a damma on the hamza in the plural, meaning: that the servants who possess great might may sadden your faces.

(and to enter the Masjid as they entered it the first time, and to destroy) meaning to annihilate and ruin. Qutrub said: to demolish. The poet said:
"Surely the people are only two doers: a doer who destroys what he builds, and another who raises."
(what they had conquered) meaning what they overcame of your lands (with complete destruction).

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿It may be that your Lord will have mercy upon you﴾. This is among the things they were informed of in their scripture. "Perhaps" (ʿasā) from Allah is a promise that He will remove the punishment from them, and "perhaps" from Allah is binding.

(That He will have mercy upon you) after His retribution against you. And so it was: their number increased and He made kings from among them.

(And if you return, We will return) Qatadah said: They returned, so Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ) against them, and they give the jizyah in humiliation. This was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. This contradicts what preceded in the hadith and elsewhere. Al-Qushayri said: The punishment befell the Children of Israel twice at the hands of disbelievers and once at the hands of Muslims. This was when they returned, and Allah returned (the punishment) against them. On this basis, Qatadah's statement is valid.

(And We have made Hell a ḥaṣīr for the disbelievers) That is, a place of confinement and a prison, from al-ḥaṣr, which means confinement. Al-Jawhari said: One says ḥaṣarahu yaḥṣuruhu ḥaṣran, meaning he constricted him and surrounded him. Al-ḥaṣīr means one who is narrow and stingy. Al-ḥaṣīr also means a woven mat. Al-ḥaṣīr also means the side (of the body). Al-Asmaʿi said: It is what lies between the vein that appears in the side of a camel or horse, running crosswise, and what is above it, up to the end of the side. Al-ḥaṣīr also means kingship, because it is veiled. Labid said:

*And a band of people with unbending necks, as if they were jinn standing at the door of the ḥaṣīr*

It is also narrated (with a variant in the margin of manuscript J: the author, Shaykh, said: it is narrated as "wa-ʿiṣābah," "and a band"):

*And a gathering with unbending necks...*

Here "unbending" (ghulb) is in apposition to "gathering," as if he said: "and many a people with unbending necks." It is narrated from Abu ʿUbayda:

*At the edge of the ḥaṣīr they stand*

That is, near the edge of the carpet of al-Nuʿman ibn al-Mundhir. Al-ḥaṣīr also means a place of confinement. Allah the Exalted said: "And We have made Hell a ḥaṣīr for the disbelievers." Al-Qushayri said: It is also said of one who spreads a ḥaṣīr (mat), because its parts are confined to one another by weaving. Al-Hasan said: That is, a bed and a cushion, going to the meaning of the mat that is spread, because the Arabs call a small carpet a ḥaṣīr. Al-Thaʿlabi said: This is a good interpretation.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 9–10:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾. When He mentioned the Mi'raj (the Night Journey and Ascension), He mentioned what He decreed to the Children of Israel, and that was a proof of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). Then He explained that the Book which Allah revealed to him is a means of guidance. The meaning of (lillati hiya aqwam) is: the path that is most straight, most just, and most correct. So "allati" is an adjective of an omitted noun, i.e., the path to a more upright matter. Al-Zajjaj said: "to the state that is the most upright of states, and it is the Oneness of Allah and belief in His messengers." Al-Kalbi and al-Farra' also said this.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And gives good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds﴾. This has already been mentioned [[See vol. 1, p. 338.]].

(Anna lahum) i.e., that for them.

(ajran kabiran) i.e., Paradise.

(Wa anna alladhina la yu'minuna bil-akhirah) i.e., and He gives them good tidings that for their enemies there is punishment. The Qur'an is mostly promise and warning. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "wa yubashshiru" with light pronunciation, with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the shin, and this has been mentioned [[See vol. 4, p. 75.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 11:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And man prays for evil as he prays for good﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas and others said: it is a man's supplication against himself and his child in a moment of impatience, with something he would not like to be granted to him, saying: "O Allah, destroy him," and the like.

(His praying for good) meaning, like his prayer to his Lord that He grant him well-being. Had Allah answered his supplication against himself for evil, he would have perished; but by His grace He does not answer him in that. Its parallel is: ﴿And if Allah were to hasten for the people the evil as they seek to hasten the good﴾, which has already been discussed [see vol. 8, p. 314]. It was also said: it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who used to pray and say: "O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment" [see vol. 7, p. 398 and vol. 8, p. 315]. It was also said: it is that a person prays for what is forbidden just as he prays for what is permitted. The poet, who was Ibn Jami', said:

I circle the House among those who circle it,
and I lift up my trailing lower garment,
and I prostrate myself through the night until morning,
and I recite from the Clear, Revealed Book.
Perhaps the reliever of worry concerning Yusuf
will make the mount of the rider subservient to me.

Al-Jawhari said: it is said, "There is no mahmal (support, reliance) for so-and-so," in the pattern of majlis, meaning he has no one to rely on. Al-Mahmal also means one of the litters of the pilgrims. Al-Mihmal, in the pattern of al-Mirjal, is the strap of a sword.

The waw was deleted from ﴿wayad'u al-insanu﴾ in pronunciation and in writing, but not in meaning, because its position is nominative; it was deleted because it came before the unvoweled lam, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Sanad'u al-zabaniyah﴾ [see vol. 20, p. 126], ﴿wayamhu Allahu al-batil﴾ [see vol. 16, p. 24], ﴿sawfa yu'ti Allahu al-mu'minin﴾ [see vol. 5, p. 425], ﴿yunad al-munad﴾ [see vol. 17, p. 27 and p. 128], and ﴿fa-ma tughni al-nudhur﴾ [see vol. 11, p. 288].

(And man has always been hasty) "meaning, his nature is haste, so he hastens to ask for evil just as he hastens to ask for good. It was also said: it refers to Adam, peace be upon him, when he rose up before the spirit had been fully breathed into him completely. Salman said: the first thing Allah the Exalted created of Adam was his head, and he began to look while his body was being created. When it reached the time of ʿAsr, his two legs remained without the spirit being breathed into them, so he said: "My Lord, hasten it before night." That is His saying: ﴿And man has always been hasty﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: when the breath reached his navel, he looked at his body and tried to stand up but could not, and that is His saying: ﴿And man has always been hasty﴾. Ibn Masʿud said: when the spirit entered his eyes, he looked at the fruits of Paradise, and that is when He says: ﴿Man was created of haste﴾ [see vol. 11, p. 288]. Al-Bayhaqi mentioned it. In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Anas ibn Malik, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah the Exalted fashioned Adam in Paradise, He left him for as long as Allah willed to leave him, and Iblis began to circle around him, looking at what he was. When he saw him hollow, he knew that he had been created a creature who cannot control himself" [which has already been discussed; see vol. 1, p. 281]. It was also said: Adam, peace be upon him, was given a captive woman, Sawda, and he spent the night moaning. She asked him, and he said: "My moaning is from the severity of the leather bindings and the captivity." So she loosened his bonds, and when she fell asleep he fled. She informed the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: "May Allah cut off your hands." When she woke in the morning she was expecting a calamity, and he, peace be upon him, said: "I asked Allah the Exalted to make my supplication fall upon those among my family who do not deserve it, because I am a human who becomes angry as humans become angry," and the verse was revealed. Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr mentioned it, may Allah have mercy on him. In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "O Allah, Muhammad is only a human who becomes angry as humans become angry, and I have taken a covenant with You which You will not break: whichever believer I have harmed, cursed, or flogged, make it for him an expiation and a means of drawing near to You on the Day of Resurrection." There are also reports on this topic from ʿAisha and Jabir. It was also said: the meaning of ﴿And man has always been hasty﴾ is that he prefers what is immediate, even if it is small, over what is deferred, even if it is great.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on surah 17, verse 12:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs﴾, meaning two indications of Our oneness, Our existence, and the perfection of Our knowledge and power. The sign in them is that each of them comes forward from a place one does not know, and withdraws to a place one does not know. The decrease of one of them through the increase of the other, and the reverse, is also a sign. Likewise the light of the day and the darkness of the night. This has already been discussed [see vol. 2, p. 192].

(*Then We erased the sign of the night*): He did not say "Then We erased the night." When He attributed the sign to the night and the day, this shows that the two signs mentioned belong to them and are not themselves the two. "Famahawna" means "We obliterated" (*tamasna*). It is reported that Allah, exalted is He, commanded Jibril, peace be upon him, so he passed his wing over the face of the moon, and it obliterated its light, and it was like the sun in brightness. The blackness seen in the moon is the trace of that erasure. Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah made the sun seventy parts and the moon seventy parts, then He erased from the light of the moon sixty-nine parts and added them to the light of the sun. So the sun has one hundred and thirty-nine parts, and the moon has one part.

It is also reported from him: Allah created two suns from the light of His Throne. He made what He knew would be a sun like the world in size, the distance between its risings and its settings, and He made the moon lesser than the sun. Then He sent Jibril, peace be upon him, who passed his wing over its face three times, while it was then a sun, and it obliterated its light and its radiance remained. So the blackness you see in the moon is the trace of the erasure. Had He left it as a sun, the night would not have been distinguished from the day. Al-Tha'labi transmitted the first report from him, and al-Mahdawi the second, and it will come later as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report.

'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) and Qatadah said: By the erasure He means the black smudge that is in the moon, so that the light of the moon is less than the light of the sun, and thereby the night is distinguished from the day.

(*And We made the sign of the day visible*): that is, We made its sun radiant to the eyes. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: that is, one sees by it. Al-Kisa'i said: This is from the saying of the Arabs, "absara al-nahar" when the day became bright and reached a state in which one can see by it. It was also said: it is like their saying "khabith, mukhbith," when its companions are wicked, and "rajul mud'if" when his riding animals are weak. Likewise the day is "mubsiran" when its people are seeing.

(*That you may seek bounty from your Lord*): meaning, to engage in earning a livelihood. He did not mention rest in the night, being content with what was mentioned about the day. He said in another place: ﴿He it is who made the night for you that you may rest therein, and the day giving sight﴾ [see vol. 8, p. 360]. (*And that you may know the number of years and the reckoning*): that is, if He had not done that, the night would not be distinguished from the day, and neither reckoning nor counting would be known.

(*And every thing We have explained in detail*): that is, of the rulings of obligation. It is like His saying: ﴿an explanation of everything﴾ [Q 16:89; see p. 164 of this part], and ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾ [Q 6:38; see vol. 6, p. 420].

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When Allah had completed His creation, and there remained of His creation nothing but Adam, He created a sun from the light of His Throne and a moon, and they were both two suns. As for what was in Allah's prior knowledge that He would leave as a sun, He created it like the world, the distance between its risings and its settings. As for what was in Allah's knowledge that He would create as a moon, He created it lesser than the sun in size. But their smallness is seen only because of the great height of the sky and its distance from the earth. Had Allah left the sun and the moon as He created them, the night would not be distinguished from the day, nor would the hired worker know until when he should work, nor the fasting person until when he should fast, nor the woman how she should observe her waiting period, nor would the times of the prayers and the pilgrimage be known, nor would debts be due, nor would they know when to sow and to plant, nor when they should rest their bodies. Allah looked upon His servants, and He is more merciful to them than they are to themselves, so He sent Jibril, who passed his wing over the face of the moon three times, while it was then a sun. It obliterated its light and its radiance remained in it. That is His saying: ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs﴾, the verse."

**The Qurtubi commentary on Surah 17, verses 13–14**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And every person We have fastened his bird (ṭā'ir) to his neck﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: Mentioning the neck is an expression for constant attachment, like a necklace that clings to the neck. Ibn 'Abbas said: "ṭā'ir" means his deeds and what he is capable of, good and evil, and it is bound to him wherever he is. Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: His good and evil are with him; they do not leave him until he is called to account for them. Mujahid said: It means his deeds and his provision. He also reported: No child is born except that on his neck is a scroll on which is written "wretched" or "fortunate." Al-Hasan said: "We have fastened his bird to him" means his wretchedness and his happiness, what has been written for him of good and evil, and what has flown to him of the decree, that is, what came to him at the division in pre-eternity. It was also said: He meant by it the obligation, that is, We have made him bound by the obligation of the Law (sharʿ), and he is in such a state that if he wished to do what he was commanded and to refrain from what he was forbidden, he would be able to do so.

﴿And We will bring forth for him on the Day of Resurrection a record that he will find spread open﴾. He means the record of his ṭā'ir, which is around his neck. Al-Hasan, Abu Raja' and Mujahid read "ṭayrahu" without an alif. From this is what is reported in a hadith: "O Allah, there is no good except Your good, and no ṭayr (omen) except Your ṭayr, and no lord besides You." Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read "wa-yakhruju" with a fatha on the yā' and a ḍamma on the rā', meaning: and the ṭā'ir will bring forth for him a record. Here "kitāban" is in the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative). It is also possible that the meaning is: the ṭā'ir will come forth and become a record. Yahya ibn Wathhab read "wa-yukhriju" with a ḍamma on the yā' and a kasra on the rā', and it is reported from Mujahid, meaning: Allah brings forth. Shayba and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqa', and it is also reported from Abu Ja'far, read "wa-yukhraju" with a ḍamma on the yā' and a fatha on the rā', as a passive verb, meaning: a ṭā'ir will be brought forth for him as a record. The rest read "wa-nukhriju" with a ḍamma on the nūn and a kasra on the rā', meaning: and We bring forth. Abu 'Amr supported this reading by the words "alzamnāhu" (We have fastened it).

Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan and Ibn 'Amir read "yalqāhu" with a ḍamma on the yā', a fatha on the lām and a shadda on the qāf, meaning: it is given to him (yu'tāhu). The rest read it with a fatha on the yā' and without shadda, meaning: he sees it spread open. He said "manshūran" (spread open) to hasten the good news for the one with good deeds and the reproach for the one with bad deeds. Abu al-Sawwar al-'Adawi recited this verse: "And every person We have fastened his bird to his neck," and said: These are two spreadings. As for what you are alive, O son of Adam, your page is the open one, so contemplate in it what you wish. When you die it is folded, and when you are raised it is spread out again.

﴿Read your record; sufficient is yourself against you this Day as a reckoner﴾. Al-Hasan said: A person reads his record, whether he is unlettered or not. ﴿Sufficient is yourself against you this Day as a reckoner﴾, that is, as one who takes account. Some of the righteous said: This is a book whose tongue is its pen, whose saliva is its ink, and whose limbs are its paper. You were the one who dictated to your guardians; nothing was added to it or removed from it. And whenever you deny anything in it, the witness against you will be from yourself.
