The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 15:

Allah's words: ﴿Whoever is guided is only guided for his own self, and whoever goes astray only goes astray to its detriment﴾. That is, every person is called to account only for himself, not for another. Whoever is guided, the reward of his guidance is his own, and whoever goes astray, the punishment for his disbelief falls upon him.

﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ has preceded in al-An'am [See vol. 7, p. 155]. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, who said to the people of Makkah: "Follow me, and disbelieve in Muhammad, and I will bear your sins." So this verse was revealed, meaning that al-Walid does not bear your sins, and the sin of each one falls only upon himself. It is said: wazara yaziru wizran and wizratan, meaning he sinned. Al-wizr (burden) is a heavy load, and its plural is awzar. From it comes ﴿they shall bear their burdens upon their backs﴾ [See vol. 6, p. 413], meaning the weights of their sins. Wazara means he carried, so the one who carries is wazir, and from it comes wazir of the ruler, the one who bears the weight of his government. The pronoun in His words [the editor notes that the word "wazirah" appears to have dropped out here, as shown by what follows] refers to the self, meaning that no sinful self is seized for the sin of another. Even a mother will meet her child on the Day of Resurrection and say: "O my son, was not my lap a bed for you? Was not my breast a water-skin for you? Was not my belly a vessel for you?" He will say: "Yes, O mother." She will say: "O my son, my sins have weighed me down, so bear for me one sin of mine!" He will say: "Away from me, O mother! For I am, today, preoccupied with my own sin."

Issue: 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, cited this verse in refuting Ibn 'Umar when he said: "The dead person is punished by the weeping of his family." Our scholars said: she was led to this because she had not heard it, and because it appeared to contradict the verse. There is no basis for rejecting it, since the narrators of this meaning are many, such as 'Umar, his son, al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah, and Qaylah bint Makhramah, and they were certain in their narration, so there is no basis for declaring them mistaken. There is also no contradiction between the verse and the hadith, for the hadith is to be understood as referring to the case where the wailing was part of the deceased's own instruction and practice, as the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic era) used to do, to the point that Tarafah said:

"When I die, then mourn me with what I am worthy of, and tear the collar for me, O daughter of Ma'bad."

And he said:

"Until the year is complete, then peace be upon you both; and whoever weeps for a full year has made his excuse."

To this view al-Bukhari inclined. A group of scholars, including Dawud, held to the apparent meaning of the hadith, that he is punished only by their wailing, because he neglected to forbid them from it before his death and to discipline them in that matter, so he is punished for his negligence in this and for abandoning what Allah commanded him, through His words: ﴿Protect yourselves and your families from a fire﴾ [See vol. 18, pp. 194 and 212], not for the sin of another. And Allah knows best.

Allah's words: ﴿And We would never punish until We have sent a messenger﴾. That is, We did not leave creation neglected, but We sent the messengers. In this is evidence that the rulings are not established except by the Shari'ah, contrary to the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school), who hold that reason determines what is good and bad, permitted and forbidden. The discussion of this was preceded in al-Baqarah [See vol. 1, p. 251]. The majority hold that this applies to the ruling of this world: that Allah does not destroy a nation with punishment except after sending a messenger to them and warning them. But one group said: this is general, applying to this world and the Hereafter, based on His words: ﴿Whenever a company is cast into it, its keepers will ask them: "Did no warner come to you?" They will say: "Yes, indeed, a warner came to us"﴾ [See vol. 18, pp. 194 and 212].

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: What the reasoning indicates is that when Adam, peace be upon him, was sent with monotheism, and the beliefs were spread among his offspring along with the establishment of proofs pointing to the Creator, and with the soundness of natural disposition (fitrah), this made it obligatory for every person in the world to believe and to follow the Shari'ah of Allah. Then this was renewed in the time of Noah, peace be upon him, after the disbelievers drowned. This verse, too, by the possibilities of its wording, may be understood in this sense regarding those who did not receive a message, namely the people of the intervals between messengers (fatrat), whose existence some scholars have estimated. As for what is reported, that Allah will send to them on the Day of Resurrection, and to the insane and the children, it is a hadith that is not authentic, and it does not conform to what the Shari'ah indicates, that the Hereafter is not an abode of obligation.

Al-Mahdawi said: It is reported from Abu Hurayrah that Allah, mighty and majestic, will send a messenger on the Day of Resurrection to the people of natural disposition, the mute, the deaf-mute, and the deaf, and whoever wished to obey him in this world will obey him, and he recited the verse. Ma'mar narrated it from Ibn Tawus, from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, and al-Nahhas mentioned it. I say: this is a mawquf (a report ending with a Companion), and it will come as marfu' (traced to the Prophet) at the end of surah Ta-Ha, if Allah wills, but it is not authentic.

Some people have used this to argue that the people of remote lands, if they heard of Islam and believed, have no obligation for what passed before, and this is correct. Whoever has not been reached by the call is not deserving of punishment by reason. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 16:

There are three issues in this.

The first: God, exalted is He, informed in the preceding verse that He does not destroy the towns before sending messengers. This is not because it would be ugly of Him to do so if He did, but it is a promise from Him, and He does not break His promise. So when He wills to destroy a town, while fulfilling His promise, as He has said, He commands its affluent people (mutrafiha) to disobedience (al-fisq) and wrongdoing (al-zulm) within it, and then the word becomes due against it for destruction. This teaches you that whoever is destroyed is destroyed by His will. He is the One who causes the causes (yusabbibu al-asbab) and drives them to their ends, so that the prior word from God may be fulfilled.[[The verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun), following what Ibn 'Abbas said as in al-Bahr: "We commanded them, so they disobeyed and transgressed," and it will come. This is the one that corresponds, like His words: "Indeed, Allah does not command immorality." As for what al-Qurtubi mentioned, like al-Zamakhshari, it requires interpretation. Verified.]]

The second: His saying, ﴿amarna﴾ (We commanded).

Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi, Abu Raja', Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Rabi', Mujahid and al-Hasan read "ammarna" with a shadda (emphatic doubling), and this is the reading of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, meaning: We empowered its wicked ones, so they disobeyed in it, and when they did that, We destroyed them. Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi said: "ammarna," with the mim doubled, means: We made them commanders (umara') who dominate, and Ibn 'Uzayz said the same. And "ta'ammara 'alayhim" means he dominated over them.

Al-Hasan also, along with Qatadah, Abu Haywah al-Shami, Ya'qub, Kharijah from Nafi', Hammad ibn Salamah from Ibn Kathir, and 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas, with variation between them, read "amarna" with a long vowel and light doubling-free form, meaning: We made its tyrants and its rulers numerous; this was said by al-Kisa'i. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "amartuhu" with the long vowel and "amartuhu" are two dialectal forms with the same meaning, "kaththartuhu" (I made him numerous), and from this is the hadith: "The best of wealth is a mare that is multiplied (mahrah ma'murah) or a row of palms that is pollinated (sikkah ma'burah).[[Al-sikkah: a row of palms set in line. Al-ma'burah: pollinated; it is said: abarat al-nakhlah and abartuha, so it is ma'burah and mu'abbarah. Sikkah is a row for tillage, and al-ma'burah is that which is improved for it. The meaning: the best wealth is offspring and crops. (Ibn al-Athir).]]" meaning abundant in offspring and progeny. Likewise Ibn 'Uzayz said: "amarna" and "ammarna" have one meaning, that is, We made them numerous. And from al-Hasan also, and Yahya ibn Ya'mar, "amirna" with a short vowel and a kasra on the mim, following the pattern "fa'iltu," and it was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. Qatadah and al-Hasan said: the meaning is "We made them numerous." Abu Zayd and Abu 'Ubayd related something similar, and al-Kisa'i denied it and said: From kathrah (abundance) one says only "amarna" with a long vowel. He said its origin is "a'amarna," which was lightened; al-Mahdawi related this.

In al-Sihah: Abu al-Hasan said: "amira malahu" (bi-l-kasr), meaning he had abundance of it, and "amira al-qawm," meaning they became numerous. The poet said:

*Amirun la yarithuna sahma al-qu'dud*
(They are numerous, not inheriting the share of the few)[[This is the second half of a verse by al-A'sha, whose first half is: "Tarafun wa-ladun kulla mubarak." Al-zarf and al-zarif: one who has many ancestors back to the great-grandfather. Al-qa'dad: one with few ancestors back to the great-grandfather.]]

And "amara Allahu malahu" (with long vowel): al-Tha'labi said: a large thing is called amir, and its verb is "amira al-qawm, ya'maruna, amran" when they became numerous. Ibn Mas'ud said: "In the Jahiliyyah we used to say of a clan when they became numerous: 'The affair of the Banu so-and-so has become numerous (amira amr)." Labid said:

*Kullu banī ḥurratin maṣīruhum... qalla wa-in akthart min al-'adad*
Every clan of free men, their end is paucity, even if you multiply them in number.

*In yughbatu yahbitu wa-in amiru... yawman yasiru lil-halki wal-nakad*
If they are envied they will perish, and if they become numerous, one day they will go to destruction and misfortune.[[He says: if they are envied for a day, they die. "Yahbizu" here means "yamutu" (die). In another version: "in ghubitu ya'batu," they die a death of "'abtah" (sudden death), as if they die without illness. (See the Diwan.) In Jim and Wa: "al-fand."]]

I say: In the authentic hadith of Heraclius: "Indeed the affair of Ibn Abi Kabshah has become great (la-qad amira amr Ibn Abi Kabshah), so that the king of the Banu al-Asfar fears him."[[He means the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The polytheists used to call the Prophet ﷺ "Ibn Abi Kabshah," likening him to Abu Kabshah, a man of Khuza'ah who opposed Quraysh in idol worship. Or it is the kunyah of Wahb ibn 'Abd Manaf, his grandfather ﷺ on his mother's side, because he was known for resembling him. Or it is the kunyah of the husband of Halimah al-Sa'diyyah.]] "That is, it became abundant." All of this is intransitive, and for this reason al-Kisa'i denied it, and Allah knows best.

Al-Mahdawi said: Whoever reads "amira" (with kasra), it is a dialect form, and the way "amira" is made transitive is that it was likened to "'amara" (to populate), since abundance is the closest thing to population, so it was made transitive as "'amara" is. The rest read "amarna" from the command (al-amr), meaning: We commanded them to obedience as a warning, admonition, intimidation and threat. So they transgressed (fasaqu), meaning they went out of obedience, disobeying Us. So the word became due against it (fa-haqqa 'alayha al-qawl), meaning the threat was incumbent upon it, according to Ibn 'Abbas. It was also said: "amarna" means We made them commanders (umara'), because the Arabs say: "amir ghayr ma'mur" (a commander who is not commanded). It was also said: its meaning is "We sent its greatest criminals." Harun said: It is the reading of Ubayy: "ba'athna akabira mujrimiha" (We sent its eminent criminals). This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. Al-Nahhas related: Harun said in the reading of Ubayy: "Wa-idha aradna an nuhlika qaryatan ba'athna fiha akabira mujrimiha fa-makaru fiha fa-haqqa 'alayha al-qawl" (When We wish to destroy a town, We send into it its greatest criminals, and they plot within it, so the word becomes due against it).

It is possible that "amarna" means "akthharna" (We made numerous), and from this is "The best of wealth is a mare that is multiplied," as previously mentioned. Some people said: "ma'murah" is a follow-up to "ma'burah," like "al-ghadaya wal-'ashaya" (the mornings and evenings), and like His saying: "Return, being burdened with sin, not rewarded." On this basis, one does not say "amarahum Allah" in the sense of "kathkarahum," but rather "amarahu" and "amarahu." Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose the reading of the majority. Abu 'Ubayd said: We chose "amarna" only because the three meanings gather in it: from command (al-amr), from leadership (al-imarah), and from abundance (al-kathrah).

Al-mutraf: the one given luxury (al-mun'am). They were singled out for the command because others follow them.

The third: His saying, ﴿fa-dammarnaha﴾ (then We destroyed it).

That is, We uprooted it by destruction.

(tadmiran)

He mentioned the verbal noun for emphasis regarding the punishment that befell them. In the Sahih, from the hadith of Zaynab bint Jahsh, wife of the Prophet ﷺ, she said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out one day, frightened, his face reddened, saying: "La ilaha illa Allah, woe to the Arabs from an evil that has drawn near. Today an opening has been made in the barrier of Ya'juj and Ma'juj like this," and he made a circle with his thumb and the finger next to it. She said: I said: "O Messenger of Allah, will we be destroyed while the righteous are among us?" He said: "Yes, when wickedness becomes abundant." The discussion of this topic has already preceded, and that when sins appear and are not changed, they become a cause of destruction for all, and Allah knows best.

How many generations have We destroyed after Noah! And your Lord is sufficient as one who is Aware and Seeing of the sins of His servants. (Qur'an 17:17)

That is, how many peoples disbelieved, and destruction (al-bawar) came upon them. It is a warning to the disbelievers of Makkah. The discussion of the word "qarn" (generation) has already been given at the beginning of Surah al-An'am [see vol. 6, p. 391], and praise be to God.

(And your Lord is sufficient as one who is Aware and Seeing of the sins of His servants.) "Khabiran": knowing of them. "Basiran": seeing their deeds. This has already been discussed [see vol. 2, p. 35].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever desires the hastened [life]﴾ means the worldly life. The intended meaning is "the hastened abode," but he used the adjective in place of the noun it describes [[In H, J, Kh: "the described noun by its adjective."]].

﴿We hasten for him therein what We will, for whomever We wish﴾, meaning We give him from it only what We will, and then We call him to account for his deeds, and his end is entry into the Fire.

﴿Blameworthy and rejected﴾, meaning expelled and distanced from the mercy of Allah. This is the description of the hypocrites, the corrupt, and the show-offers who conceal their intentions. They wear the garb of Islam and obedience in order to obtain the hastened goods of this world, such as spoils and other things. Their deeds will not be accepted in the Hereafter, and in this world they will receive only what has been apportioned for them. This was already discussed in [the commentary on] Hud [[See vol. 9, p. 13.]] that this verse restricts the unrestricted verses, so reflect on it.

﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter﴾, meaning the Hereafter abode.

﴿And strives for it with its striving﴾, meaning he performs its deeds, the acts of obedience.

﴿While he is a believer﴾, because acts of obedience are not accepted except from a believer.

﴿Those, their striving is ever appreciated﴾, meaning accepted and not rejected. It has also been said: "multiplied," meaning their good deeds are multiplied to ten, to seventy, to seven hundred fold, and to many more multiples, as was related from Abu Hurayrah when he was asked: "Did you hear the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Indeed Allah rewards one good deed with a thousand thousand good deeds'?" He said: "I heard him say: 'Indeed Allah rewards one good deed with two thousand thousand good deeds.'"

Al-Qurtubi, commentary on Surah 17, verses 20–22:

Allah's words: ﴿To each We extend, to these and to those, from the bounty of your Lord﴾. He informs that He provides for both the believers and the disbelievers.

(﴿And the bounty of your Lord has never been restricted﴾), i.e., confined and prevented, from *ḥaẓara* (حَظَرَ), *yaḥẓuru* (يَحْظُرُ), *ḥaẓran* (حَظْرًا) and *ḥiẓāran* (حِظَارًا). Then He said, Most High: See how We have made some of them exceed others in provision and in deeds, so there are those who are *muqill* (مُقِلٌّ, the one with little) and those who are *mukthir* (مُكْثِرٌ, the one with much).

(﴿And the Hereafter is greater in ranks and greater in preference﴾), i.e., for the believers. Even if the disbeliever is granted abundance in this world once, and the believer is restricted once, the Hereafter is distributed only once, according to their deeds, so whoever misses any portion of it cannot make it up there.

As for His words (﴿Do not set up with Allah another god, lest you sit down reproached and forsaken﴾), the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the intended meaning is his community. It has also been said that the address is to the human being.

(*Fa-taqʿuda* (فَتَقْعُدَ)), i.e., remain.

(*Madhmūman makhdhūlan* (مَذْمُومًا مَخْذُولًا)): you will have no helper and no protector.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verses 23–24 (part 1 of 3)**

There are sixteen issues in this passage.

**First:** *Qada'* (decreed) means He commanded, obligated, and made obligatory. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and Qatadah said: This is not a *qada'* of judgment but a *qada'* of command. In the *mushaf* (the codex) of Ibn Mas'ud the reading is *wa-wassa* ("and enjoined"). This is the reading of his companions, and also the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ali, and others. It is likewise in the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Ibn 'Abbas said: The original is *wa-wassa rabbuka* ("your Lord enjoined"), and one of the two waws was joined to the next letter, so it was read *wa-qada rabbuka* ("your Lord decreed"). For if it were a decree that could not be disobeyed, no one would have disobeyed Allah. Al-Dahhak said: For some people it was mistaken as *wassa bi-qada*, when the waw was confused with the sad at the time the *mushaf* was written. Abu Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas something like the statement of al-Dahhak. He also reported from Maymun ibn Mihran that he said: "Indeed, upon the saying of Ibn 'Abbas there is light." Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He has prescribed for you of religion what He enjoined upon Noah and what We have revealed to you﴾ [See vol. 16, p. 9]. Then Abu Hatim refused to accept that Ibn 'Abbas said this. He said: If we said this, the heretics (*zanadiqah*) would criticize our *mushaf*.

Then our scholars of theology and others said: *qada'* is used in the language in several senses. *Qada'* in the sense of command, as in His saying: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾, meaning *amara* (commanded). *Qada'* in the sense of creation, as in His saying: ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens in two days﴾ [See vol. 15, p. 342], meaning He created them. *Qada'* in the sense of judgment, as in His saying: ﴿So decide what you will decide﴾ [See vol. 11, p. 225], meaning judge what you judge. *Qada'* in the sense of completion, as in His saying: ﴿The matter about which you inquire has been concluded﴾ [See vol. 9, p. 193], meaning it has been finished. From this is His saying: ﴿And when you have completed your rites﴾ [See vol. 2, p. 431], and His saying: ﴿And when the prayer has been concluded﴾ [See vol. 18, p. 108]. *Qada'* in the sense of will, as in His saying: ﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [See vol. 4, p. 92]. *Qada'* in the sense of covenant, as in His saying: ﴿And you were not on the western side when We conveyed to Moses the command﴾ [See vol. 13, p. 291].

Since *qada'* bears these meanings, it is not permissible to say without qualification that acts of disobedience are by the decree of Allah. If by it is meant command, there is no disagreement that this is impermissible, because Allah the Exalted did not command them, for He does not command indecency.

Zakariyya ibn Sallam said: A man came to al-Hasan and said: "He divorced his wife three times." He said: "You have disobeyed your Lord, and she has become irrevocably separated from you." The man said: "Allah decreed that upon me!" Al-Hasan, who was eloquent, said: "Allah did not decree that"; that is, Allah did not command it. And he recited this verse: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾.

**Second:** Allah the Exalted commanded His worship and His oneness, and He linked kindness to parents with that, just as He linked their thanks with His thanks. He said: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and to parents, good treatment﴾. And He said: ﴿Give thanks to Me and to your parents; to Me is the destination﴾ [See vol. 14, p. 65].

In the *Sahih* of al-Bukhari, from 'Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud), who said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ): "Which deed is most beloved to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic?" He said: "Prayer at its proper time." I said: "Then which?" He said: "Then kindness to parents." I said: "Then which?" He said: "Jihad in the way of Allah." So he (ﷺ) informed that kindness to parents is the best of deeds after prayer, which is the greatest pillar of Islam. He arranged this with *thumma* ("then"), which indicates sequence and a time interval.

**Third:** Among kindness and goodness toward them is that one does not expose oneself to insulting them and does not disobey them (*'uquq*). This is a major sin (*kaba'ir*) without disagreement, and the established Sunnah has come with this. In the *Sahih* of Muslim, from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Among the major sins is a man cursing his parents." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, does a man curse his parents?" He said: "Yes. A man curses another man's father, so he curses his father, and curses his mother, so he curses his mother."

**Fourth:** Disobedience (*'uquq*) to parents is opposing them in their permissible aims, just as their kindness is agreeing with them in their aims. Accordingly, if they or one of them command their child with a command, obedience to them in it becomes obligatory, provided that command is not sinful, even if the thing commanded is originally permissible (*mubah*), and likewise if it is recommended (*mandub*). Some people have held that their commanding something permissible makes it recommended for the child, and their commanding something recommended increases its recommendation.

**Fifth:** Al-Tirmidhi reported from 'Umar, who said: "I had a wife whom I loved, and my father disliked her, so he commanded me to divorce her, but I refused. I mentioned that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'O 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, divorce your wife.'" He said: This is a hadith that is *hasan sahih* (good and sound).

**Sixth:** The Sahih reported from Abu Hurayrah, who said: A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Who is most deserving of good companionship from me?" He said: "Your mother." He said: "Then who?" He said: "Your mother." He said: "Then who?" He said: "Your mother." He said: "Then who?" He said: "Then your father." This hadith indicates that love for the mother and compassion toward her should be three times the love for the father, since the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned the mother three times and mentioned the father only in the fourth place. When this meaning is established, observation bears witness to it, because the difficulty of pregnancy, the difficulty of childbirth, and the difficulty of nursing and rearing belong to the mother alone and not the father. These are three stations from which the father is free.

It is reported from Malik that a man said to him: "My father is in the land of the Sudan, and he has written to me to come to him, but my mother prevents me from that." He said: "Obey your father, and do not disobey your mother." This statement of Malik indicates that kindness to them is equal in his view. Al-Layth was asked about this issue, and he ordered obedience to the mother, claiming that she has two-thirds of the kindness. The hadith of Abu Hurayrah indicates that she has three-quarters of the kindness, and it is the proof against those who differ. Al-Muhasibi claimed in his book *al-Ri'ayah* that there is no disagreement among the scholars that the mother has three-quarters of the kindness and the father one-quarter, according to the import of the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him. And Allah knows best.

**Seventh:** Kindness to parents is not restricted to their being Muslims. Even if they are disbelievers, one treats them well and is kind to them when they have a covenant. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion and do not expel you from your homes—from being righteous toward them﴾ [See vol. 18, p. 58 and vol. 14, p. 63].

In the *Sahih* of al-Bukhari, from Asma' (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: My mother came to me while she was a polytheist, during the time of the covenant of Quraysh and their truce, when they had made a covenant with the Prophet (ﷺ) along with her father. So I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for a ruling and said: "My mother has come, and she is *raghibah*" [Note: meaning either desiring my kindness and maintenance, or averse to Islam and hating it]. "Shall I maintain ties with her?" He said: "Yes, maintain ties with your mother."

It is also reported from Asma', who said: My mother came to me desiring (something) during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), so I asked the Prophet (ﷺ): "Shall I maintain ties with her?" He said: "Yes." Ibn 'Uyaynah said: Then Allah the Mighty and Majestic revealed concerning her: ﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion﴾. The first report is *mu'allaq* (with its chain omitted) and the second is *musnad* (with a complete chain).

**Eighth:** Among kindness to them and righteousness toward them, when jihad is not specifically obligated, is that one should not wage jihad except with their permission. The Sahih reported from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, who said: A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) asking his permission for jihad, and he said: "Are your parents alive?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then strive (jahid) for their sake." This is the wording of Muslim. In a report outside the Sahih, he said: "Yes, and I left them weeping." He said: "Go and make them laugh as you made them weep."

In another report he said: "Your sleeping with your parents on their bed, while they laugh with you and play with you, is better for you than jihad with me." This is mentioned by Ibn Khuwayz Mandad.

The wording of al-Bukhari in the book on kindness to parents: Abu Nu'aym informed us, Sufyan informed us, from 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from his father, from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, who said: A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) to pledge allegiance to him for emigration, and he had left his parents weeping. He (ﷺ) said: "Return to them and make them laugh as you made them weep."

Ibn al-Mundhir said: In this hadith is the prohibition of going out without the permission of the two parents, so long as a call to mobilize (*nafir*) has not occurred. When it occurs, going out becomes obligatory for everyone. This is clear in the hadith of Abu Qatadah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent an army of commanders... and he mentioned the story of Zayd ibn Harithah, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, and Ibn Rawahah. Then the caller of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called out afterward: "Indeed, the prayer is gathering (*jami'ah*)." The people gathered, and he praised Allah and extolled Him, then said: "O people, go forth and reinforce your brothers, and let no one remain behind." The people went out on foot and on horseback in intense heat. The Prophet's saying "go forth and reinforce your brothers" indicates that the excuse for remaining behind from jihad is only when mobilization has not occurred, along with his peace be upon him saying: "When you are called to mobilize, then mobilize."

I say: In these hadiths is evidence that when obligatory or recommended acts coincide, the more important of them is given precedence. Al-Muhasibi has fully addressed this meaning in *Kitab al-Ri'ayah*.

**Ninth:** The scholars differed regarding polytheist parents: whether one may go out to jihad with their permission when jihad is a collective obligation (*fard kifayah*). Al-Thawri used to say: One does not go on a military expedition except with their permission. Al-Shafi'i said: He may go out to fight.

Without their permission. Ibn al-Mundhir said: "Grandfathers are fathers and grandmothers are mothers, so a man should not go out to fight except with their permission. I know of no evidence that makes this obligatory with regard to others besides them, such as brothers and the rest of the relatives." Tawus used to hold that striving to support one's sisters was better than jihad in the way of Allah, mighty and majestic is He.

The tenth: Among the perfection of kindness toward them is maintaining ties with the friends of their affection. In the Sahih it is related from Ibn Umar, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Among the most meritorious acts of kindness is a man's maintaining ties with the friends of his father after he has passed away." Abu Usayd, who was one of the people of Badr, related: I was sitting with the Prophet (ﷺ) when a man from the Ansar came to him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, is there any kindness to my parents that remains for me to do after their death?" He said: "Yes. Praying for them, asking forgiveness for them, carrying out their promises after them, honoring their friends, and maintaining the ties of kinship that you have only through them. These are what remain for you." The Prophet (ﷺ) would send gifts to the friends of Khadijah out of kindness to her and loyalty to her, though she was his wife; so what do you think of the parents?

The eleventh: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Should one or both of them reach old age with you﴾. He singled out the state of old age because it is the state in which they need his kindness, due to the change in their condition through weakness and aging. So in this state he is obligated to attend to their circumstances more than he was obligated before, because in this state they have become a burden upon him, and they need him to take charge of them in old age in the same way they had to take charge of him in his childhood. Therefore He singled out this state for mention. Furthermore, prolonged companionship usually makes a person weary, boredom arises, irritation increases, and his anger toward his parents becomes apparent, his veins swell against them, and he becomes overbearing toward them through the presumption of sonship and lack of religious restraint. The least of the disliked behavior is what he shows through repeated sighs of irritation. He has been commanded to answer them with words characterized by honor, that is, words free from every fault. So He said: ﴿So do not say to them "Uff," nor repel them, but speak to them a noble word﴾. Muslim related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "May he be humbled, may he be humbled, may he be humbled." It was said: "Who, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "The one who reaches his parents in old age, one or both of them, and yet does not enter Paradise."

Al-Bukhari said in the Book of Parents: Musaddad narrated to us, Bishr ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, Abd al-Rahman ibn Ishaq narrated to us, from Abu Sa'id al-Maqbari, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "May a man be humbled in whose presence I am mentioned and he does not send blessings upon me. May a man be humbled who reaches his parents in old age, or one of them, and they do not cause him to enter Paradise. And may a man be humbled upon whom Ramadan comes and then passes before he is forgiven." Ibn Abi Uways narrated to us, my brother narrated to us, from Sulayman ibn Bilal, from Muhammad ibn Hilal, from Sa'd ibn Ishaq ibn Ka'b ibn Ujrah al-Salimi, from his father, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: Ka'b ibn Ujrah, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Bring the pulpit." When it was brought out, he ascended it; he said "Amin" upon the first step, then ascended to the second and said "Amin," then when he ascended to the third he said "Amin." When he finished and descended from the pulpit, we said: "O Messenger of Allah, we have heard from you today something we have never heard from you before." He said: "Did you hear it?" We said: "Yes." He said: "Jibril, peace be upon him, came to me and said: 'Distant is the one who lives to see Ramadan and is not forgiven.' So I said, 'Amin.' When I ascended to the second step he said: 'Distant is the one in whose presence you are mentioned and he does not send blessings upon you.' So I said, 'Amin.' When I ascended to the third he said: 'Distant is the one in whose presence his parents, or one of them, reach old age and they do not cause him to enter Paradise.' I said, 'Amin.'" Abu Nu'aym narrated to us, Salamah ibn Wardan narrated to us, I heard Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, say: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ascended a step of the pulpit and said "Amin," then ascended another step and said "Amin," then ascended the third step and said "Amin." Then he settled and sat down. His companions said: "O Messenger of Allah, for what did you say Amin?" He said: "Jibril, peace be upon him, came to me and said: 'May he be humbled in whose presence you are mentioned and who does not send blessings upon you,' and I said Amin. 'May he be humbled who reaches his parents or one of them and they do not cause him to enter Paradise,' and I said Amin." The hadith.

So the happy person is the one who hastens to seize the opportunity of kindness to them, lest it escape him at their death and he regret it. The wretched one is the one who disobeys them, especially one to whom the command to be kind to them has reached.

The twelfth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So do not say to them "Uff"﴾, meaning: do not say to them anything containing even the slightest sign of weariness. It is related from Abu Ja'far al-Utaridi that he said: "Uff" is foul, bad, subtle speech. Mujahid said: its meaning is that when you see from them in old age the excrement and urine that they saw from you in childhood, do not be disgusted by them and say "Uff." The verse is more general than this. "Uff" and "Tuff" also refer to the dirt under the fingernails. And it is said of every

What is disliked and considered burdensome: *uff* (أُفٍّ). Al-Azhari said: *tuff* (والتف) also refers to a trivial thing. It is read *uffin* (أُفٍّ) with tanwin and a kasra, as sounds are given a kasra and tanwin, as in *sahin* (صَهٍ) and *mahin* (مَهٍ). It has ten dialectal forms: أَفَّ, أَفُّ, أَفِّ, أفا, أُفٌّ, أُفَّهْ, إِفْ لَكَ (with a kasra on the hamza), أُفْ (with a damma on the hamza and sukun on the fa), and أُفًا (with a light fa). In a hadith: "He put the end of his garment over his nose, then said: *uff, uff*." Abu Bakr said: its meaning is disgust at a foul smell. Some said: the meaning of *uff* is contempt and belittling, derived from *al-uff*, which means little. Al-Qutabi said: its origin is your blowing on a thing that falls on you of ash, dust and the like, or on a place you want to clear of something so you can sit in it. So this word came to be used for anything burdensome. Abu Amr ibn al-Ala said: *al-uff* is the dirt between the fingernails, and *al-tuff* is its clipping. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of *uff* is stench. Al-Asmai said: *al-uff* is earwax, and *al-tuff* is the dirt of the fingernails; its use then became widespread until it was mentioned for everything by which one is harmed.

It is narrated from the hadith of Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If Allah knew of any act of disobedience to parents worse than *uff*, He would have mentioned it. So let the dutiful do whatever he wishes, he will not enter the Fire. And let the disobedient do whatever he wishes, he will not enter Paradise." Our scholars said: the saying "uff" to one's parents is the worst thing, because it rejects them with the rejection of ingratitude for a blessing, denies their upbringing, and rejects the command that Allah enjoined in the revelation. *Uff* is a word said for anything rejected, and for this reason Ibrahim said to his people: "Uff to you and to what you worship besides Allah" (see vol. 11, p. 302), meaning: rejection of you and of these idols with you.

Thirteenth: His saying, the Exalted: "and do not scold them" (وَلا تَنْهَرْهُما). *Al-nahr* is rebuke and harshness. "And speak to them a generous word" (وَقُلْ لَهُما قَوْلًا كَرِيماً), meaning gentle and kind speech, such as "O my father" (يَا أَبَتَاهُ) and "O my mother" (يَا أُمَّاهُ), without naming them or calling them by a kunya, said Ata. Ibn al-Baddah al-Tujibi said: I said to Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab: "I know all that the Qur'an says about honouring the parents except His saying: 'And speak to them a generous word.' What is this generous word?" Ibn al-Musayyab said: "The word of a servant who has done wrong to a harsh, rough master."

Fourteenth: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy﴾. This is a metaphor (istiʿara) for compassion and mercy towards them, and for humbling oneself before them as subjects humble themselves before a ruler and slaves before masters, as Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab pointed out. The lowering and raising of the wing is presented as an image of a bird's wing when it spreads it out over its young. *Al-dhull* means gentleness. The reading of the majority is with a damma on the dhal: from *dhalla yadhillu dhullan, dhillatan* and *madhallatan*, so he is *dhall* and *dhalil*. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn Abbas and Urwa ibn al-Zubayr read *al-dhill* with a kasra on the dhal, and it is also narrated from Asim. It comes from the expression "a dhalul animal", clearly tame; *al-dhill* in animals means one that is led and gentle, not difficult. Therefore, by the ruling of this verse, a person should make himself, with his parents, in the best state of humility: in his speech, his bearing and his gaze, and he should not fix his eyes on them, for that is the look of an angry person.

Fifteenth: The address in this verse is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and what is meant is his community, since at that time he, peace be upon him, had no parents. Humbling (*dhull*) is not mentioned in His saying: "And lower your wing to those who follow you of the believers" (see vol. 13, p. 118 onwards), and it is mentioned here because of the greatness and emphasis of the right. The *min* in His saying "min al-rahma" is for specifying the kind, meaning this lowering comes from the mercy that is settled in the soul, not that it should be mere practice. It may also be for indicating the end point. Then Allah, the Exalted, commanded His servants to show mercy to their fathers and mothers, to pray for them, and to be merciful to them as they showed mercy to you, and to be gentle with them as they were gentle with you. When they cared for you as a child, ignorant and in need, they preferred you over themselves, stayed awake through the night, went hungry so that you could be fed, went without clothes so that you could be clothed. You cannot repay them except when they reach old age in the state you were in as a child, so that you may then be the one who takes care of them as they took care of you, and then they will have the precedence of the first. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A child cannot repay a parent unless he finds him enslaved, buys him and frees him." The discussion of this hadith will come in Surat Maryam (see vol. 11, p. 159).

Sixteenth: His saying, the Exalted: "as they raised me" (كَما رَبَّيانِي). He singled out upbringing for mention so that the servant may remember the compassion of his parents and their care in raising him, which increases his compassion and tenderness towards them. All of this applies to believing parents. The Qur'an has forbidden seeking forgiveness for dead polytheists, even if they were near relatives, as has already been mentioned (vol. 8, p. 272). It is reported from Ibn Abbas and Qatada that all of this was abrogated (naskh, meaning the cancelling of a ruling by a later one) by His saying: "It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were near relatives, after it has become clear to them that they are companions of the Blazing Fire." So if a Muslim's parents are non-Muslim protected subjects (dhimmis), he should treat them as Allah has commanded here, except that praying for mercy for them after their death in disbelief is abrogated, because this alone was abrogated by the verse mentioned. It was also said: this is not a case of abrogation; it is a prayer for worldly mercy for the two polytheist parents for as long as they live, as was mentioned earlier. Or the generality of this verse is restricted by that, not to mercy in the Hereafter, especially since it was said that His saying "And say: My Lord, have mercy on them both" was revealed concerning Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas. When he embraced Islam, his mother threw herself onto the hot sand, naked. This was reported to Sa'd, and he said: "Let her die." Then the verse was revealed. It was also said: the verse is specifically about praying for two Muslim parents. The correct view is that it is general, as we have mentioned.

Ibn Abbas said: the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever spends the evening and the morning pleasing his parents, has two gates to Paradise open for him in the morning and in the evening, and if there is one parent, then one gate. Whoever spends the evening and the morning displeasing his parents, has two gates to the Fire open for him in the morning and in the evening, and if there is one parent, then one gate." A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, even if they wronged him?" He said: "Even if they wronged him, even if they wronged him, even if they wronged him."

It has been transmitted with a connected chain (isnad) from Jabir ibn Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, my father has taken my wealth." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to the man: "Bring me your father." Then Jibril, peace be upon him, descended to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, sends you His greetings and says: When the old man comes, ask him about something he said to himself that his ears did not hear." When the old man came, the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "What is the matter with your son, who complains about you? Do you want to take his wealth?" He said: "Ask him, O Messenger of Allah: do I spend it except on one of his paternal or maternal aunts, or on myself?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "*Eeh*" (إِيهِ) [a word used to ask for more or to make someone speak; with a kasra on the ha, it is a request for elaboration. When you say *iyha* with a fatha and tanwin, you are ordering silence. Ibn Sidah said: "*Eeh*" (with a kasra) is a word of rebuke meaning "enough for you", and it is given tanwin as *iyha*. He related from al-Layth: "*Eeh* and *eeh*" are for asking for more and making someone speak; "*Eeh*" and "*iyha*" are for rebuke, as in your saying: *eeh*, "enough for you", and *iyha*, "enough for you"], leave this aside. Tell me about something you said to yourself that your ears did not hear." The old man said: "By Allah, O Messenger of Allah, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has never ceased to increase us in certainty through you. I did say something to myself that my ears did not hear." He said: "Say it while I listen." He said: I said:

*I nourished you as a newborn, and I supported you as a youth, you grew strong on what I earned for you, and you were nourished.*

*When a night brought you sickness, I did not sleep, but stayed awake for your sickness, restless.*

*As if I were the one struck by what you were struck by, and my eye sheds tears.*

*My soul fears death for you, though it knows that death is an appointed time.*

*When you reached the age and the limit to which I had hoped for you,*

*you made my reward harshness and roughness, as if you were the benefactor, the one who grants favours.*

*Would that when you did not honour my fatherhood, you had acted like a near neighbour would act.*

*You gave me the right of a neighbour, and you were not stingy with me in wealth other than your own.*

He said: Then the Prophet (ﷺ) took hold of his son by the collar and said: "You and your wealth belong to your father." Al-Tabarani said: al-Lakhmi did not narrate this hadith with this full wording, nor the poetry, except through this chain, and Ubayd Allah ibn Khalsa was alone in narrating it. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verses 23–24 (part 1 of 3)**

There are sixteen issues in this passage.

**First:** *Qada'* (decreed) means He commanded, obligated, and made obligatory. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and Qatadah said: This is not a *qada'* of judgment but a *qada'* of command. In the *mushaf* (the codex) of Ibn Mas'ud the reading is *wa-wassa* ("and enjoined"). This is the reading of his companions, and also the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ali, and others. It is likewise in the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Ibn 'Abbas said: The original is *wa-wassa rabbuka* ("your Lord enjoined"), and one of the two waws was joined to the next letter, so it was read *wa-qada rabbuka* ("your Lord decreed"). For if it were a decree that could not be disobeyed, no one would have disobeyed Allah. Al-Dahhak said: For some people it was mistaken as *wassa bi-qada*, when the waw was confused with the sad at the time the *mushaf* was written. Abu Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas something like the statement of al-Dahhak. He also reported from Maymun ibn Mihran that he said: "Indeed, upon the saying of Ibn 'Abbas there is light." Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He has prescribed for you of religion what He enjoined upon Noah and what We have revealed to you﴾ [See vol. 16, p. 9]. Then Abu Hatim refused to accept that Ibn 'Abbas said this. He said: If we said this, the heretics (*zanadiqah*) would criticize our *mushaf*.

Then our scholars of theology and others said: *qada'* is used in the language in several senses. *Qada'* in the sense of command, as in His saying: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾, meaning *amara* (commanded). *Qada'* in the sense of creation, as in His saying: ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens in two days﴾ [See vol. 15, p. 342], meaning He created them. *Qada'* in the sense of judgment, as in His saying: ﴿So decide what you will decide﴾ [See vol. 11, p. 225], meaning judge what you judge. *Qada'* in the sense of completion, as in His saying: ﴿The matter about which you inquire has been concluded﴾ [See vol. 9, p. 193], meaning it has been finished. From this is His saying: ﴿And when you have completed your rites﴾ [See vol. 2, p. 431], and His saying: ﴿And when the prayer has been concluded﴾ [See vol. 18, p. 108]. *Qada'* in the sense of will, as in His saying: ﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [See vol. 4, p. 92]. *Qada'* in the sense of covenant, as in His saying: ﴿And you were not on the western side when We conveyed to Moses the command﴾ [See vol. 13, p. 291].

Since *qada'* bears these meanings, it is not permissible to say without qualification that acts of disobedience are by the decree of Allah. If by it is meant command, there is no disagreement that this is impermissible, because Allah the Exalted did not command them, for He does not command indecency.

Zakariyya ibn Sallam said: A man came to al-Hasan and said: "He divorced his wife three times." He said: "You have disobeyed your Lord, and she has become irrevocably separated from you." The man said: "Allah decreed that upon me!" Al-Hasan, who was eloquent, said: "Allah did not decree that"; that is, Allah did not command it. And he recited this verse: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾.

**Second:** Allah the Exalted commanded His worship and His oneness, and He linked kindness to parents with that, just as He linked their thanks with His thanks. He said: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and to parents, good treatment﴾. And He said: ﴿Give thanks to Me and to your parents; to Me is the destination﴾ [See vol. 14, p. 65].

In the *Sahih* of al-Bukhari, from 'Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud), who said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ): "Which deed is most beloved to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic?" He said: "Prayer at its proper time." I said: "Then which?" He said: "Then kindness to parents." I said: "Then which?" He said: "Jihad in the way of Allah." So he (ﷺ) informed that kindness to parents is the best of deeds after prayer, which is the greatest pillar of Islam. He arranged this with *thumma* ("then"), which indicates sequence and a time interval.

**Third:** Among kindness and goodness toward them is that one does not expose oneself to insulting them and does not disobey them (*'uquq*). This is a major sin (*kaba'ir*) without disagreement, and the established Sunnah has come with this. In the *Sahih* of Muslim, from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Among the major sins is a man cursing his parents." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, does a man curse his parents?" He said: "Yes. A man curses another man's father, so he curses his father, and curses his mother, so he curses his mother."

**Fourth:** Disobedience (*'uquq*) to parents is opposing them in their permissible aims, just as their kindness is agreeing with them in their aims. Accordingly, if they or one of them command their child with a command, obedience to them in it becomes obligatory, provided that command is not sinful, even if the thing commanded is originally permissible (*mubah*), and likewise if it is recommended (*mandub*). Some people have held that their commanding something permissible makes it recommended for the child, and their commanding something recommended increases its recommendation.

**Fifth:** Al-Tirmidhi reported from 'Umar, who said: "I had a wife whom I loved, and my father disliked her, so he commanded me to divorce her, but I refused. I mentioned that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'O 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, divorce your wife.'" He said: This is a hadith that is *hasan sahih* (good and sound).

**Sixth:** The Sahih reported from Abu Hurayrah, who said: A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Who is most deserving of good companionship from me?" He said: "Your mother." He said: "Then who?" He said: "Your mother." He said: "Then who?" He said: "Your mother." He said: "Then who?" He said: "Then your father." This hadith indicates that love for the mother and compassion toward her should be three times the love for the father, since the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned the mother three times and mentioned the father only in the fourth place. When this meaning is established, observation bears witness to it, because the difficulty of pregnancy, the difficulty of childbirth, and the difficulty of nursing and rearing belong to the mother alone and not the father. These are three stations from which the father is free.

It is reported from Malik that a man said to him: "My father is in the land of the Sudan, and he has written to me to come to him, but my mother prevents me from that." He said: "Obey your father, and do not disobey your mother." This statement of Malik indicates that kindness to them is equal in his view. Al-Layth was asked about this issue, and he ordered obedience to the mother, claiming that she has two-thirds of the kindness. The hadith of Abu Hurayrah indicates that she has three-quarters of the kindness, and it is the proof against those who differ. Al-Muhasibi claimed in his book *al-Ri'ayah* that there is no disagreement among the scholars that the mother has three-quarters of the kindness and the father one-quarter, according to the import of the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him. And Allah knows best.

**Seventh:** Kindness to parents is not restricted to their being Muslims. Even if they are disbelievers, one treats them well and is kind to them when they have a covenant. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion and do not expel you from your homes—from being righteous toward them﴾ [See vol. 18, p. 58 and vol. 14, p. 63].

In the *Sahih* of al-Bukhari, from Asma' (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: My mother came to me while she was a polytheist, during the time of the covenant of Quraysh and their truce, when they had made a covenant with the Prophet (ﷺ) along with her father. So I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for a ruling and said: "My mother has come, and she is *raghibah*" [Note: meaning either desiring my kindness and maintenance, or averse to Islam and hating it]. "Shall I maintain ties with her?" He said: "Yes, maintain ties with your mother."

It is also reported from Asma', who said: My mother came to me desiring (something) during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), so I asked the Prophet (ﷺ): "Shall I maintain ties with her?" He said: "Yes." Ibn 'Uyaynah said: Then Allah the Mighty and Majestic revealed concerning her: ﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion﴾. The first report is *mu'allaq* (with its chain omitted) and the second is *musnad* (with a complete chain).

**Eighth:** Among kindness to them and righteousness toward them, when jihad is not specifically obligated, is that one should not wage jihad except with their permission. The Sahih reported from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, who said: A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) asking his permission for jihad, and he said: "Are your parents alive?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then strive (jahid) for their sake." This is the wording of Muslim. In a report outside the Sahih, he said: "Yes, and I left them weeping." He said: "Go and make them laugh as you made them weep."

In another report he said: "Your sleeping with your parents on their bed, while they laugh with you and play with you, is better for you than jihad with me." This is mentioned by Ibn Khuwayz Mandad.

The wording of al-Bukhari in the book on kindness to parents: Abu Nu'aym informed us, Sufyan informed us, from 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from his father, from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, who said: A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) to pledge allegiance to him for emigration, and he had left his parents weeping. He (ﷺ) said: "Return to them and make them laugh as you made them weep."

Ibn al-Mundhir said: In this hadith is the prohibition of going out without the permission of the two parents, so long as a call to mobilize (*nafir*) has not occurred. When it occurs, going out becomes obligatory for everyone. This is clear in the hadith of Abu Qatadah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent an army of commanders... and he mentioned the story of Zayd ibn Harithah, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, and Ibn Rawahah. Then the caller of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called out afterward: "Indeed, the prayer is gathering (*jami'ah*)." The people gathered, and he praised Allah and extolled Him, then said: "O people, go forth and reinforce your brothers, and let no one remain behind." The people went out on foot and on horseback in intense heat. The Prophet's saying "go forth and reinforce your brothers" indicates that the excuse for remaining behind from jihad is only when mobilization has not occurred, along with his peace be upon him saying: "When you are called to mobilize, then mobilize."

I say: In these hadiths is evidence that when obligatory or recommended acts coincide, the more important of them is given precedence. Al-Muhasibi has fully addressed this meaning in *Kitab al-Ri'ayah*.

**Ninth:** The scholars differed regarding polytheist parents: whether one may go out to jihad with their permission when jihad is a collective obligation (*fard kifayah*). Al-Thawri used to say: One does not go on a military expedition except with their permission. Al-Shafi'i said: He may go out to fight.

Without their permission. Ibn al-Mundhir said: "Grandfathers are fathers and grandmothers are mothers, so a man should not go out to fight except with their permission. I know of no evidence that makes this obligatory with regard to others besides them, such as brothers and the rest of the relatives." Tawus used to hold that striving to support one's sisters was better than jihad in the way of Allah, mighty and majestic is He.

The tenth: Among the perfection of kindness toward them is maintaining ties with the friends of their affection. In the Sahih it is related from Ibn Umar, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Among the most meritorious acts of kindness is a man's maintaining ties with the friends of his father after he has passed away." Abu Usayd, who was one of the people of Badr, related: I was sitting with the Prophet (ﷺ) when a man from the Ansar came to him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, is there any kindness to my parents that remains for me to do after their death?" He said: "Yes. Praying for them, asking forgiveness for them, carrying out their promises after them, honoring their friends, and maintaining the ties of kinship that you have only through them. These are what remain for you." The Prophet (ﷺ) would send gifts to the friends of Khadijah out of kindness to her and loyalty to her, though she was his wife; so what do you think of the parents?

The eleventh: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Should one or both of them reach old age with you﴾. He singled out the state of old age because it is the state in which they need his kindness, due to the change in their condition through weakness and aging. So in this state he is obligated to attend to their circumstances more than he was obligated before, because in this state they have become a burden upon him, and they need him to take charge of them in old age in the same way they had to take charge of him in his childhood. Therefore He singled out this state for mention. Furthermore, prolonged companionship usually makes a person weary, boredom arises, irritation increases, and his anger toward his parents becomes apparent, his veins swell against them, and he becomes overbearing toward them through the presumption of sonship and lack of religious restraint. The least of the disliked behavior is what he shows through repeated sighs of irritation. He has been commanded to answer them with words characterized by honor, that is, words free from every fault. So He said: ﴿So do not say to them "Uff," nor repel them, but speak to them a noble word﴾. Muslim related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "May he be humbled, may he be humbled, may he be humbled." It was said: "Who, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "The one who reaches his parents in old age, one or both of them, and yet does not enter Paradise."

Al-Bukhari said in the Book of Parents: Musaddad narrated to us, Bishr ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, Abd al-Rahman ibn Ishaq narrated to us, from Abu Sa'id al-Maqbari, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "May a man be humbled in whose presence I am mentioned and he does not send blessings upon me. May a man be humbled who reaches his parents in old age, or one of them, and they do not cause him to enter Paradise. And may a man be humbled upon whom Ramadan comes and then passes before he is forgiven." Ibn Abi Uways narrated to us, my brother narrated to us, from Sulayman ibn Bilal, from Muhammad ibn Hilal, from Sa'd ibn Ishaq ibn Ka'b ibn Ujrah al-Salimi, from his father, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: Ka'b ibn Ujrah, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Bring the pulpit." When it was brought out, he ascended it; he said "Amin" upon the first step, then ascended to the second and said "Amin," then when he ascended to the third he said "Amin." When he finished and descended from the pulpit, we said: "O Messenger of Allah, we have heard from you today something we have never heard from you before." He said: "Did you hear it?" We said: "Yes." He said: "Jibril, peace be upon him, came to me and said: 'Distant is the one who lives to see Ramadan and is not forgiven.' So I said, 'Amin.' When I ascended to the second step he said: 'Distant is the one in whose presence you are mentioned and he does not send blessings upon you.' So I said, 'Amin.' When I ascended to the third he said: 'Distant is the one in whose presence his parents, or one of them, reach old age and they do not cause him to enter Paradise.' I said, 'Amin.'" Abu Nu'aym narrated to us, Salamah ibn Wardan narrated to us, I heard Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, say: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ascended a step of the pulpit and said "Amin," then ascended another step and said "Amin," then ascended the third step and said "Amin." Then he settled and sat down. His companions said: "O Messenger of Allah, for what did you say Amin?" He said: "Jibril, peace be upon him, came to me and said: 'May he be humbled in whose presence you are mentioned and who does not send blessings upon you,' and I said Amin. 'May he be humbled who reaches his parents or one of them and they do not cause him to enter Paradise,' and I said Amin." The hadith.

So the happy person is the one who hastens to seize the opportunity of kindness to them, lest it escape him at their death and he regret it. The wretched one is the one who disobeys them, especially one to whom the command to be kind to them has reached.

The twelfth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So do not say to them "Uff"﴾, meaning: do not say to them anything containing even the slightest sign of weariness. It is related from Abu Ja'far al-Utaridi that he said: "Uff" is foul, bad, subtle speech. Mujahid said: its meaning is that when you see from them in old age the excrement and urine that they saw from you in childhood, do not be disgusted by them and say "Uff." The verse is more general than this. "Uff" and "Tuff" also refer to the dirt under the fingernails. And it is said of every

What is disliked and considered burdensome: *uff* (أُفٍّ). Al-Azhari said: *tuff* (والتف) also refers to a trivial thing. It is read *uffin* (أُفٍّ) with tanwin and a kasra, as sounds are given a kasra and tanwin, as in *sahin* (صَهٍ) and *mahin* (مَهٍ). It has ten dialectal forms: أَفَّ, أَفُّ, أَفِّ, أفا, أُفٌّ, أُفَّهْ, إِفْ لَكَ (with a kasra on the hamza), أُفْ (with a damma on the hamza and sukun on the fa), and أُفًا (with a light fa). In a hadith: "He put the end of his garment over his nose, then said: *uff, uff*." Abu Bakr said: its meaning is disgust at a foul smell. Some said: the meaning of *uff* is contempt and belittling, derived from *al-uff*, which means little. Al-Qutabi said: its origin is your blowing on a thing that falls on you of ash, dust and the like, or on a place you want to clear of something so you can sit in it. So this word came to be used for anything burdensome. Abu Amr ibn al-Ala said: *al-uff* is the dirt between the fingernails, and *al-tuff* is its clipping. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of *uff* is stench. Al-Asmai said: *al-uff* is earwax, and *al-tuff* is the dirt of the fingernails; its use then became widespread until it was mentioned for everything by which one is harmed.

It is narrated from the hadith of Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If Allah knew of any act of disobedience to parents worse than *uff*, He would have mentioned it. So let the dutiful do whatever he wishes, he will not enter the Fire. And let the disobedient do whatever he wishes, he will not enter Paradise." Our scholars said: the saying "uff" to one's parents is the worst thing, because it rejects them with the rejection of ingratitude for a blessing, denies their upbringing, and rejects the command that Allah enjoined in the revelation. *Uff* is a word said for anything rejected, and for this reason Ibrahim said to his people: "Uff to you and to what you worship besides Allah" (see vol. 11, p. 302), meaning: rejection of you and of these idols with you.

Thirteenth: His saying, the Exalted: "and do not scold them" (وَلا تَنْهَرْهُما). *Al-nahr* is rebuke and harshness. "And speak to them a generous word" (وَقُلْ لَهُما قَوْلًا كَرِيماً), meaning gentle and kind speech, such as "O my father" (يَا أَبَتَاهُ) and "O my mother" (يَا أُمَّاهُ), without naming them or calling them by a kunya, said Ata. Ibn al-Baddah al-Tujibi said: I said to Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab: "I know all that the Qur'an says about honouring the parents except His saying: 'And speak to them a generous word.' What is this generous word?" Ibn al-Musayyab said: "The word of a servant who has done wrong to a harsh, rough master."

Fourteenth: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy﴾. This is a metaphor (istiʿara) for compassion and mercy towards them, and for humbling oneself before them as subjects humble themselves before a ruler and slaves before masters, as Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab pointed out. The lowering and raising of the wing is presented as an image of a bird's wing when it spreads it out over its young. *Al-dhull* means gentleness. The reading of the majority is with a damma on the dhal: from *dhalla yadhillu dhullan, dhillatan* and *madhallatan*, so he is *dhall* and *dhalil*. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn Abbas and Urwa ibn al-Zubayr read *al-dhill* with a kasra on the dhal, and it is also narrated from Asim. It comes from the expression "a dhalul animal", clearly tame; *al-dhill* in animals means one that is led and gentle, not difficult. Therefore, by the ruling of this verse, a person should make himself, with his parents, in the best state of humility: in his speech, his bearing and his gaze, and he should not fix his eyes on them, for that is the look of an angry person.

Fifteenth: The address in this verse is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and what is meant is his community, since at that time he, peace be upon him, had no parents. Humbling (*dhull*) is not mentioned in His saying: "And lower your wing to those who follow you of the believers" (see vol. 13, p. 118 onwards), and it is mentioned here because of the greatness and emphasis of the right. The *min* in His saying "min al-rahma" is for specifying the kind, meaning this lowering comes from the mercy that is settled in the soul, not that it should be mere practice. It may also be for indicating the end point. Then Allah, the Exalted, commanded His servants to show mercy to their fathers and mothers, to pray for them, and to be merciful to them as they showed mercy to you, and to be gentle with them as they were gentle with you. When they cared for you as a child, ignorant and in need, they preferred you over themselves, stayed awake through the night, went hungry so that you could be fed, went without clothes so that you could be clothed. You cannot repay them except when they reach old age in the state you were in as a child, so that you may then be the one who takes care of them as they took care of you, and then they will have the precedence of the first. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A child cannot repay a parent unless he finds him enslaved, buys him and frees him." The discussion of this hadith will come in Surat Maryam (see vol. 11, p. 159).

Sixteenth: His saying, the Exalted: "as they raised me" (كَما رَبَّيانِي). He singled out upbringing for mention so that the servant may remember the compassion of his parents and their care in raising him, which increases his compassion and tenderness towards them. All of this applies to believing parents. The Qur'an has forbidden seeking forgiveness for dead polytheists, even if they were near relatives, as has already been mentioned (vol. 8, p. 272). It is reported from Ibn Abbas and Qatada that all of this was abrogated (naskh, meaning the cancelling of a ruling by a later one) by His saying: "It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were near relatives, after it has become clear to them that they are companions of the Blazing Fire." So if a Muslim's parents are non-Muslim protected subjects (dhimmis), he should treat them as Allah has commanded here, except that praying for mercy for them after their death in disbelief is abrogated, because this alone was abrogated by the verse mentioned. It was also said: this is not a case of abrogation; it is a prayer for worldly mercy for the two polytheist parents for as long as they live, as was mentioned earlier. Or the generality of this verse is restricted by that, not to mercy in the Hereafter, especially since it was said that His saying "And say: My Lord, have mercy on them both" was revealed concerning Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas. When he embraced Islam, his mother threw herself onto the hot sand, naked. This was reported to Sa'd, and he said: "Let her die." Then the verse was revealed. It was also said: the verse is specifically about praying for two Muslim parents. The correct view is that it is general, as we have mentioned.

Ibn Abbas said: the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever spends the evening and the morning pleasing his parents, has two gates to Paradise open for him in the morning and in the evening, and if there is one parent, then one gate. Whoever spends the evening and the morning displeasing his parents, has two gates to the Fire open for him in the morning and in the evening, and if there is one parent, then one gate." A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, even if they wronged him?" He said: "Even if they wronged him, even if they wronged him, even if they wronged him."

It has been transmitted with a connected chain (isnad) from Jabir ibn Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, my father has taken my wealth." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to the man: "Bring me your father." Then Jibril, peace be upon him, descended to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, sends you His greetings and says: When the old man comes, ask him about something he said to himself that his ears did not hear." When the old man came, the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "What is the matter with your son, who complains about you? Do you want to take his wealth?" He said: "Ask him, O Messenger of Allah: do I spend it except on one of his paternal or maternal aunts, or on myself?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "*Eeh*" (إِيهِ) [a word used to ask for more or to make someone speak; with a kasra on the ha, it is a request for elaboration. When you say *iyha* with a fatha and tanwin, you are ordering silence. Ibn Sidah said: "*Eeh*" (with a kasra) is a word of rebuke meaning "enough for you", and it is given tanwin as *iyha*. He related from al-Layth: "*Eeh* and *eeh*" are for asking for more and making someone speak; "*Eeh*" and "*iyha*" are for rebuke, as in your saying: *eeh*, "enough for you", and *iyha*, "enough for you"], leave this aside. Tell me about something you said to yourself that your ears did not hear." The old man said: "By Allah, O Messenger of Allah, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has never ceased to increase us in certainty through you. I did say something to myself that my ears did not hear." He said: "Say it while I listen." He said: I said:

*I nourished you as a newborn, and I supported you as a youth, you grew strong on what I earned for you, and you were nourished.*

*When a night brought you sickness, I did not sleep, but stayed awake for your sickness, restless.*

*As if I were the one struck by what you were struck by, and my eye sheds tears.*

*My soul fears death for you, though it knows that death is an appointed time.*

*When you reached the age and the limit to which I had hoped for you,*

*you made my reward harshness and roughness, as if you were the benefactor, the one who grants favours.*

*Would that when you did not honour my fatherhood, you had acted like a near neighbour would act.*

*You gave me the right of a neighbour, and you were not stingy with me in wealth other than your own.*

He said: Then the Prophet (ﷺ) took hold of his son by the collar and said: "You and your wealth belong to your father." Al-Tabarani said: al-Lakhmi did not narrate this hadith with this full wording, nor the poetry, except through this chain, and Ubayd Allah ibn Khalsa was alone in narrating it. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 25:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Your Lord knows best what is in your souls﴾, i.e., of belief in mercy towards them both and tenderness toward them, or of anything other than that, such as disobedience (ʿuquq), or of making the outward display of their goodness a matter of showing off (riya'). Ibn Jubayr said: it means the sudden lapse that escapes a person toward his parents or one of them, which he does not intend any harm by, such as a slip or a fault. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿If you are righteous﴾, i.e., truthful in the intention of goodness toward the parents, for indeed Allah forgives the sudden lapse. And His saying: ﴿for indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back (awwabin)﴾ is a promise of forgiveness together with the condition of righteousness and returning (awba) to the obedience of Allah, glorified and exalted is He. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: it is the servant who repents, then sins, then repents, then sins. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the awwab is the one who keeps watch, who, when he remembers his sins, seeks forgiveness for them. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr said: they are those who recall their sins in seclusion (al-khalaʾ) [[al-khalaʾ: privacy, being alone.]] and then seek forgiveness from Allah, mighty and majestic. These statements are closely related. ʿAwn al-ʿUqayli said: the awwabun are those who perform the prayer of ad-duha (ṣalat al-ḍuha, the forenoon prayer). And in the Sahih: "The prayer of the awwabin is when the young camels are scorched by the heat" [[It means when the sand becomes heated, so the young camels kneel from the intensity of its heat and their hooves are burned.]]. The literal meaning of the word (that it is) from āba, yaʾūbu, meaning to return.

There are three issues here.

The first concerns the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And give the near of kin his right﴾. That is, just as you observe the rights of the two parents, maintain the ties of kinship (silat al-rahim), then give charity to the poor and to the wayfarer (ibn al-sabil).

Ali ibn al-Husayn (Zayn al-Abidin) said, concerning the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿And give the near of kin his right﴾: they are the kinsmen of the Prophet (ﷺ). The Prophet (ﷺ) commanded that their rights be given to them from the public treasury (bayt al-mal), that is, from the share of the near of kin (dhawi al-qurba) in the spoils of war and booty. This is addressed to the rulers or to those who stand in their place. The right in this verse is what is required of maintaining kinship ties, meeting needs, helping with wealth when there is a need, and giving assistance in every way.

The second issue concerns the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And do not squander﴾, that is, do not be extravagant in spending on what is not right. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Tabdhir (wasteful squandering) is spending wealth in other than its right, and there is no tabdhir in doing good." This is the view of the majority.

Ashhab said, on the authority of Malik: "Tabdhir is taking wealth from its right and placing it in other than its right, and this is israf (extravagance), and it is prohibited, because of the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the squanderers are brothers of the devils﴾." The word "brothers" means that they are in their ruling, since the squanderer strives in corruption like the devils; or that they do what their souls prompt them to do; or that they will be joined with them tomorrow in the Fire. These are three opinions. The word "ikhwan" (brothers) here is the plural of akh (brother) in a non-blood sense, and from this is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿The believers are only brothers﴾ [see vol. 16, p. 322]. And the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And Satan has ever been ungrateful to his Lord﴾ mean: beware of following him and of resembling him in corruption. "Shaytan" is a generic noun. Al-Dahhak recited "ikhwan al-shaytan" in the singular, and this is also how it is recorded in the Mushaf of Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him.

The third issue: whoever spends his wealth on desires beyond the measure of needs, and thereby exposes it to depletion, is a squanderer. Whoever spends the profit of his wealth on his desires while preserving the capital or the principal, he is not a squanderer. Whoever spends a single dirham on something unlawful is a squanderer, and he is placed under hajr (interdiction, restriction of his disposal of property) concerning the dirham he spends on the unlawful; he is not placed under interdiction for spending on desires unless depletion of his wealth is feared.
