Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 28:

There are three issues in this.

The first: Allah, glorified and exalted be He, singled out His Prophet ﷺ with His saying: ﴿And if you turn away from them, seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for﴾. This is a wondrous act of discipline and a subtle, marvelous saying, meaning: do not turn away from them with the turning away of one who disdains, out of a sense of wealth and power, so that you deprive them. You may only turn away from them when there is a helplessness that overtakes you and an obstacle that hinders you. In that case, you hope from Allah, glorified and exalted be He, for the opening of a door of goodness, so that you may reach through it the consoling of the petitioner. If the situation keeps you in that state, then ﴿say to them a gentle word﴾.

The second: concerning the occasion of its revelation. Ibn Zayd said: the verse was revealed concerning a people who used to ask the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he would refuse to give them, because he knew that they spent wealth in corruption. So he would turn away from them, desiring the reward for withholding from them, so that he would not be helping them in their corruption. And 'Ata' al-Khurasani said, regarding the saying of the Exalted, ﴿And if you turn away from them, seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for﴾, he said: this is not in the mention of the parents. People from Muzayna came to the Prophet ﷺ asking him to provide them with mounts. He said: "I do not find anything to carry you on." So they turned away, their eyes overflowing with tears from sorrow. Then Allah, the Exalted, revealed: ﴿And if you turn away from them, seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for﴾. And the mercy here means the fay' [[In J, H: al-ghina (wealth).]].

The third: the saying of the Exalted, ﴿So say to them a gentle word﴾. He commanded him to pray for them, meaning: ease their poverty upon them by your supplication for them. It was also said: pray for them with a prayer that includes opening (of provision) for them and betterment. It was also said: the meaning of "And if you turn away" is: if you turn away, O Muhammad, from giving them because of constraint of hand, then ﴿say to them a gentle word﴾, meaning: speak well, extend excuse, pray for them for abundance of provision, and say: "When I find, I will act and give generously," for that works in the soul's gladness the effect of consolation. When he, peace be upon him, was asked and had nothing to give, he would remain silent, waiting for provision to come from Allah, glorified and exalted be He, out of disliking to refuse. Then this verse was revealed, and whenever he ﷺ was asked and had nothing to give, he would say: "May Allah grant us and you from His bounty." So the mercy, according to this interpretation, is the awaited provision. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and 'Ikrimah.

And ﴿a gentle word﴾ means soft, gentle, good, a passive participle used in the sense of an active one, derived from the word yusr (ease), like al-maymun (blessed), meaning a beautiful promise, according to what we have explained. And how well has the one said:

If there is no silver one day with which I may be generous to the seekers, then I am a pliant stick (of generosity).

The seekers do not lack goodness from my character, whether it is my giving or the goodness of my refusal.

You say: "yassartu laka kadha" (I prepared such-and-such for you) when you have prepared it.

In it there are four issues.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾. This is a metaphor (majaz), by which He refers to the miser who cannot, in his heart, bring himself to part with any of his wealth. So He struck for him the example of the shackle that prevents the hand from acting freely. In the Sahih of al-Bukhari and Muslim, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) struck an example of the miser and the one who gives charity: they are like two men wearing coats of iron, their hands forced up to their breasts and collarbones. Whenever the one who gives charity gives a charity, the coat expands [[i.e., the coat spreads out from him]] about him until it covers his fingertips and conceals his footprints [[i.e., the traces of his walking, due to its fullness]]. And whenever the miser intends to give charity, the coat contracts [[i.e., it gathers in and rises up]] and each ring holds to its place. Abu Hurayrah said: "So I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) [[The Arabs use the word "qala" (said) to refer to all actions and apply it to other than speech and the tongue; so they say: "qala bi-yadihi" meaning he took, and "qala bi-rijlihi" meaning he walked. All of this is metaphorical and extended usage.]] saying with his two fingers thus at his collar; were you to see him, you would see him widen it, yet it would not widen." [[The answer to "law" (if) is omitted, meaning: you would be amazed.]]

The second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not extend it with complete extension﴾. He struck the extending of the hand as an example of the loss of wealth, for closing the palm holds what is in it, while extending it lets go of what is in it. All of this is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), while what is meant is his community; this is frequent in the Qur'an, for the Prophet (ﷺ), since he was their leader and their intermediary to their Lord, was addressed on their behalf, following the Arab custom in this. Also, he, upon him be blessings and peace, did not store anything for the morrow, and he would go hungry until he tied a stone on his belly from hunger. Many of the Companions spent all their wealth in the way of Allah, and the Prophet (ﷺ) did not rebuke them nor disapproved of them, because of the soundness of their certainty and the strength of their insight. Allah, glorified and exalted, only forbade excess in spending and in giving out what his hand holds of wealth to the one who fears regret over what has left his hand. As for the one who trusts in the promise of Allah, mighty and majestic, and in His abundant reward for what he spent, he is not intended by the verse, and Allah knows best. It has also been said: this address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning himself specifically, teaching him the manner of spending and commanding him to moderation. Jabir and Ibn Mas'ud said: A boy came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "My mother asks you for such and such." He said: "We have nothing today." He said: "Then she says to you: clothe me in your shirt." So he took off his shirt, gave it to him, and sat in the house naked. In the narration of Jabir: Bilal called the adhan for the prayer and waited for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to come out, and hearts were occupied; some of them entered and found him naked, and this verse was revealed. All of this concerns spending on good. As for spending on corruption, its little and its much are unlawful, as has preceded.

The third: This verse forbids exhausting one's wealth (wujd) [[al-wujd (with a triple vowel on the waw): means affluence and abundance.]] in what first comes up of the requests of the believers, lest there remain after that someone who comes with nothing for himself, or lest the spender neglect his dependents. A similar saying of wisdom is: I have never seen extravagance except that with it there is a neglected right. This is among the verses of the jurisprudence of circumstance, so its ruling is not clarified except by considering each individual person.

The fourth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so you sit blameworthy, stripped bare﴾. Ibn 'Arafah said: He means: do not be wasteful and do not squander your wealth, lest you remain stripped bare, cut off from spending and disposing, like the exhausted camel, which is the one whose strength has gone so there is no movement in it. From this is His saying, exalted is He: "Then the gaze will return to you humbled while it is exhausted" [[See vol. 18, p. 209.]], that is, weary and cut off. Qatadah said: that is, regretful over what has passed from you, so he made it from regret (hasrah). This is far-fetched, because the one who experiences regret is "hasir" and "hasran," and one does not say "mahsur." "Al-malum" is the one who is blamed for destroying his wealth, or the one whom the one he does not give to blames.

This verse was not discussed by the author, and it does not appear in the copies of the book available to us. Perhaps he discussed it and the copyists omitted it. The wording of Ibn Jarir al-Tabari in his discussion of the verse, as it appears in his tafsir, is:

"He, exalted is His remembrance, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): Indeed your Lord, O Muhammad, extends provision to whomever He wills of His servants, so He widens it for him, and He decides it with measure for whomever He wills," and says: "and He restricts it for whomever He wills of them, so He constricts it for him."

﴿Indeed He is ever, of His servants, Acquainted and Seeing.﴾ "He says: Indeed your Lord is one who has knowledge of His servants, and of who is made right by abundance in provision and who is corrupted by it, and of who is made right by restriction and constriction and who is destroyed by it." ﴿Seeing.﴾ "He says: He is one who has sight of their management and their governance. And He says: So, O Muhammad, refer to Our command regarding what We have commanded you and forbidden you concerning the extending of your hand, in what you extend it to and to whom you extend it, and concerning the withholding of it from whom you withhold it and in what you withhold it. So We are more knowing of the good of the servants than you and than all of creation, and more seeing of their management."

**First issue:** Al-Qurtubi's commentary on this verse has already been discussed in Surat al-An'am, and all praise is due to Allah [see vol. 7, p. 30].

*Al-imlaq* (poverty and the lack of possessions): *amlaqa al-rajul* means that nothing remained to him except *al-malaqat*, which are large, smooth stones. The Hudhali poet, describing a hunter, said:

*Uti'a laha Uqayder dhu Hashif... idha sama 'ala al-malaqat sama*

(Its singular is *malaqa*.) *Al-Uqayder* is the diminutive of *al-aqdar*, meaning a short man. *Al-Hashif* refers to worn-out clothing. *Sama* means "passed by." Shimr said: *amlaqa* is both intransitive and transitive. *Amlaqa* means he became poor, and *amlaqa al-dahr ma biyadihi* means time took what was in his hand. Aws said:

*Wa amlaqa ma 'indi khutub tanbul*
[The first half of the verse is: *Lamma ra'aytu al-'adama qad naa'ili*]

**Second issue:** Allah's words (*khit'an*). The recitation of the majority is *khi'an*, with a kasra on the *kha'*, a sukun on the *ta'*, a hamza, and a short vowel (*qasr*). Ibn 'Amir recited *khata'an*, with a fatha on the *kha'* and the *ta'* and a hamza with qasr, and this is the recitation of Abu Ja'far Yazid. These two recitations are derived from *khati'a*, meaning to commit a sin deliberately. Ibn 'Arafa said: it is said *khati'a fi dhanbihi khata'an* when one sins in it, and *akhta'a* when one takes a wrong course, whether deliberately or not. He said: it is also said that *khati'a* has the same meaning as *akhta'a*. Al-Azhari said: it is said *khati'a yakhta'u khit'an* when one deliberately commits error, like *athima ya'thamu ithman* (to commit a sin). And *akhta'a* when one does not intend it: *ikhta'an* and *khata'an*. The poet said:

*Da'ini innama khat'i wa sawbi... 'alayya wa in ma ahlaktu mal*
[In the originals: "wa in ma ahlaktu mali." The correction is from *Kitab al-Shi'r wa al-Shu'ara'* by Ibn Qutayba, *Tabaqat al-Shu'ara'* by Ibn Sallam in the biography of Aws ibn Ghalfa', and *Lisan al-Arab* under the root *sawb*. It is also said that this verse is:

*Ala qalat Umama yawma Ghawl... taqta'u ya ibn Ghalfa' al-hibal*

He means: what I destroyed was only wealth, and wealth is cheap, and I did not damage anyone's honor. Ghawl was a place where the Arabs fought a battle, in which Dabba fought against Banu Kilab.
(See Mu'jam Yaqut.)]] *Al-khata'* is the noun that stands in place of *ikhta'*, and it is the opposite of *al-sawab* (correctness). It has two forms: *al-qasr* (the short form), which is the better one, and *al-madd* (the long form), which is less common. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, *khata'an* with a fatha on the *kha'*, a sukun on the *ta'*, and a hamza. Ibn Kathir recited with a kasra on the *kha'*, a fatha on the *ta'*, and a long hamza. Al-Nahhas said: I do not know any basis for this recitation, and for this reason Abu Hatim considered it an error. Abu 'Ali said: it is a verbal noun of *khai'a yukhati'u*, although we do not find *khai'a* used, but we find *takhata'a*, which is the reflexive of *khata'a*, so this points to it. From this is the poet's saying:

*Takhata'at al-nablu ahshaa'uhu... wa akhkhara yawmi fa lam u'ajjil*
[*Akhkhara*: meaning *yata'akhkharu* (is delayed). It is permissible to read *akhkhara* with a damma on the hamza and a shadda on the *kha'* with a kasra.]

Another poet, describing a female antelope, said:

*Takhata'ahu al-qannas hatta wajadtuhu... wa khurtumuhu fi manqa' al-ma' rasibu*

Al-Jawhari said: *takhata'ahu* means *akhta'ahu* (he missed him). Awfa ibn Matar al-Mazini said:

*Ala ablighaa khullati Jabiran... bi-anna khalilaka lam yuqtali*

*Takhata'at al-nablu ahshaa'ahu... wa ukhkhira yawmi fa lam ya'jali*

Al-Hasan recited *khata'an*, with a fatha on the *kha'* and the *ta'* and a long hamza. Abu Hatim said: this is not known in the language, and it is an unacceptable error. Abu al-Fath said: *al-khata'* is derived from *akhta'tu*, in the same pattern as *al-'ata'* from *a'taytu*. It is a noun with the meaning of a verbal noun. It is also reported from al-Hasan *khata*, with a fatha on the *kha'* and the *ta'*, tanwin, and no hamza.

There is one issue here. The scholars said: God's words ﴿And do not approach adultery﴾ are more emphatic than saying "and do not commit adultery," for their meaning is "do not draw near to adultery." The word الزنى (az-zina) may be pronounced with a long or a short first vowel; both are valid dialect forms (lughatan). The poet said:

"It was an obligation, as you say, just as
the zina was an obligation for stoning."

The word سبيلا (sabilan) is in the accusative as a tamyiz (specification of the noun, a grammatical term meaning a clarifying accusative). The sense is: "and evil is its path, a path," meaning that it leads to the Fire. Zina is among the major sins (al-kaba'ir), and there is no disagreement about it or about its ugliness, especially with the wife of a neighbour. It also results in the adoption of another man's child and treating him as one's son, and in other matters of inheritance, and in the corruption of lineages through the mixing of waters (of semen).

In the Sahih it is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) was brought, [[The phrase "atā bi-imra'a" means that he passed by a woman during some of his journeys. "Al-muhijj" (with a damma on the mim, a kasra on the jim, and an unpointed ha') is an adjective for a woman, meaning a pregnant woman whose delivery is near. His words "and said: perhaps ..." etc. contain an ellipsis; the intended sense is: he asked about her, and they said: she is the slave-woman of so-and-so, that is, his captive. The meaning of "yulimma biha" is that he has intercourse with her. She was a pregnant captive, and it is not permissible to have intercourse with her until she gives birth. His words "how can he inherit him ... etc." mean: her delivery may be delayed by six months, so that it is possible the child is from this captor, and it is also possible that he was from someone before him. If the child is from the captor, he is his son and they inherit from each other. If the child is not from the captor, then neither he nor the captor inherit from each other, since there is no kinship, but he may use him as his property, because he is his slave. The meaning of the hadith is that he may claim him and make him his son and let him inherit with him, though it is not permissible for him to make him an heir because he is not from him, and it is not permissible to make him an heir and to compete with the other heirs. He may also employ him as a slave and make him a possession he owns, although it is not permissible for him to do that because the child may be his. If she gives birth within a period in which the child could belong to either of them, he must refrain from having intercourse with her out of fear of this prohibited outcome.

(See Sharh al-Nawawi ala Sahih Muslim, the Book of Marriage, chapter: the prohibition of having intercourse with a pregnant captive.)]] to a woman who was pregnant and near delivery at the door of a tent, and he said: "Perhaps he wants to have intercourse with her." They said: "Yes." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I was about to curse him with a curse that would enter with him into his grave. How can he make him an heir when it is not lawful for him? How can they make him a servant when it is not lawful for them?"

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 17, verse 33:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right﴾. The discussion of this has already passed in Surat al-An'am [[see vol. 7, p. 130.]].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have certainly given his heir (wali) authority, but let him not commit excess in killing; indeed, he is supported﴾. In it are three issues.

**The first:** His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿whoever is killed wrongfully﴾, meaning without a cause that makes killing obligatory.

(﴿We have certainly given his heir﴾), that is, to the one entitled to his blood. Khuwayz said: the *wali* must be male, because He singled him out for the guardianship (wilaya) with the masculine form. Isma'il ibn Ishaq mentioned, regarding His saying ﴿his heir﴾, what indicates that a woman is excluded from the general meaning of the word *wali*. Therefore, women have no right in retaliation (qisas) by this verse, and they have no standing and no right to carry it out. The opponent said: the intended meaning of *wali* here is the heir. Allah has said: ﴿And the believing men and believing women are allies (awliya') of one another﴾ [[see vol. 8, p. 202, p. 55, and p. 58.]], and He said: ﴿And those who believed but did not emigrate, you have no guardianship (wilaya) over them at all﴾ [[see vol. 8, p. 202, p. 55, and p. 58.]], and He said: ﴿And those of blood relationship are more entitled to one another in the Book of Allah﴾. This implies establishing retaliation for all the heirs. As for what they mentioned, that the word *wali* in its outward form is masculine and singular, as is what has the sense of a genus in which masculine and feminine are equal, its full treatment is in the books of disputation (khilaf).

(*Sultanan*, authority): that is, an empowerment. If he wishes, he may kill; if he wishes, he may pardon; and if he wishes, he may take the blood money (diyya). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and by al-Dahhak, Ashhab, and al-Shafi'i. Ibn Wahb said: Malik said, "*Sultan* is the command of Allah." Ibn 'Abbas said: "*Sultan* is the proof (hujja)." It has also been said: "*Sultan* is his pursuit of the matter until it is delivered to him." Ibn al-'Arabi said: these sayings are close in meaning, and the clearest of them [[in manuscript J: "the most apparent of them."]] is the saying of Malik, that it is the command of Allah. Then, the command of Allah, mighty and majestic, was not stated explicitly, so the scholars differed about it. Ibn al-Qasim said, on the authority of Malik and Abu Hanifa: it is killing specifically. Ashhab said: it is the choice, as we mentioned just above, and al-Shafi'i held the same. This meaning has already passed in Surat al-Baqara [[see vol. 2, p. 244 and following.]].

**The second:** His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿let him not commit excess in killing﴾. Regarding it there are three opinions: (1) he should not kill other than the killer; this was said by al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, Mujahid, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. (2) He should not kill two people in place of his wali, as the Arabs used to do. (3) He should not mutilate the killer; this was said by Talq ibn Habib. All of these are intended, because each is excess, which is forbidden. The matter has been fully treated in Surat al-Baqara [[see vol. 2, p. 244 and following.]].

The majority read ﴿yusrif﴾ with a *ya'*, referring to the *wali*. Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read ﴿tusrif﴾ with a *ta'* on top, and this is the recitation of Hudhayfa. Al-'Ala' ibn 'Abd al-Karim related from Mujahid that he said: it refers to the first killer. Our meaning is: "So do not commit excess, O killer." Al-Tabari said: it is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to the imams after him, meaning: do not kill other than the killer. In the codex of Ubayy, it reads: "So do not commit excess in killing."

**The third:** His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿indeed, he is supported﴾, that is, assisted, meaning the *wali*. If it is said: how many a *wali* is forsaken and does not reach his right? We say: the support may come through the manifestation of proof at one time, through its execution at another, and through both together at a third; whichever of these occurs is a victory from Allah, glorified and exalted. Ibn Kathir related from Mujahid that he said: the one who was killed was supported. Al-Nahhas said: the meaning of His saying is that Allah gave him victory through his *wali*. It was related that in the recitation of Ubayy it reads: "So do not commit excess in killing; indeed, the *wali* of the one killed was supported." Al-Nahhas said: the reading with *ya'* is clear, and it refers to the *wali*, because it is said "he does not commit excess" only if he has the right to kill, and this applies to the *wali*. It is also permissible with *ta'*, and it refers to the *wali* as well, except that it then requires a shift of address. Al-Dahhak said: this is the first thing revealed of the Qur'an concerning killing, and it is Meccan [[what is related from al-Hasan is that it is Medinan, as in al-Alusi. The latter is the more apparent, because it concerns rulings.]].

There are two issues concerning this verse.

The first is His saying, ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best manner, until he reaches his maturity﴾. The discussion of it has already passed in (Surat) al-An'am [[see vol. 7, p. 130.]].

The second is His saying, ﴿And fulfil the covenant﴾. The discussion of it has already passed in more than one place [[see vol. 1, p. 332.]]. Al-Zajjaj said: Everything that God has commanded and forbidden is part of the covenant.

"Indeed, the covenant was something to be asked about" (17:34), meaning about it, and the preposition was omitted, as in His saying, "and they do what they are commanded" [[see vol. 18, p. 196.]], meaning, what they are commanded to do. It was also said: the covenant is questioned in order to rebuke the one who breaks it, so it is said to him, "Why did you break it?" just as the buried infant girl is questioned in order to rebuke the one who buried her [[see vol. 19, p. 230 onward.]].

**First issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And give full measure when you measure﴾. This has already been discussed in Surat al-An'am [see vol. 7, p. 130]. This verse implies that the measuring is the responsibility of the seller, and this was already covered in Surat Yusuf, so there is no point in repeating it [see vol. 9, p. 254]. Al-Qistas (with a ḍamma or a kasra on the qaf) means the balance in the language of the Romans, so said Ibn 'Uzayr. Al-Zajjaj said: al-qistas is the balance, whether small or large. Mujahid said: al-qistas is justice, and he used to say: it is a Roman word, as if the people were told: weigh with equity in your weighing. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr read "al-qustas" with a ḍamma on the qaf. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read "bil-qistas" with a kasra on the qaf, and both are dialectal variants.

**Second issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is better and more excellent in outcome﴾. That is, fulfilling the measure and upholding the weight is better with your Lord and more blessed.

(And more excellent in outcome) means in its consequence. Al-Hasan said: It was related to us that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No man has the power to commit a sin and then abandons it, having nothing that drives him except fear of Allah, the Exalted, except that Allah replaces it for him in the worldly life, before the Hereafter, with something better than that."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 36:

There are six issues in this.

The first: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And do not pursue (wa-la taqfu)﴾, that is, do not follow what you have no knowledge of and what does not concern you. Qatadah said: Do not say "I saw" when you did not see, or "I heard" when you did not hear, or "I know" when you did not know. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said the same. Mujahid said: Do not denounce anyone with what you have no knowledge of. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, also said this. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah said: It is false testimony (shahadat al-zur). Al-Qutabi said: The meaning is, do not follow conjecture and suppositions. All of these are close in meaning. The root of qafw is slander and hurling baseless accusations, and from it is the saying of the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace: "We are the sons of al-Nadr ibn Kinanah; we do not slander our mother nor disown our father," meaning, we do not revile our mother. Al-Kumayt said:

"I do not wrong the innocent without fault,
nor do I slander the chaste women, even if they slander me."

It is said: qafawtuhu aqfuhu, and qaftuhu aqufuhu, and qaffaytuhu, when one follows his trace. From it comes al-qafah (the trackers), because they follow traces; and qafiyat kull shay' (the rhyme of everything) is its last part, and from it qafiyat al-shi'r (the rhyme of a poem), because it follows the verse. From it also is the name of the Prophet, peace be upon him, al-Muqaffi (the Final), because he came last of the prophets. From it also is al-qa'if, who follows the traces of resemblance. It is said: qaffa al-qa'if yaqufu when he does this. And you say: faqawtu li-l-athar, with the fa' placed before the qaf. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This may be one of the Arabs' playful alterations in some words, as they said: ra'amli for la'amri (by my life). Al-Tabari related from a group that they said: qafa and qaf, like 'ata and 'at. Mundhir ibn Sa'id held that qafa and qaf are like jabadha and jadhaba. In sum, this verse forbids false speech and slander, and whatever resembles them of lying and vile words.

Some reciters, as al-Kisa'i related, read "taqfu" with a damma on the qaf and a sukun on the fa'. Al-Jarrah read "wal-fu'ad" (wal-fa'ad) with a fatha on the fa', and this is a dialect of some people, though Abu Hatim and others rejected it. [[In the irregular readings: al-fu'ad with a fatha on the fa' and waw. Al-Jarrah was the judge of Basra.]]

The second: Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: This verse includes the ruling on qafah (tracking by resemblance), because when He said, "And do not pursue what you have no knowledge of," this indicates the permissibility of what we have knowledge of. So whatever a person knows or whose probability predominates in his assessment is permissible to rule by. On this basis we have argued for establishing the lot (qur'ah) and estimation (kharsh), because it is a form of predominant assumption, and it is sometimes called knowledge by extension. The qa'if attributes the child to his father through the resemblance between them, just as the jurist attaches the branch to the root through resemblance. In the Sahih, from 'A'ishah: The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, entered upon me joyful, the lines of his face shining, and said: "Did you not see that Mujazziz looked at Zayd ibn Harithah and Usamah ibn Zayd, and they were covered with a cloak with their heads covered and their feet exposed, and he said: 'Indeed some of these feet are from others'?" In the hadith of Yunus ibn Yazid: "And Mujazziz was a qa'if."

The third: The Imam Abu 'Abdullah al-Mazari said: The Jahiliyyah used to cast doubt on the lineage of Usamah because he was very black, while his father Zayd was white of complexion. Thus Abu Dawud related it from Ahmad ibn Salih. Al-Qadi 'Iyad said: Other than Ahmad said that Zayd was fair-complexioned and Usamah was very dark-skinned. Zayd ibn Harithah was a pure Arab from Kalb, who was taken captive, as will come in Surat al-Ahzab, Allah willing. [[See vol. 14, p. 118.]]

The fourth: The majority of scholars used as evidence for resorting to the qafah in disputes over a child the Prophet's joy at the words of this qa'if, and the Prophet, peace be upon him, was not one who rejoices in falsehood or is pleased by it. Abu Hanifah, Ishaq, al-Thawri and their companions did not adopt this, holding that the Prophet, peace be upon him, disregarded resemblance in the hadith of li'an, as will come in Surat al-Nur, Allah willing. [[See vol. 12, p. 191.]]

The fifth: Those who adopted the statements of the qafah differed over whether this applies to the children of free women and slave women, or is restricted to the children of slave women, on two views. The first is the view of al-Shafi'i and Malik, may Allah be pleased with them, in the narration of Ibn Wahb from him, while the well-known position of his school restricts it to the child of a slave woman. The sound view is what Ibn Wahb related from him. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Because the hadith which is the basis in this matter concerned free persons, for Usamah and his father were both free. How then can the cause that prompted the evidence for the ruling be disregarded, when it is the very motive behind it? This is not permissible according to the usulis. Likewise these scholars differed over whether the statement of one qafah suffices or two are required, since it is testimony. Ibn al-Qasim held the first, and it is the apparent meaning of the report, indeed its explicit text. Malik and al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with them, held the second.

The sixth: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed the hearing, the sight and the heart, all of those will be questioned about it﴾, that is, each of them will be asked about what it acquired. The heart is asked about what it contemplated and believed, and the hearing and sight about what they perceived and heard. It was also said: The meaning is that Allah, glorified and exalted, will question the human being about what his hearing, sight and heart encompassed. A parallel is the Prophet's saying, peace be upon him: "Each of you is a shepherd and each of you is responsible for his flock." So the human being is a shepherd over his limbs, as if He said, "Of all these the human being will be questioned," so it is an elision of a modifier (hadhf mudaf). The first meaning is more eloquent in argument, for his denial will come from his own limbs, and that is the utmost disgrace, as He said: "Today We seal their mouths, and their hands speak to Us, and their feet bear witness to what they used to earn" and His saying: "Their hearing and their sights and their skins will bear witness against them for what they used to do." He described the hearing, sight and heart with "those" (ulaika) because they are faculties that perceive, and in this verse He made them questioned, so they are in the state of one who reasons, and therefore He referred to them with ulaika. Sibawayh, may Allah have mercy on him, said regarding His saying, "I saw them prostrating to me": He said "ra'aytuhum" about the stars because when He attributed prostration to them, which is an act of the rational, He referred to them with the pronoun of the rational. This has already been mentioned. Al-Zajjaj related that the Arabs refer to what is rational and what is not rational with ulaika, and he and al-Tabari recited:

"Blame the dwellings after the abode of al-Liwa,
and life after those days..."

This is a matter to be pondered. As for the line, the narration in it is "al-aqwam" (the peoples), and Allah knows best.

This is the commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surahs 17:37–38:

There are five issues (masa'il) in this.

**The first issue:** God's words, ﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾. This is a prohibition of arrogance and a command to humility. *Al-maraḥ* means intense joy. It is also said to mean arrogance in walking, and to mean a person exceeding his proper station. Qatada said it is conceit in walking. It is also said to mean insolence and exultant pride (*al-bataru wal-ashar*), and it is said to mean vigor (*al-nashat*). These meanings are close to one another, but they divide into two kinds: one blameworthy and the other praiseworthy. Arrogance, insolence, conceit, and a person exceeding his station are blameworthy, while joy and vigor are praiseworthy. God has described Himself with one of the two, as in the sound hadith: "God is more delighted (*la-Allahu afraḥu*) with the repentance of a servant than a man ..." and so on. Laziness (*al-kasal*) is blameworthy in the Sharia, and vigor is its opposite. Arrogance and what is similar to it may also be praiseworthy, namely against the enemies of God and against wrongdoers. Abu Hatim ibn Hibban related with his chain of narration from Ibn Jabir ibn Atik, from his father, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "Among jealousy (*al-ghayra*) is that which God, Mighty and Majestic, hates, and among it is that which God, Mighty and Majestic, loves. Among arrogance (*al-khuyala'*) is that which God loves, and among it is that which God hates. As for the jealousy that God loves, it is jealousy in religion. The jealousy that God hates is jealousy in other than religion. The arrogance that God loves is a man's pride in himself at the time of fighting and at the time of giving charity. The arrogance that God hates is arrogance in falsehood." Abu Dawud recorded it in his *Musannaf* and others.

They also recited:

*Do not walk upon the earth except in humility,*
*for beneath it are people who were higher than you in aspiration.*

*Even if you are in might, protection, and power,*
*how many people have died who were stronger than you in their defenses.*

**The second issue:** A person's devoting himself to hunting and the like out of haughtiness, without any need for it, falls under this verse. It also involves torturing animals and making them run for no purpose. As for a man who rests on a rare day, or for an hour of his day, and in that time relaxes and takes his ease so that he may be strengthened thereby for a work of righteousness, such as studying knowledge or prayer, he is not included in this verse.

**God's words, ﴿maraḥan﴾:** The reading of the majority is with a *fatḥa* on the *rā'*. The reading of a group, as transmitted by Ya'qub, is with a *kasra* on the *rā'*, in the form of the active participle (*ism al-fa'il*). The first is more eloquent, for your saying *jā'a Zayd rakḍan* ("Zayd came running") is more eloquent than your saying *jā'a Zayd rākiḍan* ("Zayd came running," as a participle). Likewise your saying *maraḥan*. The verbal noun (*al-maṣdar*) *al-maraḥ* is more eloquent than saying *marihan*.

**The third issue:** God's words, ﴿Indeed, you will never tear through the earth﴾, meaning you will never penetrate its depths so as to know what is in it, ﴿and you will never reach the mountains in height﴾, meaning you will never equal the mountains in your height or in your exaltation. It is said: *kharaqa al-thawb*, meaning he tore the garment, and *kharaqa al-arḍ*, meaning he cut across the earth. *Al-khark* is the wide expanse of the earth. That is, you will never tear through the earth by your pride and your walking upon it.

﴿And you will never reach the mountains in height﴾ by your greatness. That is, your power does not reach this level. Rather, you are a humble servant, encompassed from beneath you and from above you. The one who is encompassed is confined and weak, and arrogance does not befit you.

The meaning of "tearing through the earth" here is piercing it, not crossing it by distance, and God knows best. Al-Azhari said: its meaning is that you will never cross it. Al-Nahhas said: this is clearer, because it is derived from *al-khark*, which is the wide desert. It is said: "So-and-so is more *akhraq* than so-and-so," meaning he travels more, and is more powerful and more protected.

It is related that Saba' subdued the earth with his armies, east and west, plain and mountain. He killed the nobles and took captives, and it is from him that Saba' (the place/people) is named. The creatures submitted to him. When he saw this, he withdrew from his companions for three days, then came out to them and said: "When I attained what no one else had attained, I saw that the beginning should be the thanking of these blessings. I found nothing more fitting for that than prostration to the sun when it rises." So they prostrated to it, and that was the first worship of the sun. This is the outcome of pride, arrogance, and exultance. We seek refuge with God from that.

**The fourth issue:** God's words, ﴿All of that, its evil is hateful in the sight of your Lord﴾. *Dhālika* is a reference to the whole of what has been mentioned before, of what He commanded and what He forbade. *Dhālika* may be used for the singular, the plural, the feminine, and the masculine.

ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza, al-Kisa'i, and Masruq read *sayyi'uhu* as an idafa of *sayyi'* to the pronoun. For this reason He says *makruhan* (hateful), which is put in the accusative as the predicate of *kāna*. *Al-sayyi'* is the hateful, which is what God, Mighty and Majestic, does not approve of and does not command. God, glorified and exalted, has mentioned in these verses, from His words "and your Lord has decreed" to His words "was its evil," things that are commanded and things that are forbidden. So He does not describe all of them as evil, lest what is commanded enter into what is forbidden. Abu ʿUbayd chose this reading. Also, in the reading of Ubayy, "all of that, its evils (*sayyi'atuhu*)" is found, and that can only be an idafa.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Abu ʿAmr read *sayyi'atan* with tanwin, meaning: everything that God and His Messenger forbade is an evil. On this view, the speech ends at His words "and better in interpretation." Then He says, "and do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge," and "and do not walk," then He says, "All of that was an evil," with tanwin.

It is also said that from His words "and do not kill your children" to this verse, all of it was evil, with no good in it. So they made *kull* encompass only what is forbidden, not other things. His words *makruhan* are not an adjective of *sayyi'atan*, but a substitute (*badal*) for it. The implied meaning is: it was an evil and it was hateful.

It has also been said that *makruhan* is a second predicate of *kāna*, with *kull* construed according to its wording, while *sayyi'atan* is construed according to the meaning across all of these things mentioned before.

Some said it is an adjective of *sayyi'atan*, because its feminine gender is not real, so it is permissible to describe it with a masculine word. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi weakened this and said: when a feminine is made masculine, it should properly be a masculine modifier. What is permitted is that the verb attributed to a feminine comes first while being in the form of what is attributed to a masculine. Do you not see the poet's words:

*No cloud has rained its rain,*
*and no earth has put forth its vegetation.*

This is considered repulsive by them. But if someone said *abqala ardun* ("the earth put forth vegetation"), it would not be ugly. Abu ʿAli said: but in His words *makruhan* it is permissible that it be a substitute for *sayyi'atan*, and it is permissible that it be a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun in *ʿinda rabbika*, with *ʿinda rabbika* in the position of a qualifier of *sayyi'atan*.

**The fifth issue:** The scholars have used this verse as evidence for the blameworthiness of dancing and indulging in it. Abu al-Wafa' Ibn ʿAqil said: The Qur'an has explicitly prohibited dancing when He said, "and do not walk upon the earth exultantly," and He censured the arrogant. Dancing is the extreme of exultance and insolence. Are we not those who analogized *nabidh* (a date drink) to wine because they agree in intoxication and exhilaration? Why then do we not analogize dancing, the rhythmic swaying of poetry along with it, and the lute, the flute, and the drum, because they are gathered together? How ugly it is for one with a beard! How much more so when he resembles a woman, dancing and clapping to the rhythm of melodies and rods, especially if there are the voices of women and beardless youths! Is it fitting for one who has before him death, questioning, resurrection, and the Sirat, while he is heading toward one of the two abodes, to shake himself with dancing like a beast of burden, and to clap like women? By God, I have seen in my life elders for whom not a tooth showed through smiling, let alone laughter, despite my constant company with them.

Abu al-Faraj Ibn al-Jawzi, may God have mercy on him, said: Some of the shaykhs related to me from Imam al-Ghazali, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "Dancing is foolishness between the shoulders, which does not go away except by playing." The fuller explanation of this subject will come, God willing, in the commentary on *al-Kahf* [the editor's note refers to p. 365 of this volume] and elsewhere [the editor's note refers to vol. 14, p. 51 onward].

﴿Indeed, you are saying a monstrous saying﴾, i.e., in its sinfulness before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 41:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly diversified﴾, meaning: We have made clear. And it was said: We have repeated.

(in this Qur'an) It was said: "fi" is superfluous, and the construction is: "And We have certainly diversified in this Qur'an", like: "and set right for me in my offspring [[See vol. 16, p. 195.]]", meaning: set right my offspring. And al-tasrif (diversification) is turning a thing from one direction to another. The intended meaning of this diversification is clarification and repetition. And it was said: variation, meaning We varied the admonitions so that they might remember, take heed, and be admonished. The reading of the majority is "sarrafna" with the doubled letter, indicating intensification wherever it occurs. Al-Hasan read it with the single letter. And His statement, "in this Qur'an", means the parables, lessons, wisdom, admonitions, rulings, and signs. Al-Tha'labi said: I heard Abu al-Qasim al-Husayn say in the presence of the Imam, Shaykh Abu al-Tayyib: His statement, exalted is He, "sarrafna" has two meanings. The first: He did not make it one single type, but rather promise and threat, decisive and ambiguous, prohibition and command, abrogating and abrogated, reports and parables, like the diversification of the winds: the east wind, the west wind, the south wind, and the north wind; and the diversification of verbs: the past, the future, the imperative, the prohibitive, the active and the passive, and the like. The second: it was not sent down all at once but in installments, like His statement, "and a Qur'an We have divided [[See p. 139 of this part.]]", and its meaning: We multiplied the sending of Jibril, peace be upon him, to you.

(so that they might remember) The reading of Yahya, al-A'mash, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i is "liyadhdhakaru" with a single letter, and likewise in al-Furqan: "And We have certainly diversified it among them so that they might remember [[See vol. 13, p. 57 and p. 294 onward.]]". The rest read it with the doubled letter. Abu 'Ubayd preferred this, because its meaning is "liyatadhakkaru" and "liyatta'izu" (so that they might reflect and take admonition). Al-Mahdawi said: whoever doubles "liyadhdhakaru" intends reflection, and so does whoever reads "liyadhdhakaru". Its parallel for the first is: "And We have certainly caused the word to reach them, that they might remember [[See vol. 13, p. 57 and p. 294 onward.]]", and for the second: "and remember what is in it [[See vol. 1, p. 436.]]".

(And it increases them only in aversion) That is, the diversification and the reminder.

(only in aversion) Meaning: distance from the truth and heedlessness toward reflection and consideration. This is because they believed about the Qur'an that it was a trick, sorcery, soothsaying, and poetry.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 42–43:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: If there were with Him other gods﴾. This is connected to His saying, the Exalted: "And do not set up with Allah another god," and it is a refutation of the worshippers of idols.

(as they say) Ibn Kathir and Hafs read "yaqulun" with the ya'. The rest read "taqulun" with the ta', as direct address.

(then they would have sought) meaning the gods.

(a way to the Owner of the Throne) Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: they would have sought with Allah contention and fighting, as the kings of the world do, some against others. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the meaning is that they would have sought a path to reach Him in order to remove His dominion, since they are His partners. Qatadah said: the meaning is that the gods would have sought a means of nearness to the Owner of the Throne, and would have desired closeness to Him, because they are below Him; and the people believed that the idols brought them near to Allah in nearness. So when they believe that the idols are in need of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, then it is established that they are not gods.

(Glory be to Him and exalted far above what they say, a great exaltation) He declared Himself free of, and sanctified and glorified Himself above, what is not fitting for Him. And tasbih (glorification) means tanzih (declaring Allah free of imperfection). It has been mentioned before [[see vol. 1, p. 276.]].

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 44:**

His statement, the Exalted: ﴿The seven heavens and the earth glorify Him, and whoever is in them﴾. He returned the pronoun for the heavens and the earth to the form used for rational beings (*man ya'qilu*), because He attributed to them an action of a rational being, which is glorification (*tasbih*, the glorifying of Allah). His words "and whoever is in them" mean the angels, humans, and jinn. Then He generalized to all things in His words: ﴿And there is not a thing but that it glorifies Him with His praise﴾.

Scholars differed over whether this generality is specified (*mukhassas*, restricted) or not. One group said: it is not specified, and what is meant is the glorification of indication (*tasbih al-dalalah*), since every created thing bears witness to itself that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is a Creator and All-Powerful. Another group said: this glorification is literal, and everything, in its generality, glorifies in a way that humans neither hear nor comprehend. If what the earlier scholars said were correct, namely that it is a trace of the craftsmanship and an indication, it would be an understandable matter, but the verse states that this glorification is not comprehended. They responded that the meaning of His words "you do not comprehend" refers to the disbelievers who turn away from reflection, so they do not grasp the wisdom of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, in things.

A group said: His words "a thing" are general, but their meaning is specific to every living thing and every sleeping thing, and this does not apply to inanimate objects. From this is the statement of Ikrimah: "The tree glorifies, and the pillar does not glorify." Yazid al-Raqashi said to al-Hasan, while they were eating and the tablecloth had been brought: "Does this tablecloth glorify, O Abu Sa'id?" He said: "It used to glorify once." He meant that the tree, in the time of its fruit and its freshness, used to glorify, but now it has become a greased tablecloth.

I say: this view may be supported from the Sunnah by what is established from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Prophet ﷺ passed by two graves and said: "Indeed, they are being punished, and they are not being punished for something great. As for one of them, he used to walk about with tale-bearing; and as for the other, he did not guard himself from urine." He said: Then he asked for a fresh palm frond, split it into two, and planted one piece on this grave and one piece on that. Then he said: "Perhaps it will lighten their punishment as long as they have not dried out." His statement, peace and blessings be upon him, "as long as they have not dried out," indicates that while they are fresh, they glorify, and when they dry out, they become inanimate.

And Allah knows best. In the Musnad of Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi: "A palm frond is placed on one of them, half, and on the other, half." And he said: "Perhaps it will ease their punishment as long as there remains something of their moistness." Our scholars said: From this is derived the planting of trees and the recitation of the Qur'an at graves. If they are lightened by trees, how much more by the recitation of a believing man of the Qur'an. We have explained this meaning fully in (the book *al-Tadhkirah*), and that the reward of what is gifted to the dead reaches them. Praise be to Allah for that. According to the second interpretation, this is not needed, since everything, including inanimate objects and others, glorifies.

I say: this interpretation and this view may be supported from the Book by His words, Glorified and Exalted: ﴿And mention Our servant Dawud, the possessor of strength; indeed, he was one who turned back in repentance. Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify [Allah] with him in the evening and at sunrise﴾ [see vol. 15, p. 158 onward], and His words: ﴿And indeed, among them is that which descends out of fear of Allah﴾ [see vol. 1, p. 462 onward], according to the view of Mujahid, and His words: ﴿And the mountains will collapse in ruin that they attribute to the Most Merciful a son﴾ [see vol. 11, p. 155 onward].

Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned in (*Daqa'iqihi*): Mis'ar informed us, from Abd Allah ibn Wasil, from Awf ibn Abd Allah, who said: Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Indeed, a mountain says to a mountain: 'O so-and-so, has someone remembering Allah, Mighty and Majestic, passed by you today?' If he says yes, he rejoices." Then Abd Allah recited: ﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son"﴾, the verse. He said: "Do you think they hear falsehood but do not hear good?"

In the same work, from Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "There is no morning or evening but that the parts of the earth call out to one another: 'O neighbor, has a servant passed by you today who prayed to Allah or mentioned Allah upon you?' Some say no, and some say yes. When one says yes, it sees for itself a merit over the others."

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "No jinn, no human, no tree, no stone, no clod, and nothing hears the voice of the muezzin but that it will bear witness for him on the Day of Resurrection." Ibn Majah related it in his Sunan, and Malik in his Muwatta, from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him.

Al-Bukhari related from Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "We used to hear the glorification of food while it was being eaten." In another narration from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "We used to eat with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ the food, and we were hearing its glorification."

In Sahih Muslim, from Jabir ibn Samurah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed, I know a stone in Makkah that used to greet me before I was sent as a prophet. Indeed, I know it even now." It was said: It is the Black Stone, and Allah knows best.

The reports on this meaning are numerous. We have mentioned a portion of them in (*al-Lam' al-Lu'lu'iyyah fi Sharh al-IshrinIyyat al-Nabawiyyah*) of al-Fadari, may Allah have mercy on him. The report of the trunk (of the palm tree) is also well known in this regard, and al-Bukhari related it in several places in his book. If this is established for a single inanimate object, it is permissible for all inanimate objects, and there is no impossibility in any of that. So everything glorifies, in its generality.

Likewise, al-Nakha'i and others said: It is general regarding what has a soul and what has no soul, even to the creaking of a door. They argued with the reports we have mentioned.

It was also said: The glorification of inanimate objects is that they call the one who looks at them to say: "Glory be to Allah!" because of their lack of perception. The poet said:

*They are struck with a glorification wherever they turn,*
*and they settle in the heart of the beholder with a trembling.*

That is, whoever sees them says: "Glory be to their Creator."

So the correct view is that all things glorify, based on the reports that indicate this. If that glorification were only glorification of indication, then there would be no specification for Dawud. Rather, that is glorification of speech, by the creation of life and making them speak the glorification, as we have mentioned. The Sunnah has explicitly stated what the apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates, namely the glorification of everything, so holding this view is preferable. And Allah knows best.

Al-Hasan, Abu Amr, Ya'qub, Hafs, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read ﴿*tafqahuna*﴾ with a *ta'* (you comprehend) because the subject is feminine. The rest read it with a *ya'* (they comprehend). Abu Ubayd preferred this, and said: because of the intervening element between the verb and the feminine marker.

﴿Indeed, He was Forbearing﴾: toward the sins of His servants in this world.

﴿Forgiving﴾: toward the believers in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 45:

On the authority of Asma' bint Abi Bakr (may Allah be pleased with them both), she said: When the surah "Tabbat yada Abi Lahab" (Surah al-Masad) was revealed [[See vol. 20, p. 234.]], al-'Awra' Umm Jamil bint Harb came forward, wailing, with a fihr in her hand [[al-Fihr (with a kasra): a stone the size of the palm. It is also said: a stone in general.]], and she was saying:

"We have disobeyed Mudhammam,
and we have rejected his command,
and we have spurned his religion."

[[This is what appears in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham. In the manuscripts of the original text it reads: "Mudhammaman ataynaa... wa dinahu qalaynaa" (We have come to Mudhammam... and we have hated his religion).]]

The Prophet (ﷺ) was sitting in the mosque, and with him was Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him). When Abu Bakr saw her, he said: "O Messenger of Allah, she has come, and I fear that she will see you!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, she will not see me." And he recited a Qur'an and sought refuge in it, as he had said. He recited: "And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a hidden barrier." She then stood before Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) and did not see the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and she said: "O Abu Bakr, I have been informed that your companion has satirised me!" He said: "No, by the Lord of this House, he has not satirised you." She said: She turned away, saying: "The Quraysh have known that I am the daughter of their chief."

Sa'id ibn Jubayr (may Allah be pleased with him) said: When "Tabbat yada Abi Lahab wa tabb" was revealed, the wife of Abu Lahab came to the Prophet (ﷺ), and with him was Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him). Abu Bakr said: "If only you would move away from her, so that she does not hear from you what would hurt you, for she is a vile woman." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, it will be made that a barrier stands between me and her." So she did not see him. She said to Abu Bakr: "O Abu Bakr, your companion has satirised us!" He said: "By Allah, he does not speak poetry, nor does he compose it." She said: "Indeed, you are one who confirms (him)," and she hurried back. Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "O Messenger of Allah, did she not see you?" He said: "No. An angel continued to stand between me and her, shielding me, until she left."

Ka'b (may Allah be pleased with him) said concerning this verse: The Prophet (ﷺ) used to conceal himself from the polytheists by three verses: the verse in al-Kahf, "Indeed, We have placed over their hearts coverings lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness" [[See vol. 11, p. 4 onward.]]; the verse in al-Nahl, "Those are the ones whom Allah has sealed upon their hearts and their hearing and their sight" [[See p. 191 of this part.]]; and the verse in al-Jathiyah [[In some copies: al-Shari'ah. It is one of the names of al-Jathiyah.]], "Have you seen one who takes his desire as his god, and Allah has led him astray knowingly, and has sealed upon his hearing and his heart, and placed upon his sight a covering?" [[See vol. 16, p. 166 onward.]] — the verse. So whenever the Prophet (ﷺ) recited these, he would conceal himself from the polytheists.

Ka'b (may Allah be pleased with him) said: I related these to a man from the people of Syria, and he went to the land of the Romans and remained there for a time. Then he left fleeing, and they went out in pursuit of him. He recited these verses, and they would come to be with him on his path without seeing him.

Al-Tha'labi [[In some copies: "al-Kalbi".]] said: This which they narrate from Ka'b, I related to a man from the people of al-Ray, and he was captured by the Daylam. He remained for a time, then left fleeing, and they went out in pursuit of him. He recited these verses until their garments were touching his garments, yet they did not see him.

I say: To this verse may be added the beginning of Surah Ya-Sin up to His words: "So they do not see." In the Sirah, concerning the Hijrah of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the staying of 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) in his bed, it is said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out, took a handful of dust in his hand, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, took their sight away from him, so they did not see him. He began scattering that dust over their heads while reciting these verses of Ya-Sin: "Ya-Sin. By the wise Qur'an, indeed you are among the messengers, upon a straight path, a revelation of the Mighty, the Merciful," up to His words: "And We have placed before them a barrier and behind them a barrier, and We have covered them, so they do not see." Until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) finished these verses, and there was not a man among them but that he had put dust upon his head. Then he departed to wherever he intended to go.

I say: There also happened to me in our land of al-Andalus, at the fortress of Manthur [[So it is in the originals.]] in the districts of Qurtubah, something similar to this. I had fled from the enemy and withdrawn to one side of it, and it was not long before two horsemen came out in pursuit of me while I was sitting in an open space of the land with nothing concealing me from them. I was reciting the beginning of Surah Ya-Sin and other parts of the Qur'an. They passed by me, then returned from where they had come, and one of them said to the other: "This is a dayba[[A French word, meaning: a jinn. It is likely so in Latin as well.]]," meaning a devil. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, blinded their sight so they did not see me, and all praise is due to Allah, abundant praise, for that.

It was also said: The hidden barrier is that Allah has sealed upon their hearts so that they do not understand it and do not perceive the wisdom in it; this was said by Qatadah. Al-Hasan said: That is, because of their turning away from your recitation and their heedlessness of you, they are like one between whom and you there is a barrier, in not seeing you, as if there were coverings upon their hearts.

It was also said: It was revealed concerning a people who used to harm the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he recited the Qur'an, namely Abu Jahl, Abu Sufyan, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Umm Jamil the wife of Abu Lahab, and Huwaytib. So Allah, glorified and exalted, placed a barrier between His Messenger (ﷺ) and their sight during the recitation of the Qur'an, and they would pass by him without seeing him. This was said by al-Zajjaj and others. This is the same meaning as the first opinion, and it is the more apparent in the verse, and Allah knows best.

As for His words "mastur" (screened), there are two views: The first is that the barrier is screened from you, so you do not see it. The second is that the barrier conceals from you what is behind it, and "mastur" here is in the sense of "satir" (concealing).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 46:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾. "Akinnah" (coverings) is the plural of "kinan," which is that which conceals a thing. This has already been discussed in (surah) al-An'am [[See vol. 6, p. 404.]]. "That they understand it" means lest they understand it, or out of aversion to their understanding it, that is, that they comprehend what it contains of commands, prohibitions, wisdom and meanings. This is a refutation of the Qadariyyah (the Qadariyyah, a early theological school that affirmed human free will in its strong form).

﴿And in their ears a deafness﴾, that is, deafness and heaviness. In the speech there is an implied elision, meaning: so that they do not hear it.

﴿And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an﴾, that is, when you say: there is no god but Allah, while you are reciting the Qur'an. Abu al-Jawza' Aws ibn Abd Allah said: Nothing drives the devils away from the heart more than the saying "There is no god but Allah." Then he recited: "And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an, they turn away on their backs in aversion." Ali ibn al-Husayn said: it is His saying "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful." This has already been discussed under the basmalah [[See vol. 1, p. 9 onward.]].

﴿They turn away on their backs in aversion﴾. It has been said: this refers to the polytheists. It has also been said: the devils. "Nufur" (aversion) is the plural of "nafir," like "shuhud" the plural of "shahid" and "qu'ud" the plural of "qa'id," and it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal). It may also be a verbal noun of a form other than the usual verbal noun, since "wallaw" (they turned away) carries the sense of "nafaru" (they fled).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 47:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We are best aware of what they listen to when they listen to you﴾. It has been said: the bāʾ in "bihi" (ﺑِﻪ) is extra (zāʾidah), meaning "they listen to it." They used to listen to the Qur'an from the Prophet (ﷺ), then they would turn away and say, "He is a sorcerer and one who is bewitched," as Allah, may He be exalted, reported about them. This was said by Qatadah and others.

﴿And when they hold secret counsel﴾, meaning they confer secretly about your affair. Qatadah said: Their secret counsel was their saying that he is a madman, that he is a sorcerer, that he brings the fables of the ancients, and other such things. It has also been said: it was revealed when ʿUtbah invited the nobles of Quraysh to a meal he had prepared for them. The Prophet (ﷺ) entered upon them, recited the Qur'an to them, and called them to Allah, and they conferred secretly, saying, "He is a sorcerer and a madman." It has also been said: the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded ʿAli to prepare a meal and invite to it the nobles of Quraysh among the polytheists. ʿAli did so, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered upon them, recited the Qur'an to them, and called them to monotheism, and said, "Say: There is no god but Allah, so that the Arabs will obey you and the non-Arabs will submit to you." But they refused. They used to listen to the Prophet (ﷺ) and say to one another in secret conference, "He is a sorcerer, and he is bewitched," and so the verse was revealed. Al-Zajjaj said: al-najwa (النَّجْوَى, secret counsel) is a noun used as a verbal noun, meaning "when they are possessors of secret counsel," i.e., private whispering.

﴿When the wrongdoers say﴾: Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, and those like them.

﴿You follow only a man bewitched﴾, meaning one who has been affected by magic, so that his affair has become confused for him. They say this in order to turn people away from him. Mujahid said: "Mashūrān" (مَسْحُوراً) means deceived, like His saying: ﴿Then how are you deluded?﴾ meaning, "From where are you being deceived?" [See vol. 12, p. 144.] Abu ʿUbaydah said: "Masḥūr" (مَسْحُوراً) means that he has a sahr, i.e., a windpipe (ri'ah), so he cannot do without food and drink; thus he is like you and not an angel. The Arabs say of a coward, "His sahr has swollen." Anyone among humans or others who eats or drinks is called masḥūr and musaḥḥar. Labid said:

"So if you ask us what we are about, indeed we are sparrows from this nourished humankind."

And Imru' al-Qays said:

"We see ourselves hastening toward an unseen matter ... and we are beguiled with food and drink."

That is, we are nourished and diverted. In a hadith from ʿAisha, may Allah be pleased with her, she said: "Who is this one who vies with me among the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) died between my sahr and my nahr?" [She means that he (ﷺ) died while leaning against her chest and what corresponds to her sahr, which is (the lung).]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 48:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Look how they coin comparisons for you﴾. He marvels at their conduct, how they say at one time "a sorcerer," at another time "a madman," and at another time "a poet."

(So they have strayed, and they cannot find a way.) That is, they have no stratagem for turning people away from you. It has also been said: they have strayed from the truth, so they do not find a way, that is, a way to guidance. And it has been said: an exit, because of the contradiction in their speech when they say "madman," "sorcerer," and "poet."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 49:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Shall we, when we are bones and crumbled dust, truly be raised up as a new creation?﴾ That is, they said while conferring secretly among themselves, when they heard the Qur'an and heard the mention of resurrection: "If he were not bewitched, he would not have said this." Ibn 'Abbas said: al-rufat (crumbled dust) is the powder (al-ghubar). Mujahid said: it is the dust (al-turab). Al-rufat is that which has broken and decayed from anything, like al-futat (crumbs), al-hutam (debris) and al-rudad (fragments). This is related from Abu 'Ubayda, al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Akhfash. One says from it: rufita al-shay' rafthan, meaning it was smashed, so it is marfut (smashed).

﴿Shall we truly be raised up as a new creation?﴾ "A 'innA" is an interrogative, and what is intended by it is denial and rejection. "Khalqan" is in the accusative case because it is a verbal noun (masdar), meaning a new resurrection (ba'than jadidan). And this was the utmost of their denial.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 50–51:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Be you stones or iron﴾, meaning: say to them, O Muhammad, "Be stones or iron, in hardness and strength," by way of disabling them. Al-Tabari said: That is, if you wonder at Allah's creating you with bones and flesh, then be you stones or iron, if you are able. ʿAli ibn ʿIsa said: Its meaning is that even if you were stones or iron, you could not escape Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, if He wished you, except that it came out in the form of a command, because that is more forceful in binding (the listener). It was also said: its meaning is that if you were stones or iron, He would restore you as He originated you, and cause you to die and then give you life. Mujahid said: the meaning is, "Be whatever you wish, for you will be brought back." al-Nahhas said: This is a good opinion, because they are not able to become stones; rather the meaning is that they had acknowledged their Creator but denied the resurrection, so it was said to them: consider that you be whatever you wish, yet if you were stones or iron you would be resurrected just as you were created the first time.

(Or a creation of what is greater in your breasts.) Mujahid said: it means the heavens, the earth and the mountains, because of their greatness in souls. This is also the meaning of Qatadah's saying: "Be whatever you wish, for Allah will cause you to die and then resurrect you." Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar, ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid also (in another report), ʿIkrimah, Abu Salih and al-Dahhak said: it means death, because there is nothing greater in the soul of the son of Adam than it. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"And death has a dreadful form in souls."

He means: even if you were created from stones or iron, or were death itself, I would cause you to die and resurrect you, because the power by which I originated you is the power by which I will return you. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿So they will say: Who will restore us? Say: He who originated you the first time.﴾ In a hadith it is related that death will be brought on the Day of Resurrection in the form of a white-flecked ram, and it will be slaughtered between Paradise and the Fire. It was also said: He meant by it the resurrection, because it was greater in their breasts; this was said by al-Kalbi. "Fatarakum" means "created you and brought you into being."

(So they will shake their heads at you) That is, they will move their heads in mockery. It is said: nagha his head (nagha, yanughu / yanghu, naghdan, nuguwdan), meaning it moved; and anghada his head, meaning he moved it, like one who is amazed at something. From this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So they will shake their heads at you﴾. The rajiz (poet) said:

"He shook his head toward me and raised it (to the sky)."

It is also said: naghada fulan his head, meaning he moved it, transitive and intransitive, related by al-Akhfash. It is said: "His tooth moved (naghadat sinnuh)," meaning it became loose and fell out. The rajiz said:

"And from old age their teeth became loose."

Another said:

"When she saw me, she made her head shake for me."

Another said:

"There is no water in the cistern if it does not rise, with a rope over the great pulley (al-mihal al-nughad)."

Al-Mihal and al-Mihalah: the great pulley by which camels are watered.

(And they say: When is it?) That is, the resurrection and the restoration, and this time.

(Say: It may be that it is near.) That is, it is near, because "ʿasa" and "ahabba" (in such contexts denote certainty). Its parallel is His saying: ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ [see vol. 14, p. 284], and ﴿The Hour is perhaps near﴾ [see vol. 16, p. 15]. And everything that is to come is near.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Be you stones or iron﴾, meaning: say to them, O Muhammad, "Be stones or iron, in hardness and strength," by way of disabling them.
