It has already been discussed in al-A'raf [[See vol. 7, p. 205.]] ..

This verse is said to be Medinan, as has been mentioned at the beginning of the surah. Ibn ‘Abbas said: The Jews envied the Prophet's (ﷺ) residence in Medina, so they said: "Prophets were only sent to the Levant (al-Sham). If you are a prophet, then go there, for if you go out to it we will believe you and have faith in you." This thought entered his heart because of his desire for their Islam, so he set out from Medina by one stage (marhalah), and Allah revealed this verse.

‘Abd al-Rahman ibn Ghanm said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) undertook the expedition of Tabuk, intending nothing but al-Sham. When he halted at Tabuk, there came down ﴿And indeed they almost provoked you to drive you out of the land﴾ after the surah had been completed, and he was ordered to return.

It is also said that it is Meccan. Mujahid and Qatadah said: It was revealed concerning the plan of the people of Mecca to expel him. Had they expelled him, they would not have been given respite. But Allah commanded him to emigrate (hijrah), and he went out. This is the more sound view, because the surah is Meccan, and because what precedes it is a report about the people of Mecca, and no mention of the Jews has occurred.

As for the phrase ﴿from the land﴾, it means the land of Mecca, like His saying: ﴿So I will not leave the land﴾ (12:80), meaning the land of Egypt. Its evidence is His saying: ﴿And how many a city was stronger in power than your city which has expelled you﴾ (47:13), meaning Mecca. The meaning is that its people planned to expel him, and for this reason He attributed the expulsion to it and said ﴿has expelled you﴾. [[In the original manuscripts: "إليهم" (to them), which is an error.]]

It is also said: All the disbelievers planned to drive him out of the land of the Arabs by uniting against him, but Allah prevented them. Had they driven him out of the land of the Arabs, they would not have been given respite, and this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And then they would not remain after you except a little﴾.

ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abi Rabah recited ﴿lā yulabbathūna﴾ with the bā' doubled, and ﴿khalfaka﴾ [after you]. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu Bakr and Abu ‘Amr [read it this way], and its meaning is "after you." Ibn ‘Amir, Hafs, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿khilafaka﴾, and Abu Hatim chose this reading, considering His saying: ﴿Those who stayed behind rejoiced in their seats, contrary to (khilaf) the Messenger of Allah﴾ (9:81). Its meaning is also "after you." The poet said:

"The abodes have been effaced after them (khilafahum), so it is as though
The palm-splitting women had spread mats of reed between them."

[Al-Mawardi reports: "spread by the Bawasit."] It is said: the woman splits the palm fronds (shatabat al-mar'ah al-jarid) when she splits them to make mats from them. Abu ‘Ubayd said: Then the splitter (al-shatibah) passes it on to the one who cleans it (al-munaqqiyah).

It is also said: ﴿khalfaka﴾ means "after you," and ﴿khilafaka﴾ means "your opposition (mukhalafatika)," as mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

As for ﴿illa qalilan﴾ (except a little), there are two views. The first: the period they remained after him is the interval between their expulsion of him and their being killed at the Battle of Badr. This is the view of those who said they were the Quraysh. The second: the interval between that and the killing of Banu Qurayzah and the exile of Banu al-Nadir. This is the view of those who said they were the Jews.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 77:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The way (sunnah) of those whom We sent before you of Our messengers﴾, meaning: they will be punished in the same way as (kasunnati) those whom We sent. It is put in the accusative (nussiba) by supposing an implied verb, "yu'adhdhabun" (they will be punished). Then, when the preposition was dropped, the verb took effect (governed the noun). This is what al-Farra' said. It was also said: it is in the accusative on the meaning of "sanannā sunnata man qad arsalnā" (We established the way of those whom We sent). It was also said: it is in the accusative by supposing the removal of the kaf (the particle "like"), the sense being: "they will not remain after you except a little, like the way of those whom We sent." So, according to this supposition, one does not pause at His saying "illa qalilan" (except a little). One pauses at the first and the second: "qablaka min rusulina" is a good place to pause (waqf hasan). (And you will not find any change in Our way.) That is, there is no failure in its promise.

**Question one:** Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun﴾. When He mentioned the schemes of the polytheists, He commanded His Prophet, peace be upon him, to be patient and to maintain the prayer, and in this there is a request for victory over the enemies. A similar verse is: "And We know that your breast is constrained by what they say. So exalt your Lord with praise and be among those who prostrate [[See p. 64 of this volume.]]." The meaning of establishing the prayer was discussed at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 164.]]. This verse, by the consensus of the exegetes (ijma', the scholarly consensus), refers to the obligatory prayers.

The scholars differed over the meaning of *duluk* (the decline of the sun) according to two opinions:

First, it is the sun's passing from the middle of the sky (zawal). This was said by ʿUmar, his son, Abu Hurayrah, Ibn ʿAbbas, and a group of others from among the scholars of the Successors and others.

Second, *duluk* is sunset (maghrib). This was said by ʿAli, Ibn Masʿud, and Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, and it is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Al-Mawardi said: Whoever takes *duluk* to mean the sun's setting does so because a person rubs his eyes with his palm to see it at the time of its setting. Whoever takes it to mean its passing from the middle of the sky does so because a person rubs his eyes due to the intensity of its rays.

Abu ʿUbayd said: Its *duluk* is its setting, and *dalakat Barah* means the sun, i.e., it set. Qutrub recited:

*"This is the standing place of the feet of Rabah... he kept lashing until Barah (the sun) set."*

*Barah* (with a fatha on the *ba'*) is on the pattern of *Hizam* and *Qatam*, and *Raqas* is a name among the names of the sun [[So in the originals. The correct reading is that these are women's names.]]. Al-Farra' narrated it with a kasra on the *ba'* [[That is, the *ba'* of the preposition.]], and it is the plural of *rahah*, which means the palm, i.e., it set while he was looking at it with his palm placed over his eyebrow. From the same usage is the verse of al-Ajjaj:

*"The sun had nearly become exhausted; I push it with the palm so that it slides down."*

Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: *al-Zuhlufah* is a smooth, sloping place, because people slide down on it. He said: *al-Zahlafah* is like *al-Dahraja* and *al-Daf'* (rolling or pushing); one says: "I made him slide, so he slid." It is also said: "The sun *dalakat*," meaning it set. Dhu al-Rummah said:

*"Lamps that are not led by the wandering ones, nor by the stars that set and vanish [al-dawalik]."*

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: *Duluk* in the language means inclination. Its beginning is the zawal and its end is the setting. From the time of the zawal until sunset it is called *duluk*, because the sun is in a state of inclination. So Allah, the Exalted, mentioned the prayers that occur during the *duluk* and at it, and this includes Zuhr, ʿAsr, and Maghrib, and it is possible that Maghrib is included in *ghasaq al-layl* (the darkness of the night). Some people held that the time of Zuhr extends from the zawal until sunset, because Allah, glory be to Him, linked its obligation to *duluk*, and all of this is *duluk*. This was said by al-Awzaʿi, and Abu Hanifah held it with some detail. Malik and al-Shafiʿi indicated it in a case of necessity.

**Second question:** Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿until the darkness of the night﴾. Malik narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "*Duluk* of the sun is its inclination, and *ghasaq* of the night is the gathering of the night and its darkness." Abu ʿUbaydah said: *al-Ghasaq* is the blackness of the night. Ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat said:

*"Indeed this night has become dark (ghasaqa), and I have complained of worry and sleeplessness."*

It has also been said: *ghasaq al-layl* is the disappearance of the twilight (shafaq). It has also been said: it is the approach of its darkness. Zuhayr said:

*"She kept giving generously with her hand while being careless, until the darkness and the ghasaq inclined."*

One says: *ghasaq al-layl, ghusuqan*. *Al-Ghasaq* is a noun with a fatha on the *sin*. The root of the word is from flowing; one says: "The eye *ghasaqat*" when it flows, and "The wound *ghasaq*, *ghasaqan*" when yellowish water flows from it. *Aghsaq al-muʾadhdhin* means he delayed the Maghrib until the darkness of the night. Al-Farra' related: *ghasaqa al-layl* and *aghsaqa*, *zalama* and *aẓlama*, *dajā* and *adjā*, *ghabasa* and *aghbasa*, *ghabasha* and *aghbasha*. Al-Rabiʿ ibn Khuthaym [[This is the vocalization of al-Taqrib. What is in al-Khulasah is with a fatha on the *mu'jamah* and the *muthallathah* with a sukun on the *tahtaniyyah* between them, and this is the well-known form.]] used to say to his muezzin on a cloudy day: "*Aghsiq, aghsiq!*" He meant: delay the Maghrib until the night becomes dark, which is its darkness.

**Third question:** The scholars differed over the end of the time of Maghrib. It was said that its time is a single time, and it has no time except when the sun is hidden. This is clear in the account of Jibril leading the prayer, for he prayed it on the two days at one time, which is the setting of the sun. This is the apparent position of Malik's school according to his companions. It is also one of al-Shafiʿi's two opinions and the well-known view from him, and al-Thawri also said it. Malik said in the *Muwatta'*: "When the twilight (shafaq) has disappeared, one has left the time of Maghrib and the time of ʿIsha has entered." Abu Hanifah and his companions, al-Hasan ibn Hayy, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, and Dawud said this, because the time from sunset until the twilight is all *ghasaq*. It is also based on the hadith of Abu Musa, in which the Prophet, peace be upon him, prayed Maghrib with the questioner on the second day, delaying it until the disappearance of the twilight. Muslim narrated it. They said: This is more preferable than the reports about Jibril leading the prayer, because it is later in Madinah, while Jibril's leading was in Makkah, and the later practice and command take precedence, because it abrogates what came before.

Ibn al-ʿArabi claimed that this position is the well-known view of Malik's school, and it is what he stated in his *Muwatta'*, which he read throughout his life and dictated during his lifetime. The key point in this is whether the rulings attached to names are linked to their beginnings, their ends, or the ruling is tied to all of them. The stronger view on reflection is that the ruling is tied to their beginnings, so that mentioning them is not idle; once it is tied to their beginnings, consideration of its extension to the whole until the end follows.

I say: The view of extension (*tawsi'ah*) is more likely correct. The Imam and memorizer Abu Muhammad ʿAbd al-Ghani ibn Saʿid narrated from the hadith of al-Ajlah ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Kindi, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ left Makkah close to the setting of the sun, and did not pray Maghrib until he reached Sarif, which is nine miles away."

As for the claim of abrogation (naskh), it is not clear, even if the chronology is known, because the reconciliation (jam') is possible. Our scholars said: The hadiths of Jibril are to be understood as indicating the preference (afdaliyyah) in the time of Maghrib, and for this reason the community agreed on hastening it and promptly performing it at the moment of sunset. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: "We do not know of any Muslim who delayed the establishment of Maghrib in a congregational mosque beyond the time of sunset." The hadiths of extension clarify the time of permissibility, so the contradiction is removed and reconciliation is valid. This is preferable to preponderance (tarjih), by the agreement of the scholars of legal theory (usuliyyun), because it gives effect to each of the two evidences, whereas the claim of abrogation or preponderance drops one of them. And Allah knows best.

**Fourth question:** Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿and the Qur'an of dawn﴾. *Qur'an* is in the accusative case for two reasons. First, it is in conjunction with *al-salat* (the prayer): the meaning is "and establish the Qur'an of dawn," i.e., the dawn prayer (salat al-subh). This was said by al-Farra'. The people of Basra said that it is in the accusative as an incitement (al-ighra'), meaning "then hold fast to the Qur'an of dawn." Al-Zajjaj said this. The prayer was described by the term "Qur'an" specifically and not by other prayers, because the Qur'an is the greatest part of it, since its recitation is long and recited aloud, as is well known and recorded. This is also from al-Zajjaj.

I say: The practice of Madinah has settled on recommending a lengthy recitation in Subh, to an extent that does not harm those behind (the imam), reciting in it the long surahs of the *mufassal*. Zuhr and Friday prayer come next in this respect. Recitation in Maghrib is shortened, and in ʿAsr and ʿIsha it is of medium length. It has been said that for ʿAsr it is shortened like Maghrib. As for what occurs in Sahih Muslim and elsewhere of lengthening in what has settled as shortened, or shortening in what has settled as lengthened, such as his recitation of the two *Mu'awwidhatayn* in Fajr, as narrated by al-Nasa'i, and his recitation of al-A'raf, al-Mursalat, and al-Tur in Maghrib, that is abandoned in practice. There is also his denunciation of Mu'adh for lengthening when he led his people in ʿIsha and began with Surat al-Baqarah; this was recorded in the Sahih. And there is his command to imams to be brief, when he said: "O people, among you are those who cause aversion. Whoever leads the people in prayer should be brief, for among them are the young, the old, the sick, the weak, and the one with need." And he said: "When one of you prays alone, let him make it as long as he wishes." All of this is recorded in the sound hadith collections.

**Fifth question:** Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿and the Qur'an of dawn﴾. This is evidence that there is no prayer except with recitation, because He called the prayer "Qur'an." The scholars differed over recitation in the prayer. Most of them held that the recitation of Umm al-Qur'an (al-Fatihah) is obligatory for the imam and the one praying alone in every rak'ah. This is the well-known view of Malik. He also held that it is obligatory in most of the prayer. This is the view of Ishaq. He also held that it is obligatory in one rak'ah only; this was said by al-Mughirah and Sahnun. He also held that recitation is not obligatory in any part of the prayer; this is the most unusual of the reports from him. It is also reported from Malik that it is obligatory in half the prayer, and al-Awza'i held this view. It is also reported from al-Awza'i and Ayyub that it is obligatory for the imam, the one praying alone, and the follower in all circumstances; this is one of al-Shafi'i's two views. This has been discussed fully under al-Fatihah [[See vol. 1, p. 117 onward.]].

**Sixth question:** Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿…was witnessed﴾. Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ, concerning His saying: "And the Qur'an of dawn; indeed the Qur'an of dawn was witnessed," that he said: "The angels of the night and the angels of the day witness it." This is a hadith that is good and sound (hasan sahih). It was also narrated by ʿAli ibn Mushir, from al-Aʿmash, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayrah and Abu Saʿid, from the Prophet ﷺ.

Al-Bukhari narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "The virtue of congregational prayer over the prayer of one person is twenty-five degrees, and the angels of the night and the angels of the day gather at the dawn prayer." Abu Hurayrah said: "Recite, if you wish: 'And the Qur'an of dawn; indeed the Qur'an of dawn was witnessed.'"

For this same meaning, Malik and al-Shafi'i said: performing Subh in the darkness (taghlis) is more excellent. Abu Hanifah said: The more excellent is to combine the darkness and the lightening (isfar); if one misses that, then isfar is preferable to taghlis. This contradicts what the Prophet, peace be upon him, used to do, namely his constant practice of taghlis. Also, it causes the loss of witnessing by the angels of the night. And Allah knows best.

**Seventh question:** Some scholars used the saying of the Prophet ﷺ, "The angels of the night and the angels of the day witness it," as evidence that the dawn prayer is neither of the night prayer nor of the day prayer. I say: According to this, the ʿAsr prayer would also be neither of the night prayer nor of the day prayer, for in the Sahih, from the Prophet ﷺ, peace be upon him, as narrated by Abu Hurayrah, he said: "Angels of the night and angels of the day succeed one another among you, and they gather at the ʿAsr prayer and the Fajr prayer," and the hadith continues. It is known that the ʿAsr prayer belongs to the day, so the dawn prayer would likewise belong to the night, and that is not the case. Rather, it belongs to the day, like ʿAsr, as shown by the evidence of fasting and faith. And this is clear.

There are six issues in it.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿min al-layl﴾ ("from the night"), where "min" is partitive (lil-tab'id). The "fa" in His saying "fatahajjad" (﴿fatahajjad﴾, "so perform tahajjud") coordinates with an implied element, meaning "so stand up and perform tahajjud."

"(bihi)" means "with it," i.e., with the Qur'an. Tahajjud (nocturnal prayer after sleep) derives from al-hujud, which is one of the words with opposite meanings (al-adhdad). It is said: hajada means "he slept," and hajada also means "he stayed awake," in opposite senses. The poet said:

"Has she not visited the people of Mina, the sleepers, / and would that her phantom would return to Mina."

Another said:

"Did she not visit us while the company was asleep, / so she spent the night giving with the pretexts of al-nawal [[al-'illah (here): that by which one makes an excuse, like al-ta'illah.]]."

He means "sleeping." Hajada and tahajjada have the same meaning. Hajjadtuhu means "I made him sleep," and hajjadtuhu also means "I woke him up." Tahajjud is becoming alert after a sleep, and it became a term for the prayer because one awakens for it. So tahajjud is rising from sleep to pray. This was said by al-Aswad, 'Alqamah, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Aswad, and others.

Isma'il ibn Ishaq al-Qadi related from the hadith of al-Hajjaj ibn 'Umar, a companion of the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Does one of you think, if he stands for the whole night, that he has performed tahajjud? Tahajjud is only prayer after a sleep, then prayer after a sleep, then prayer after a sleep." This was how the prayer of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was.

It is also said: al-hujud means sleep. It is said: "al-rajul tahajjada" when he stayed awake and cast off al-hujud, which is sleep. Whoever stands for prayer is called mutahajjid, because the mutahajjid is the one who casts off from himself the hujud, which is sleep. This verb follows the pattern of tahawwaba, tahar-raja, ta'athtama, tahannatha, taqadhdhara, and tanajjasa, when one removes those things from oneself. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿fazaltum tafakkahun﴾ ("you would have been left wondering"), meaning "you would regret," i.e., you cast off amusement from yourselves, and it is the relaxing and happiness of the souls. It is said: "rajul fakih" when he is very joyful and laughs. The meaning in the verse is: "And at a time of the night stay awake with it in prayer and recitation."

The second: His saying, ﴿nafilatan laka﴾ ("as an extra [prayer] for you"), i.e., as an honour for you, said by Muqatil. The scholars differed about singling out the Prophet (ﷺ) in mention without his community. It was said: night prayer was obligatory upon him, based on His saying ﴿nafilatan laka﴾, meaning an obligation additional to the obligation prescribed for the community. I say: this interpretation is far-fetched for two reasons. The first is calling an obligation "nafl" (supererogatory), which is metaphorical, not literal. The second is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Five prayers, which Allah has enjoined upon the servants," and His saying: ﴿hunna khamsun wa hunna khamsuna﴾ ("they are five, and they are fifty"), ﴿ma yubaddalu al-qawlu ladayya﴾ ("the word is not changed with Me"). This is explicit, so how can it be said that a prayer beyond five was made obligatory upon him? This is not valid. Although it has been related from him (peace be upon him): "Three are obligatory upon me and a voluntary matter for my community: night prayer, witr, and the siwak."

It was also said: night prayer was voluntary for him, and at the beginning it was obligatory upon everyone, then the obligation was abrogated (naskh), so night prayer became a voluntary act after an obligation, as 'A'ishah said. This will be explained in detail in the commentary on Surat al-Muzzammil, if Allah the Exalted wills. On this view, the command to perform the voluntary prayer is by way of recommendation, and the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), because he was forgiven. So when he performs what is not obligatory upon him, it is an increase in ranks. For the rest of the community, their voluntary acts are expiations and makeup for a flaw that occurs in the obligatory acts. This was said by Mujahid and others.

It was also said: it is a gift, because a servant does not attain a better gift of felicity than success in worship.

The third: His saying, ﴿'asa an yab'athaka rabbuka maqaman mahmudan﴾ ("It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station"). The scholars differed about al-maqam al-mahmud (the praiseworthy station) in four statements.

The first, which is the most authentic of them, is intercession (al-shafa'ah) for people on the Day of Resurrection. This was said by Huthayfah ibn al-Yaman. In Sahih al-Bukhari, from Ibn 'Umar, he said: "People will become kneeling groups [[juthan (plural of juthwah, like khutwah and khutha): meaning groups.]] on the Day of Resurrection, each community following its prophet, saying: 'O so-and-so, intercede,' until the intercession reaches the Prophet (ﷺ). That is the day on which Allah raises him to the praiseworthy station." In Sahih Muslim, from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) told us: 'When the Day of Resurrection comes, people will surge toward one another, and they will come to Adam and say to him: "Intercede for your descendants." He will say: "I am not fit for it, but go to Abraham, for he is the friend of Allah." They will come to Abraham, and he will say: "I am not fit for it, but go to Moses, for he is the one Allah spoke to." They will come to Moses, and he will say: "I am not fit for it, but go to Jesus, for he is the spirit of Allah and His word." They will come to Jesus, and he will say: "I am not fit for it, but go to Muhammad (ﷺ)." I will come, and I will say: "I am fit for it."'" He then mentioned the hadith. Al-Tirmidhi related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, concerning His saying ﴿'asa an yab'athaka rabbuka maqaman mahmudan﴾, when he was asked about it: "It is the intercession." He said: "This is a hasan sahih hadith."

Since it is established that the praiseworthy station is the matter of intercession, which the prophets (peace be upon them) push onward until the matter reaches our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), and he intercedes this intercession for the people of the place of gathering, so that their reckoning may be hastened and they may find rest from the terror of their standing, and this is specific to him (ﷺ). For this reason he said: "I am the master of the descendants of Adam, and I say so without boasting." Al-Naqqash said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has three intercessions: the general one, an intercession for entry into Paradise, and an intercession for the people of major sins. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The well-known view is that there are two only: the general one, and an intercession for bringing sinners out of the Fire. This second intercession is not one the prophets push onward; rather, the prophets intercede, and the scholars intercede.

Qadi Abu al-Fadl 'Iyad said: The intercessions of our Prophet (ﷺ) on the Day of Resurrection are five: the general one. The second is for admitting a people into Paradise without reckoning. The third is for a people among the monotheists of his community who deserve the Fire because of their sins; our Prophet (ﷺ) intercedes for them, and whomever Allah wills intercede, and they enter Paradise. This is the intercession that the innovators, the Khawarij and the Mu'tazilah, denied, rejecting it on their corrupt principles, which are the rational entitlement based on the doctrine of goodness and evil (al-tahsin wa al-taqbih). The fourth is for those among the sinners who entered the Fire, and they come out by the intercession of our Prophet (ﷺ), the other prophets, the angels, and their believing brothers. The fifth is the increase of ranks in Paradise for its people and their elevation. The Mu'tazilah do not deny this, nor do they deny the intercession of the first gathering.

Qadi 'Iyad said: It is known by widespread transmission that the righteous predecessors (al-salaf al-salih) asked for the intercession of the Prophet (ﷺ) and longed for it. On this basis, one should not pay attention to the statement of whoever says that it is disliked to ask Allah to grant you the intercession of the Prophet (ﷺ), because it is only for sinners. For it may be, as we have mentioned, for lightening the reckoning and increasing ranks. Furthermore, every intelligent person acknowledges shortcoming, needs pardon, does not rely on his deeds, and fears being among the ruined. This speaker must then not ask for forgiveness and mercy, since these are for the owners of sins as well, and all of this contradicts what is known of the supplications of the predecessors and successors.

Al-Bukhari related from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says, when he hears the call to prayer: 'O Allah, Lord of this perfect call and this established prayer, grant Muhammad (ﷺ) al-wasilah and al-fadilah, and raise him to the praiseworthy station that You have promised him,' my intercession will be lawful for him on the Day of Resurrection."

The second statement: the praiseworthy station is his being given the banner of praise (liwa' al-hamd) on the Day of Resurrection. I say: there is no contradiction between this statement and the first, for he will have the banner of praise in his hand and will intercede. Al-Tirmidhi related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I am the master of the descendants of Adam on the Day of Resurrection, and I say so without boasting. In my hand is the banner of praise, and I say so without boasting. There is no prophet, from Adam onward, but he is under my banner." This is the hadith.

The third statement: what al-Tabari related from a group, among them Mujahid, that they said: the praiseworthy station is that Allah, exalted is He, seats Muhammad (ﷺ) with Him on His throne (kursi). They related a hadith concerning this. Al-Tabari supported the permissibility of this with an excessive statement, which does not come out except through a subtle interpretation of its meaning, and it is far-fetched. Nevertheless, it is not rejected that it be transmitted, and knowledge interprets it. Al-Naqqash mentioned from Abu Dawud al-Sijistani that he said: Whoever denies this hadith, we regard him as suspect; the people of knowledge have always related this. Whoever denies its permissibility, let him do so with its interpretation.

Abu 'Umar said, and Mujahid said: Even if one of the imams interprets the Qur'an, he has two statements that are abandoned among the people of knowledge. One of them is this, and the second is in the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿wujuhun yawma'idhin nadiratun, ila rabbiha nazirah﴾ ("Faces that day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord"). He said: "It means awaiting the reward, not seeing." I say: this has been mentioned in the chapter on Ibn Shihab in the hadith of the revelation. It is also related from Mujahid in this verse that he said: "He will seat him upon the Throne ('arsh)." This is an interpretation that is not impossible, because Allah, exalted is He, existed before creating all things, with the Throne subsisting by its own essence. Then He created things without any need for them, but to manifest His power and wisdom, and so that His existence, His oneness, the perfection of His power, and His knowledge of all His perfectly wrought acts may be known, and He created for Himself a Throne upon which He established Himself as He willed, without being in contact with it, nor was the Throne a place for Him. It was said: He is now in the state in which He was before He created place and time. On this view, it is equal in permissibility whether Muhammad sits upon the Throne or upon the earth, for Allah's establishment upon the Throne does not mean movement, cessation, or change of states from standing and sitting, nor the states that occupy the Throne; rather, He is

...seated upon His Throne as He informed about Himself, without asking how. The seating of Muhammad upon the Throne does not make him possess the attribute of lordship (rububiyyah), nor does it remove him from the attribute of servanthood ('ubudiyyah). Rather, it is an elevation of his station and an honouring of him above His creation. As for His saying in the report, "with Him" (ma'ahu), it is in the same sense as His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 356.]], and "My Lord, build for me a house with You in Paradise" [[See vol. 8, p. 202.]], and ﴿Indeed, Allah is with the doers of good﴾ [[See vol. 13, p.]], and similar expressions. All of these refer to rank, standing, favour, and high degree, not to place.

The fourth: his bringing people out of the Fire through his intercession for whoever comes out, as related by Jabir ibn Abd Allah. Muslim recorded it. We have mentioned it in (Kitab al-Tadhkira), and Allah is the Granter of success.

The sixth: The scholars differed over whether standing in prayer at night is a cause for attaining the praised station (al-maqam al-mahmud), on two views. One: that the Creator, exalted is He, makes whatever of His actions He wills a cause for His bounty, without knowing the wisdom in it, or with knowing the wisdom in it. The second: that standing in prayer at night involves solitude with the Creator and private supplication away from people, so one is granted solitude with Him and intimate conversation with Him during that standing, and this is the praised station. People vary in it according to their degrees, and the most exalted of them in degree is Muhammad ﷺ, for he is given what no one else is given, and he intercedes in what no one else can intercede. The "'asa" (perhaps) from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is binding. "Maqaman" is in the accusative as an adverb of place, meaning "in a station" or "to a station." Al-Tabari mentioned from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The praised station is the station in which I will intercede for my community." So the maqam is the place where a person stands for great matters, like the standings before kings.

The meaning is: "Make my death a death of truthfulness, and raise me on the Day of Resurrection with a raising of truthfulness," so that it connects with His words ﴿Perhaps your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾. It is as if, when He promised him that, He commanded him to supplicate so that the promise would be fulfilled for him. It was also said: "Cause me to enter in what is commanded and bring me out of what is forbidden." It was also said: He taught him what to supplicate with in his prayer and otherwise, namely that He bring him out from among the polytheists and cause him to enter a place of security, so He brought him out of Makkah and led him to Madinah. Al-Tirmidhi narrated this meaning from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Prophet ﷺ was in Makkah, then he was commanded to emigrate, and so the following was revealed: ﴿And say, "My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance and cause me to exit a sound exit, and grant me from Yourself a supporting authority."﴾ He said: This is a hasan sahih hadith. Al-Dahhak said: It refers to his leaving Makkah and his entering Makkah safely on the Day of Conquest. Abu Sahl said: [It refers to] when he returned from Tabuk, after the hypocrites had said: ﴿Surely the more honorable will expel the more humble from it﴾. He meant: entering with honor and exiting with victory to Makkah. [See vol. 18, p. 129.]

It was also said: The meaning is: "Cause me to enter into the matter with which You have honored me, namely prophethood, with a sound entrance, and cause me to exit from it with a sound exit when You cause me to die." This was said by Mujahid. The words al-mudkhal and al-mukhraj (with a ḍammah on the mīm) carry the sense of al-idkhal (causing to enter) and al-ikhraj (causing to exit), as in His words ﴿Cause me to land at a blessed landing place﴾, meaning a landing in which I see nothing I dislike. This is the reading of the majority. Al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliyah and Nasr ibn 'Asim read mudkhal and mukhraj with a fatḥah on both mīms, with the sense of entering and exiting. The first is quadriliteral (rubā'ī) and this is triliteral (thulāthī). Ibn Abbas said: "Cause me to enter the grave with a sound entrance at death, and cause me to exit with a sound exit at resurrection."

It was also said: "Cause me to enter wherever You cause me to enter with truthfulness, and cause me to exit with truthfulness," that is, "Do not make me one who enters with one face and exits with another, for the one with two faces will not be honored before You."

It was also said: The verse is general, covering everything that is undertaken among matters, attempted among journeys and deeds, and awaited from the disposition of decrees in death and life. So it is a supplication, and its meaning is: "My Lord, set right my affairs in all matters."

As for His words ﴿and grant me from Yourself a supporting authority﴾, al-Sha'bi and 'Ikrimah said: That means a firm proof. Al-Hasan held that it is might, victory, and the manifestation of His religion over all religions. He said: So God promised him that He would surely strip the kingdom of Persia and Rome and others, and give it to him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 81:

There are three issues in this.

The first: al-Bukhari and al-Tirmidhi narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) entered Makkah in the year of the Conquest, and around the Ka'bah were three hundred and sixty idols (nusub). The Prophet (ﷺ) began to strike them with a mikhsarah [[What a person holds in his hand, grasping it as a stick, a cane, a whip, or a rod, and which he may lean upon.]] in his hand — and perhaps he said "with a stick" — and he would say: "Truth has come and falsehood has vanished; indeed falsehood was ever bound to vanish" (Jaa'a al-haqqu wa zahaqa al-batilu inna al-batila kana zahuqan). "Truth has come, and falsehood neither originates nor restores" (Jaa'a al-haqqu wa ma yubdi'u al-batilu wa ma yu'id). [[See vol. 14, p. 313.]] This is the wording of al-Tirmidhi, who said: this is a hasan sahih hadith. Likewise in the hadith of Muslim, "nusuban." In another narration, "sanaman" (an idol).

Our scholars said: they were of this number because they used to venerate one idol each day, and they would single out the greatest of them with two days. As for his words, "he began to strike them with a stick in his hand," it is said that they were fixed in place with lead, and whenever he struck one of them on its face, it would fall on its back, or if he struck it on its back, it would fall on its face. And he would say: "Truth has come and falsehood has vanished; indeed falsehood was ever bound to vanish." This was related by Abu 'Umar and al-Qadi 'Iyad. Al-Qushayri said: no idol remained except that it fell on its face, then he ordered them to be broken.

The second: In this verse there is evidence for breaking the idols of the polytheists and all idols when one has the upper hand over them. The breaking of every instrument of falsehood also serves the meaning, as does the breaking of whatever is fit for nothing but disobedience to God, such as the tanburs, the 'idan (lutes), and the mazamir (flutes) which have no purpose except diversion with them from the remembrance of God Most High. Ibn al-Mundhir said: included in the meaning of idols are images made of clay, wood, and the like, and everything people make that has no benefit except the forbidden diversion. It is not permitted to sell any part of these, except the idols made of gold, silver, iron, or lead, when they are altered from their form and become nuqar [[The nuqrah: an ingot.]] or pieces; then it is permissible to sell them and to buy with them. Al-Muhallab said: whatever is broken of the instruments of falsehood, and whose retention after breaking still has benefit, its owner has more right to it broken, unless the ruler sees fit to burn it with fire as a means of severity and punishment in property. The burning by Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, has already been mentioned [[What was mentioned earlier concerning Ibn 'Umar is that he spoiled the children's toys. See vol. 8, p. 340.]]. The Prophet (ﷺ) also intended to burn the houses of those who stayed away from the congregational prayer. This is a principle of punishment in property, together with his saying, peace be upon him, concerning the she-camel that was cursed by its owner: "Leave her, for she is cursed," so he removed her ownership from her, as a discipline for her owner and a punishment for her for what she had been cursed with. Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, also poured out milk that had been mixed with water, belonging to its owner.

The third: What we have mentioned of the interpretation of the verse is to be considered alongside his saying (ﷺ): "By Allah, Jesus son of Mary will surely descend as a just judge, and he will surely break the cross, kill the swine, abolish the jizyah, and the she-camels (al-qilas [[al-qilas (with a kasrah on the qaf, plural of al-qalus with a fathah), which is the young she-camel.]]) will be left so that none will be pursued for them," the hadith. It was narrated by the two Sahihs. From this category is the Prophet's (ﷺ) tearing down of the curtain that bore images, and that too is evidence for spoiling images and instruments of amusement, as we have mentioned. All of this necessitates prohibiting their making and requires that the owner change them. Indeed the owners of these images will be punished on the Day of Resurrection, and it will be said to them: "Bring to life what you have created," and that is enough for you! This meaning will come again in (Surah) al-Naml, [[See vol. 13, p. 221.]] God willing, Most High.

His words, Most High: "And say: Truth has come" — that is, Islam. It was also said: the Qur'an, said Mujahid. It was also said: jihad.

"And falsehood has vanished" — it was said: shirk. It was said: Satan, said by Mujahid. The correct view is to generalize the wording to the fullest possible extent, so the interpretation is: the Sharia has come with all that it encompasses. "Falsehood has vanished": falsehood has perished. From this is the zuhuq of the soul, which is its perishing. It is said: his soul zahaqat, yazhaqu, zuhuqan, and I zahhaqtuha (caused it to perish).

"Indeed falsehood was ever bound to vanish": that is, it has no permanence, whereas the truth is what endures.

There are seven issues concerning this verse.

The first concerns God's words, ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing﴾. The majority of readers recite ﴿nunazzilu﴾ with a *nun*. Mujahid recited ﴿yunzilu﴾ with a *ya'* and a light (*khafifa*) pronunciation [[So it is in the originals. Perhaps it should be: *nun* with light pronunciation.]], and al-Marwazi transmitted it from Hafs. The *min* in ﴿min al-Qur'an﴾ may indicate the starting point, and it may also be explanatory of the kind, as if He said: "We send down, of the Qur'an, that which is a healing." The report says: "Whoever does not seek healing through the Qur'an, may God not heal him." Some interpreters rejected that the *min* is partitive (*tab'id*), because this would imply that some of it contains no healing. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This does not follow. It is valid for the *min* to be partitive, in view of the fact that its sending down is itself partial. It is as if He said: 'We send down from the Qur'an a portion that is a healing, though all of it is healing.'"

The second issue concerns whether it is a healing, on which the scholars differ in two views. The first: it is a healing for the hearts, by removing ignorance from them, dispelling doubt, and lifting the veil from the heart's sickness of ignorance, so that it can grasp the miracles and the matters that point to God, may He be exalted. The second: it is a healing from apparent illnesses through *ruqya* (incantation, spiritual healing) and seeking refuge in God, and the like. The imams have reported, and the wording is that of al-Daraqutni, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent us on an expedition (*sariyya*) of thirty riders. He said: "We alighted near a people among the Arabs, and asked them to host us, but they refused. Then the chief of the tribe was stung, and they came to us and said: 'Is there anyone among you who can perform *ruqya* for the scorpion sting?'" In the version of Ibn Qatta: "Indeed the king is dying." He said: "I said: 'Yes, but I will not do it until you give us something.' They said: 'We will give you thirty sheep.' So I recited over him ﴿Al-hamdu lillahi rabbi al-'alamin﴾ seven times, and he was cured." In the version of Sulayman ibn Qatta from Abu Sa'id: "He came to himself and was healed. They sent us provisions and sent us sheep, and I and my companions ate the food, but they refused to eat from the sheep, until we came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and I informed him of the matter. He said: 'How do you know that it is a *ruqya*?' I said: 'O Messenger of God, something was cast into my heart.' He said: 'Eat, and feed us from the sheep.'" He recorded it in the *Kitab al-Sunan*.

Al-Daraqutni also recorded, in the *Kitab al-Madih* [[In some originals: "al-madhbah" (the slaughterhouse); we have not verified the correction.]], from the hadith of al-Sari ibn Yahya, who said: Al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman told me, from Layth ibn Abi Sulaym, from al-Hasan, from Abu Umama, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), that he said: "It benefits, by the permission of God, the Most High, from leprosy, madness, elephantiasis, abdominal disease, tuberculosis, fever, and the soul, [if] one writes with saffron or with *mishq* (that is, *al-maghra*, red ochre): 'I seek refuge in the perfect words of God and all His names, from the harm of every poisonous and general [affliction], and from the evil of the afflicting eye, and from the evil of an envier when he envies, and from Abu Farwa and what he begets.'" Thus he said, and he did not say "from the evil of Abu Qitra" [[Abu Qitra (with a *kasra* on the *qaf* and a silent *ta'*): a kunya of Iblis.]].

*Al-'ayn al-lamma* is the eye that afflicts with harm. It is said: "I seek refuge for him from every *hamma lamma*." As for his words, "I seek refuge for him from the calamities of *al-lamma*," [it is said that] it means the age (*al-dahr*), and it is also said that it means hardship. *Al-samma* means the specific (or poison). One says: "How are the *sammah* and the *ammah*?" And *al-sammah* is poison. [He said:] "And from Abu Farwa and what he begets."

He also said: "Thirty-three angels came to their Lord, mighty and majestic, and said: 'An ailment is in our land.' He said: 'Take some dust from your land and wipe your foreheads' [or he said: 'your foreheads'] [[In *j*: "bi-wasbikum," i.e., with your ailment. The word *ruqya* would then be in the accusative as an incitement.]], the *ruqya* of Muhammad (ﷺ). Whoever conceals it will never prosper, or who takes a reward (*safd*) for it [[*Al-safd*: gift.]]." Then one writes the Opening of the Book (*Fatiha*), four verses from the beginning of al-Baqara, the verse in which the turning of the winds is mentioned, the Verse of the Throne, the two verses after it, and the final verses of al-Baqara from the words ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ to the end; ten verses from the beginning of Al 'Imran and ten from its end; the first verse of al-Nisa'; the first verse of al-Ma'ida; the first verse of al-An'am; the first verse of al-A'raf; and the verse in al-A'raf, ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 218.]], until you complete the verse; and the verse in Yunus from the words ﴿Moses said: "What you have brought is magic. Indeed, Allah will expose it. Indeed, Allah does not reform the work of corrupters"﴾ [[See vol. 8, p. 367.]]; and the verse in Ta-Ha: ﴿And throw what is in your right hand; it will swallow what they have made. What they have made is only the trick of a magician, and the magician will not succeed wherever he comes﴾ [[See vol. 11, p. 221 onward.]]; and ten verses from the beginning of al-Saffat; and ﴿Say, He is Allah, One﴾; and the two protective surahs (*al-Mu'awwidhatayn*). They are written in a clean vessel, then washed three times with clean water. Then the afflicted person takes three handfuls of it, then performs ablution with it as he would for prayer, after first purifying himself before performing ablution with it. Then he pours it over his head, chest, and back, and does not use it for cleansing after excretion. Then he prays two *rak'as* and seeks healing from God, the Mighty and Majestic. He does this for three days, as much as one writes a book each day."

In another version: "And from the evil of Abu Qitra and what he begets." And he said: "Wipe your foreheads" [[In *j*: "bi-wasbikum."]], and he did not doubt.

Al-Bukhari reported from 'A'isha that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to blow upon himself with the two protective surahs during the illness in which he died. When he became heavy [with illness], I used to blow upon him with them and wipe his body with his own hand, seeking its blessing. I asked al-Zuhri how he would blow, and he said: "He would blow upon his hands, then wipe his face with them." [The questioner was 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, the narrator of the hadith.]

Malik reported from Ibn Shihab, from 'Urwa, from 'A'isha that the Messenger of God (ﷺ), whenever he was ill, would recite over himself the two protective surahs and spit or blow [*tafala aw nafatha*].

Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari said: The linguists say that the interpretation of *nafatha* is to blow [*nafakha*] a breath without saliva, while the meaning of *tafala* is to blow with saliva. The poet said:

*fa-in yabra' falam unfith 'alayhi
wa-in yafqid fa-haqqa lahu al-fuqud*

And Dhu al-Rumma said:

*wa-min jawfi ma'in 'armad al-hawli fawqahu
mata yahas minhu ma'ih al-qawmi yatfil*

[[*Al-'armad*: the green growth that rises on water, which is the *ramad*, the *'alaq* and the *tuhlub* (algae). *Al-ma'ih* (with a hamza): one who goes down into the well and fills the bucket. *Al-matih* (with a *ta'*): one who pulls up the bucket.]]

Al-Qurtubi's commentary on surah 17, verse 82 (part 2 of 2):

He intended to blow (on the wound) with saliva. The scholars' views on blowing (*nafth*) will come in the commentary on Surah al-Falaq, God willing. [[See vol. 20, p. 257 and following.]]

Third: Ibn Mas'ud narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) disliked incantations (*ruqa*) except those using the Mu'awwidhat. Al-Tabari said: This is a report whose kind may not be used as evidence in religion, since among its transmitters is someone who is not known. And if it were sound, it would either be an error or abrogated, because of his saying (peace be upon him) about al-Fatihah: "How do you know that it is an incantation?" If it is permissible to recite incantations with the two Mu'awwidhat, which are two surahs of the Qur'an, then reciting incantations with the rest of the Qur'an is equally permissible, since all of it is Qur'an.

It is also narrated from him (peace be upon him) that he said: "The healing of his community is in three: a verse from the Book of God, or a lick of honey, or a cut from a cupping-horn." [[We have not located this narration. The well-known version, as in al-Bukhari and others, is: "The healing of my community is in three: a cut of the cupping-horn, a drink of honey, or a branding with fire..."]]

Al-Ghanawi Raja' said: Whoever does not seek healing through the Qur'an, there is no healing for him.

Fourth: The scholars differed concerning the *nushrah* (a remedy by which a spell is undone). It consists of writing something of the names of God or of the Qur'an, then washing it with water, then wiping the sick person with it or giving it to him to drink. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib permitted it. He was asked: "A man has been bound (magically) from his wife; may he be released from it through *nushrah*?" He said: "There is no harm in it, and what benefits is not forbidden."

Mujahid did not approve of writing verses of the Qur'an, then washing them, and then giving them to drink to one afflicted with fright (*fazå'*).

'A'ishah used to recite the two Mu'awwidhat over a vessel of water, then order it to be poured over the sick person.

Al-Mazari Abu 'Abd Allah said: The *nushrah* is a well-known practice among the practitioners of incantation (*al-ta'zim*), and it was named so because it "unties" (*tanshuru*) the affliction from its owner, that is, it releases him.

Al-Hasan and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i prohibited it. Al-Nakha'i said: "I fear that it may bring a calamity upon him," and it seems he held that what is erased of the Qur'an is more likely to bring a calamity than to bring a cure.

Al-Hasan said: I asked Anas, and he said: "They mention from the Prophet (ﷺ) that these are from Satan."

Abu Dawud has narrated from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about the *nushrah*, and he said: "It is from the work of Satan."

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: These are weak reports, and they admit of several possible interpretations. It has been said that this is to be understood as referring to cases where the practice departs from what is in the Book of God and the Sunnah of His Messenger (peace be upon him), and from the known forms of medical treatment.

The *nushrah* belongs to the category of medicine, for it is the washing-water of something that has merit, and it is like the ablution water of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

He (ﷺ) also said: "There is no harm in incantations so long as they contain no shirk. Whoever among you is able to benefit his brother, let him do so."

I say: We have already mentioned the text concerning the *nushrah* as a hadith traced to the Prophet, and that it can only be (valid) if it is from the Book of God, so let one rely upon that.

Fifth: Malik said: There is no harm in hanging writings that contain the names of God, mighty and majestic, upon the necks of the sick, seeking blessing through them, so long as the one who hangs them does not intend by hanging them to ward off the evil eye. This is its meaning before any affliction from the evil eye has befallen. The consensus of the scholars on this view is that it is not permissible to hang any amulets upon healthy animals or human beings out of fear that the evil eye may strike. But whatever is hung after an affliction has come down, of the names of God and His Book, hoping for relief and recovery from God, the Exalted, is like the permitted incantation whose permissibility the Sunnah has established, for the evil eye and other ailments.

Abd Allah ibn 'Amr narrated: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "If any of you is frightened in his sleep, let him say: I seek refuge in the perfect words of God from His wrath, from the evil of His punishment, from the evil of the satans, and from their presence (with me)." 'Abd Allah used to teach it to his children, those who had reached discernment; and for those who had not, he would write it and hang it upon them.

If it is said: It has been narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever hangs something, he will be left to it." Ibn Mas'ud saw a tied *tamimah* (amulet) on the neck of his concubine, so he yanked it violently, cut it off, and said: "The family of Ibn Mas'ud are too self-sufficient for shirk." Then he said: "Indeed, amulets (*tama'im*), incantations (*ruqa*), and love charms (*tiwalah*) are shirk." It was asked: "What is the *tiwalah*?" He said: "That by which a woman makes herself beloved to her husband."

It is narrated from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir al-Juhani, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "Whoever hangs a *tamimah*, may God not perfect (His favour) for him; and whoever hangs a *wada'ah*, may God not grant him a heart at rest." Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad said: The *tamimah* is a necklace containing charms (*'uwadh*), and the *wada'ah* is a bead.

Abu 'Umar said: The *tamimah* in the speech of the Arabs is a necklace, and its meaning according to the scholars is what is hung on the necks as necklaces out of fear of the evil eye or other kinds of affliction. The meaning in the hadith is: whoever hangs (something) out of fear of what may or may not befall him before it befalls him, then God will not perfect his health and well-being. And whoever hangs a *wada'ah*, which is similar to it in meaning, then God will not grant him *wada'ah*, that is, God will not bless him in the well-being in which he is.

And God knows best.

All of this is a warning against what the people of the Jahiliyyah used to do, namely hanging amulets and necklaces, believing that they protect them and turn away affliction from them. Yet that turns away nothing except God, the Mighty and Majestic, who is the Giver of health and the One who tests, with no partner. So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) forbade them from what they used to do of that in their pre-Islamic ignorance.

It is narrated from 'A'ishah that she said: Whatever is hung after an affliction has come down is not of the amulets.

Some scholars disliked hanging the *tamimah* in every case, both before and after the affliction came. The first view is more sound in both transmission and reasoning, God willing.

As for what is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, it may be that what he disliked hanging was other than the Qur'an: things taken from the Iraqis and the soothsayers. For seeking healing through the Qur'an, whether hung or not, is not shirk. And as for his saying (peace be upon him): "Whoever hangs something, he will be left to it," then whoever hangs the Qur'an should rely upon God and not leave it to anyone else, for He, the Exalted, is the One sought and the One relied upon in seeking healing through the Qur'an.

Ibn al-Musayyib was asked about the *ta'widh* (charm): Is it to be hung? He said: If it is in a reed-case or a piece of cloth in which it is kept safe, there is no harm in it. This is on the basis that what is written is Qur'an.

It is narrated from al-Dahhak that he saw no harm in a man hanging something from the Book of God when he puts it aside during intercourse and when relieving himself.

Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn 'Ali permitted a *ta'widh* hung upon children. Ibn Sirin saw no harm in a person hanging something of the Qur'an.

Sixth: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And a mercy for the believers﴾, (the Qur'an is) the relief of distresses, the purification of faults, and the expiation of sins, together with the reward that He, may He be exalted, bestows for its recitation, as al-Tirmidhi narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites a letter from the Book of God, he will have a good deed for it, and the good deed is multiplied tenfold. I do not say that Alif-Lam-Mim is a letter, but Alif is a letter, Lam is a letter, and Mim is a letter." He said: This is a hadith that is good, sound, and gharib. It has already been mentioned earlier.

﴿And it does not increase the wrongdoers except in loss﴾, because of their denial. Qatadah said: No one sits with the Qur'an without rising from it with an increase or a decrease. Then he recited: ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers﴾, and so on. A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿Say: It is for those who believe a guidance and a healing; and as for those who do not believe, in their ears is deafness, and it is blindness for them﴾. [[See vol. 15, p. 368.]]

It has also been said: It is a healing in matters of obligations and rulings, because of the clarification it contains.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 83:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And when We bestow favour upon man, he turns away and distances himself, [turning] his side [from Us]﴾. That is: the characteristic of these people, whom the Qur'an increases only in loss, is turning away from reflecting upon the signs of Allah and being ungrateful for His blessings. It was also said: it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira.

The meaning of "nata bi-janibihi" (distanced himself by his side) is: he became arrogant and kept away. Na'a is a metathesized form of it (na'a from na'a, by inversion of its letters), and the meaning is: he went far from discharging the rights of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It is said: na'a al-shay' (the thing became distant), meaning it was far off. NA'ataHu and na'aytu 'anhu carry the same sense: I went far from it. Anya'tuhu fa-intaa (I made him distant, so he became distant). Tana'aw (they distanced themselves from one another) means they moved apart. Al-muntaa' means a far-off place. The poet al-Nabigha said:

"Indeed you are like the night which will overtake me, and even if I thought that the far place from you was wide..."

Ibn 'Amir, in the narration of Ibn Dhakwan, read "na'a" on the pattern of "ba'a", with the hamza placed after the letter 'ayn; this is by way of metathesis from "na'a", just as it is said "ra'a" and "ra'a" (the same verb with its letters transposed). It was also said that it derives from al-nawu, which means rising and standing up; and nawu is also used for falling and sitting, being one of the words with opposite meanings (al-adداd). "Wa-nai'a" was also read, with fatha on the nun and kasra on the hamza. The common reading is "na'a" on the pattern of "ra'a".

(And when evil touches him, he is despairing) That is: when hardship reaches him, whether from poverty, sickness or misfortune, he despairs and loses hope, because he does not trust in the bounty of Allah the Exalted.

**The Qur'an, 17:84:** "Say, 'Each acts according to his own manner (shakilatihi).'" Ibn 'Abbas said: its side (nahiyatuhu). Al-Dahhak said the same. Mujahid said: his nature (tabi'atuhu). Also from him: his disposition (hiddatuhu). Ibn Zayd said: according to his religion (dinihi). Al-Hasan and Qatada said: his intention (niyyatuhu). Muqatil said: his innate constitution (jibillatuhu). Al-Farra' said: according to his path and his way, which he has been formed upon (jubila 'alayhi). It has also been said: "Each acts according to what is most fitting (ashkal) to him and most correct in his belief." It has also been said that the word is derived from *shakl* (form), as in the saying: "You are not of my *shakl* nor my *shakila*." The poet said:

*Every person is like his deeds,*
*A man is worthy of what he does.*

So *shakl* means likeness, counterpart, and kind, as in His saying ﴿and other punishments of similar kind (min shaklihi azwaj)﴾ [see vol. 15, pp. 220 onward and p. 289]. *Al-shikl* (with a kasra on the shin) means outward form or appearance; one says: "a girl of good *shikl*." All these sayings are closely related. The meaning is that each person acts according to what accords with his origin and the character habits he has grown accustomed to. This is a censure of the disbeliever and a praise of the believer.

The verse and the one before it were revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, as mentioned by al-Mahdawi.

**﴿Your Lord knows best who is best guided in the way﴾**, that is, He knows the believer and the disbeliever and what will come from each of them. It has also been said: "more guided in the way" means quicker to accept. It has also been said: better in religion.

It is related that the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, discussed the Qur'an, and Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I have read the Qur'an from its beginning to its end, and I have not found in it a verse more hopeful and better than His saying, blessed and exalted: ﴿Say, each acts according to his manner﴾, for only disobedience is fitting for the servant, and only forgiveness is fitting for the Lord." 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I have read the Qur'an from its beginning to its end, and I have not seen in it a verse more hopeful and better than His saying, the Exalted: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Ha Mim. The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Mighty, the All-Knowing. Forgiver of sin and acceptor of repentance, severe in punishment, the Possessor of bounty﴾ [see vol. 15, pp. 220 onward and p. 289]," which puts the forgiveness of sins before the acceptance of repentance, and in this is a sign for the believers. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I have read the entire Qur'an from its beginning to its end, and I have not found a verse better and more hopeful than His saying: ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ [see p. 34 of this part]." 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I have read the Qur'an from its beginning to its end, and I have not found a verse better and more hopeful than His saying: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah; indeed Allah forgives all sins; indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ [see vol. 15, p. 267]."

I say: I have also read the Qur'an from its beginning to its end, and I have not found a verse better and more hopeful than His saying: ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing, those will have security, and they are the guided﴾ [see vol. 7, p. 9 onward].

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) who said: "While I was with the Prophet (ﷺ) in a field, and he was leaning on a palm-frond stalk, some Jews passed by. Some of them said to others: 'Ask him about the spirit (rūḥ).' He said: 'What prompted you to ask him about something whose consequences you fear, that he might confront you with something you dislike?' Some of them said: 'He will not confront you with anything you dislike.' They said: 'Ask him.' So they asked him about the spirit, and the Prophet (ﷺ) remained silent and gave them no answer. I knew then that he was receiving revelation, so I remained standing in my place. When the revelation descended, he said: ﴿They ask you about the spirit. Say: The spirit is of the command of my Lord, and you have been given of knowledge only a little.﴾" This is the wording of al-Bukhari. In Muslim's version it reads: "So the Prophet (ﷺ) fell silent," and in it: "and what they were given (mā ūtū)."

Scholars have differed about which spirit was being asked about. It has been said that it is Gabriel; this was the view of Qatadah, who added: "Ibn Abbas used to conceal it." It has also been said that it is Jesus, and that it is the Qur'an, as will be explained at the end of Surah al-Shura (see vol. 16, p. 54 onward). Ali ibn Abi Talib said: it is an angel among the angels who has seventy thousand faces, each face has seventy thousand tongues, each tongue has seventy thousand languages, and it glorifies Allah with all those languages; Allah creates from every act of glorification an angel who flies with the angels until the Day of Resurrection. Al-Tabari transmitted this. Ibn Atiyyah said: "I do not think this statement is authentically transmitted from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him."

I say: Al-Bayhaqi narrated with his chain (asnada): Abu Zakariyya informed us, from Abu Ishaq, who informed us from Abu al-Hasan al-Tara'ifi, who related to us from Uthman ibn Sa'id, who related to us from Abdullah ibn Salih, from Mu'awiyah ibn Salih, from Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿They ask you about the spirit﴾, that he said: "The spirit is an angel." And with the same chain, from Mu'awiyah ibn Salih: Abu Hirran (with a kasra on the ha) Yazid ibn Samura told me, from one who narrated to him, from Ali ibn Abi Talib, that he said regarding the words of the Exalted: ﴿They ask you about the spirit﴾, he said: "It is an angel among the angels, who has seventy thousand faces..." the hadith with its wording and meaning.

Ata narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The spirit is an angel who has eleven thousand wings and a thousand faces, glorifying Allah until the Day of Resurrection." This was mentioned by al-Nahhas. And from him (Ibn Abbas): "It is one of the hosts of Allah, who have hands and feet and eat food." This was mentioned by al-Ghaznawi. Al-Khattabi said: "Some of them said: it is an angel among the angels, with a description they have fixed from the greatness of its creation." Most of the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) went to the view that they asked him about the spirit by which the body has life. The people of reasoning among them said: they only asked about the manner and the reality of the spirit, and how it is located in the human body, how it is mixed with the body and how life connects to it; and this is something only Allah, Mighty and Majestic, knows. Abu Salih said: "The spirit is a creation like the creation of the children of Adam, but they are not children of Adam; they have hands and feet."

The sound position is to leave it undetermined (al-ibhām), because of His saying: ﴿Say: The spirit is of the command of my Lord﴾, which is evidence [i.e., He alone created the spirit and knows its secret, and no one among mankind can grasp it] of the creation of the spirit. That is, it is a great matter and a major affair from the command of Allah, left unspecified and its details left aside, so that a person may know with certainty his inability to know the reality of his own self, while knowing that it exists. If a person is this way regarding knowledge of his own self, then his inability to grasp the reality of the Truth is all the more certain. The wisdom in this is to show the intellect's incapacity to grasp the knowledge of a created thing close to it, as an indication that it is even more incapable of grasping its Creator.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And you have been given of knowledge only a little﴾. Scholars have differed about who is addressed by this. One group said: only the questioners. Others said: the intended meaning is the Jews as a whole. On this view it is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, "mā ūtū" (what they were given), and he narrated it from the Prophet (ﷺ). Another group said: the intended meaning is the whole world, and this is the sound view; the reading of the majority is "mā ūtītum" (what you were given).

The Jews had said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "How is it that we have been given only a little knowledge, when we have been given the Torah, which is wisdom, and whoever is given wisdom has been given abundant good?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) countered them with the knowledge of Allah, and they were defeated. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explicitly stated in some hadiths, by his saying "kullan" (all of them), that the intended meaning of "mā ūtītum" is the whole world. That is because the Jews said to him: "Do you mean us, or your people?" He said: "Kullan." In this sense the verse was revealed: ﴿And if whatever trees on the earth were pens...﴾ (see vol. 14, p. 76). Al-Tabari, may Allah have mercy on him, related this.

It has also been said that the ones asking about the spirit were the Quraysh. The Jews had said to them: "Ask him about the People of the Cave, about Dhu al-Qarnayn, and about the spirit. If he tells you about two of them and remains silent about one, then he is a prophet." So he informed them of the story of the People of the Cave and the story of Dhu al-Qarnayn, as will come. And regarding the spirit he said: ﴿Say: The spirit is of the command of my Lord﴾, meaning: of the matter that none knows but Allah. This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi and others among the exegetes, from Ibn Abbas.

﴿And if We willed, We could surely take away that which We have revealed to you﴾. He means the Qur'an, that is: just as We were able to send it down, We are able to remove it, until people forget it. This connects with His words: ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾. That is, even if I willed to take away that little, I would be able to do so.

﴿Then you would not find for yourself concerning it any advocate against Us﴾, that is, any helper who would restore it to you.

﴿Except as a mercy from your Lord﴾. He means: but the preservation of it is a mercy from your Lord. So this is an exception that is not part of the earlier statement. It was also said: ﴿except that your Lord shows you mercy, and so does not take it away﴾.

﴿Indeed, His bounty upon you has been great﴾, for He made you the master of the children of Adam, gave you the praiseworthy station (al-maqam al-mahmud), and gave you this Mighty Book. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: "The first thing you will lose of your religion is trustworthiness, and the last thing you will lose is prayer. This Qur'an will be taken from you as if it had already been removed, so that you will wake up one day with none of it among you." A man said: "How can that be, O Abu Abd al-Rahman? We have fixed it in our hearts and written it in our copies. We teach it to our sons, and our sons teach it to their sons until the Day of Resurrection!" He said: "It will be carried away by night, and what is in the copies and what is in the hearts will be taken, and people will become like cattle." Then Abdullah recited: ﴿And if We willed, We could surely take away that which We have revealed to you﴾, to the end of the verse.

Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah narrated it in meaning, saying: Abu al-Ahwas informed us, from Abd al-Aziz ibn Rafi', from Shaddad ibn Ma'qil, who said: Abdullah, meaning Ibn Mas'ud, said: "This Qur'an that is among you is about to be taken away from you." I said: "How can it be taken from us when Allah has established it in our hearts and we have written it in our copies?" He said: "It will be made to pass over it (i.e., taken) in a single night, so what is in the hearts will be removed, what is in the copies will be gone, and people will become destitute of it." Then he recited: ﴿And if We willed, We could surely take away that which We have revealed to you﴾. This chain (isnad) is sound.

From Ibn Umar: "The Hour will not come until the Qur'an returns to where it was sent down from. It will have a humming like the humming of bees. Allah will say: 'What is the matter with you?' It will say: 'O my Lord, I came out from You and to You I return. I am recited, but I am not acted upon; I am recited, but I am not acted upon.'"

I say: The meaning of this has come as a raised (marfu') hadith from the narration of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As and Hudhayfah. Hudhayfah said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Islam will wear away as the embroidery of a garment wears away, until it is not known what fasting is, nor prayer, nor rite, nor charity. Then the Book of Allah, the Exalted, will be taken away in a single night, and not a single verse of it will remain on earth. Groups of people will remain: the old man and the old woman, who will say: 'We found our fathers upon this word: La ilaha illa Allah (there is no god but Allah),' while they do not know what prayer is, nor fasting, nor rite, nor charity."

Silah (Silah ibn Zufar al-Absi), one of the narrators of the chain, said to him: "What good is La ilaha illa Allah to them, when they do not know what prayer is, nor fasting, nor rite, nor charity?" Hudhayfah turned away from him. He repeated it three times, and each time Hudhayfah turned away from him. Then Hudhayfah turned to him and said: "O Silah! It saves them from the Fire," three times. Ibn Majah recorded it in his Sunan.

Abdullah ibn Umar said: The Prophet ﷺ came out with his head bound because of an ailment, and he smiled. He ascended the pulpit, praised Allah and extolled Him, then said: "O people, what are these books that you write? Is it a book other than the Book of Allah? It is about to be that Allah becomes angry for His Book and leaves no page or heart without it being taken from it." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, what then of the believing men and believing women on that day?" He said: "Whoever Allah intends good for, He will keep La ilaha illa Allah in his heart." Al-Tha'labi, al-Ghaznawi and others mentioned it in their tafsir.

﴿And if We willed, We could surely take away that which We have revealed to you﴾. He means the Qur'an, that is: just as We were able to send it down, We are able to remove it, until people forget it. It is about to be that Allah becomes angry for His Book and leaves no page or heart without it being taken from it."
