Al-Tha'labi, al-Ghaznawi and others mentioned it in their tafsir.

That is, a helper (ʿawnan) and a supporter (naṣīran), just as poets help one another in composing a line of verse and then complete it. It was revealed when the disbelievers said: "If we wished, we could say the like of this," and God refuted them. The discussion of the i'jaz al-Qur'an (the inimitability of the Qur'an) has already passed at the beginning of the book [see vol. 1, p. 69]. Praise be to God.

The answer to the oath (jawab al-qasam) does not come with the verb يَأْتُونَ after لَئِنِ, though it may be jussive (yujzam) when the conditional is intended. The poet says:

"If what I have been told today is true, then let me stay in the heat of the day, exposed to the sun."

[The version in Khizanat al-Adab, at the 934th witness, reads: "asimm fi nahar al-qayz..." etc.]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly diversified for the people in this Qur'an from every example﴾. That is, We directed the discourse in it toward every example by which reflection (i'tibar) is obligatory: signs, lessons, encouragement and warning, commands and prohibitions, the stories of the earlier peoples, and Paradise, Hell and the Resurrection.

﴿But most of the people refused except disbelief﴾. He means the people of Makkah. He made the truth clear to them, opened the way for them, and gave them respite until it became evident to them that it is the truth. Yet they refused except disbelief at the very time the truth had become clear.

Al-Mahdawi said: The Qadari (a follower of the Qadariyyah, who affirm human power over their own acts in a way that denies divine predestination) has no proof in their saying, "Refusal (aba) is said only of one who refuses to do what he is able to do." This is because the disbeliever, although he is not able to believe by reason of God's judgment against him, through his turning away from the truth and the sealing of his heart, was nevertheless able, at the time of ease and respite, to seek the truth and to distinguish it from falsehood.

﴿And they say, "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth"﴾ [17:90]. The verse was revealed concerning the leaders of Quraysh, such as Utbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabi'ah, Abu Sufyan, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Abu Jahl, Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, Abu al-Bakhtari, al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, and others. This was because, when they were unable to produce a rival to the Qur'an and did not accept it as a miracle, they gathered, as Ibn Ishaq and others related, after sunset near the back of the Ka'bah. Then some of them said to others: "Send to Muhammad (ﷺ), speak with him and dispute with him, so that we may be excused regarding him." So they sent to him: "The nobles of your people have gathered to speak with you, so come to them." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to them, thinking that perhaps something had become apparent to them regarding what they had spoken to him about. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was eager, loving their guidance and grieved by their distress, until he sat down with them. They said to him: "O Muhammad! We have sent for you so that we may speak with you. By Allah, we know of no man among the Arabs who has brought upon his people what you have brought upon your people. You have reviled the forefathers, found fault with the religion, reviled the gods, belittled the wisdom of the people, and divided the community. Nothing ugly has remained that you have not brought into the affair between us and you," or as they put it. "If you brought this message seeking wealth, we will gather for you of our wealth until you are the richest of us. If you seek nobility among us, we will make you our lord. If you want kingship, we will make you king over us. And if what comes to you is a jinn companion (ra'iyy) that has overpowered you — they used to call the jinn companion a ra'iyy — then we will spend our wealth seeking a cure for you until we cure you of it, or we are excused regarding you." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: "There is nothing in me of what you say. I did not bring what I have brought to you seeking your wealth, nor nobility among you, nor kingship over you. But Allah sent me to you as a messenger, revealed to me a Book, and commanded me to be a bringer of good news and a warner to you. So I conveyed to you the messages of my Lord and gave you sincere counsel. If you accept from me what I have brought you, it is your share in this world and the Hereafter. If you reject it from me, I will be patient with the command of Allah until Allah judges between me and you," or as he (ﷺ) said. They said: "O Muhammad, if you will not accept from us anything of what we have offered you, then you know that there is no people more confined in land, less in water, or harder in life than us. So ask your Lord who sent you with what He sent you with to remove these mountains from us that have constricted us, to spread out our lands, to cause rivers to flow for us in them like the rivers of Syria, and to raise up for us those of our forefathers who have passed away, and let Qusayy ibn Kilab be among those raised for us, for he was a man of truth. Then we will ask them about what you say: is it true or false? If they confirm you and you do what we ask, we will confirm you, and we will know by it your rank with Allah the Exalted, and that He sent you as a messenger as you claim." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, said to them: "I was not sent to you with this. I have only brought you from Allah, the Exalted, what He sent me with, and I have conveyed to you what I was sent with to you. If you accept it, it is your share in this world and the Hereafter. If you reject it from me, I will be patient with the command of Allah until Allah judges between me and you." They said: "Then if you will not do this for us, then take for yourself! Ask your Lord to send with you an angel who will confirm what you say and answer us on your behalf, and ask Him to make for you gardens, palaces, and treasures of gold and silver, which will make you independent of what we see you seeking, for you walk in the markets and seek livelihood as we do, so that we may know your favor and your rank with your Lord, if you are a messenger as you claim." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: "I will not do this, nor am I one who asks his Lord for this. I was not sent to you with this. Rather, Allah sent me as a bringer of good news and a warner," or as he said. "If you accept from me what I have brought you, it is your share in this world and the Hereafter. If you reject it from me, I will be patient with the command of Allah until Allah judges between me and you." They said: "Then make the sky fall upon us in pieces, as you claimed your Lord would do if He willed, for we will not believe you unless you do." He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "That is up to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. If He wills to do it to you, He will do it." They said: "O Muhammad, does your Lord not know that we will sit with you, ask you what we asked about, and seek from you what we seek, so that He would send ahead to you and inform you of what He will answer us with, and tell you what He will do with us since we did not accept from you what you brought us? It has reached us that only a man from Yamamah called al-Rahman teaches you this. By Allah, we will never believe in al-Rahman. We have made our excuse to you, O Muhammad. By Allah, we will not leave you and what you have conveyed to us until we destroy you or you destroy us." One of them said: "We worship the angels, and they are the daughters of Allah." Another said: "We will not believe you until you bring Allah and the angels before us as a tribe (qabilan)." When they said this to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he rose from them, and with him rose Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah ibn al-Mughirah ibn Abd Allah ibn Umar ibn Makhzum, who was his paternal aunt's son; his mother was Atikah bint Abd al-Muttalib. He said to him: "O Muhammad, your people offered you what they offered, and you did not accept it from them. Then they asked you for things for themselves, so that they might know by them your rank with Allah as you claim, and so that they might confirm you and follow you, but you did not do it. Then they asked you to take for yourself what they might know by which to recognize your favor over them and your rank with Allah, but you did not do it. Then they asked you to hasten for them some of what you warn them of of punishment, but you did not do it," or as he said to him. "By Allah, I will never believe in you until you take a ladder to the sky, climb up it while I look on, until you reach it, and then come with you a document with four angels who testify for you that you are as you say. By Allah, even if you did that, I would not think that I would confirm you." Then he turned away from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned to his family, grieved and saddened by what he had lost of what he hoped for from his people when they called him, and by what he saw of their distance from him. All of this is the wording of Ibn Ishaq.

Al-Wahidi related from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas: Then Allah revealed ﴿And they say, "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth"﴾.

"Yanbu'an" means springs, according to Mujahid. It is of the form fa'ul, from nabaa'a, yanba'u. Asim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "tafjura lana" with a light (unshaddahed) form. Abu Hatim preferred this because yanbu' is singular. They did not differ that the gushing of the rivers (tafajjur al-anhar) is with the doubled (shaddah) form. Abu Ubayd said: The first is like it. Abu Hatim said: It is not like it, because the first is followed by yanbu', which is singular, while the second is followed by al-anhar, which is plural, and doubling indicates multiplicity. It is answered that although yanbu' is singular, what is meant by it is plural, as Mujahid said: yanbu' is a spring of water, and its plural is yanabi'.

Qatadah read: ﴿Or there be for you a garden﴾.

(Khilalaha) means in its midst.

(Or you cause the sky to fall) is the reading of the majority. Mujahid read: ﴿Or the sky fall﴾, attributing the verb to the sky.

(Kisafan) means pieces, according to Ibn Abbas and others. Kasaf, with a fatha on the sin, is the plural of kisfah, and this is the reading of Nafi', Ibn Amir, and Asim. The rest read kasafan with a sukun on the sin. Al-Akhfash said: Whoever reads kisfan min al-sama' takes it as singular, and whoever reads kasafan takes it as plural. Al-Mahdawi said: Whoever reads the sin with a sukun may take it as the plural of kisfah, or as a verbal noun from kasaftu al-shay' when I covered it, as if they said: drop it upon us in a covering layer. Al-Jawhari said: The kisfah is a piece of a thing; one says: give me a kisfah of your garment, and its plural is kisaf and kisf. It is also said: kisfah is singular.

(Or you bring Allah and the angels as a tribe) means face to face (mu'ayanah), according to Qatadah and Ibn Jurayj. Al-Dahhak and Ibn Abbas said: as a guarantor (kafilan). Muqatil said: as a witness (shahidan). Mujahid said: it is the plural of qabilah, meaning with kinds of angels, tribe by tribe. It is also said: sureties who guarantee to us your coming with it.

(Or there be for you a house of gold) means of gold, according to Ibn Abbas and others. Its root meaning is adornment; al-muzakhraf is the adorned. The zakhaaruf of water are its currents. Mujahid said: I did not know what zukhruf was until I saw it in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "a house of gold." That is, we will not submit to you with this poverty that we see.

(Or you ascend into the sky) means you climb. One says: raqaytu fi al-sullam arqa ruqiyyan wa raqyan, idha sadadtu, and irtaqaytu is similar.

(And we will not believe in your ascent) means on account of your ascent. It is a verbal noun, like mada yamdi mudiyyan and hawa yahwi huwiyyan. Similarly raqia yarqa ruqiyyan.

(Until you send down upon us a book that we may read) means a book from Allah, the Exalted, to each man among us, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Nay, every man of them desires to be given scrolls spread out﴾ [74:52]. [See vol. 19, p. 88.]

(Say: Glory be to my Lord) The people of Mecca and Syria read "Qala Subhana Rabbi" (He said), meaning the Prophet (ﷺ), that is, he said this to glorify Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, above being unable to do anything, or being opposed in any action. It is also said: all of this is an expression of wonder at the extreme of their disbelief and their proposals. The rest read "Qul" as an imperative, meaning: Say to them, O Muhammad: ﴿Am I but a mortal messenger?﴾ That is, I am not, except that I follow what is revealed to me from my Lord, and Allah does what He wills of these things which are not within the power of a human being. Have you heard of any human who brought these signs? Some of the atheists said: This is not a convincing answer. They erred, because he answered them by saying: I am only a human; I am not able to do anything of what you ask me, and it is not for me to choose over my Lord. The messengers before me did not bring their peoples everything they desired and wanted, and my way is their way. They would limit themselves to what Allah gave them of His signs indicating the truth of their prophethood. When they established the proof against their people, it was not necessary for their people to propose other than these. If it were obligatory upon Allah to bring them everything they proposed of signs, it would be obligatory upon Him to bring them whatever messengers they chose, and it would be obligatory for every person to say: I will not believe until I am given a sign other than what another asked. This leads to the affair being left to people, whereas the disposition belongs only to Allah, the Exalted.

﴿And they say, "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth"﴾ [17:90]. The verse was revealed concerning the leaders of Quraysh, such as Utbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabi'ah, Abu Sufyan, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Abu Jahl, Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, Abu al-Bakhtari, al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, and others. This was because, when they were unable to produce a rival to the Qur'an and did not accept it as a miracle, they gathered, as Ibn Ishaq and others related, after sunset near the back of the Ka'bah. Then some of them said to others: "Send to Muhammad (ﷺ), speak with him and dispute with him, so that we may be excused regarding him." So they sent to him: "The nobles of your people have gathered to speak with you, so come to them." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to them, thinking that perhaps something had become apparent to them regarding what they had spoken to him about. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was eager, loving their guidance and grieved by their distress, until he sat down with them. They said to him: "O Muhammad! We have sent for you so that we may speak with you. By Allah, we know of no man among the Arabs who has brought upon his people what you have brought upon your people. You have reviled the forefathers, found fault with the religion, reviled the gods, belittled the wisdom of the people, and divided the community. Nothing ugly has remained that you have not brought into the affair between us and you," or as they put it. "If you brought this message seeking wealth, we will gather for you of our wealth until you are the richest of us. If you seek nobility among us, we will make you our lord. If you want kingship, we will make you king over us. And if what comes to you is a jinn companion (ra'iyy) that has overpowered you — they used to call the jinn companion a ra'iyy — then we will spend our wealth seeking a cure for you until we cure you of it, or we are excused regarding you." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: "There is nothing in me of what you say. I did not bring what I have brought to you seeking your wealth, nor nobility among you, nor kingship over you. But Allah sent me to you as a messenger, revealed to me a Book, and commanded me to be a bringer of good news and a warner to you. So I conveyed to you the messages of my Lord and gave you sincere counsel. If you accept from me what I have brought you, it is your share in this world and the Hereafter. If you reject it from me, I will be patient with the command of Allah until Allah judges between me and you," or as he (ﷺ) said. They said: "O Muhammad, if you will not accept from us anything of what we have offered you, then you know that there is no people more confined in land, less in water, or harder in life than us. So ask your Lord who sent you with what He sent you with to remove these mountains from us that have constricted us, to spread out our lands, to cause rivers to flow for us in them like the rivers of Syria, and to raise up for us those of our forefathers who have passed away, and let Qusayy ibn Kilab be among those raised for us, for he was a man of truth. Then we will ask them about what you say: is it true or false? If they confirm you and you do what we ask, we will confirm you, and we will know by it your rank with Allah the Exalted, and that He sent you as a messenger as you claim." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, said to them: "I was not sent to you with this. I have only brought you from Allah, the Exalted, what He sent me with, and I have conveyed to you what I was sent with to you. If you accept it, it is your share in this world and the Hereafter. If you reject it from me, I will be patient with the command of Allah until Allah judges between me and you." They said: "Then if you will not do this for us, then take for yourself! Ask your Lord to send with you an angel who will confirm what you say and answer us on your behalf, and ask Him to make for you gardens, palaces, and treasures of gold and silver, which will make you independent of what we see you seeking, for you walk in the markets and seek livelihood as we do, so that we may know your favor and your rank with your Lord, if you are a messenger as you claim." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: "I will not do this, nor am I one who asks his Lord for this. I was not sent to you with this. Rather, Allah sent me as a bringer of good news and a warner," or as he said. "If you accept from me what I have brought you, it is your share in this world and the Hereafter. If you reject it from me, I will be patient with the command of Allah until Allah judges between me and you." They said: "Then make the sky fall upon us in pieces, as you claimed your Lord would do if He willed, for we will not believe you unless you do." He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "That is up to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. If He wills to do it to you, He will do it." They said: "O Muhammad, does your Lord not know that we will sit with you, ask you what we asked about, and seek from you what we seek, so that He would send ahead to you and inform you of what He will answer us with, and tell you what He will do with us since we did not accept from you what you brought us? It has reached us that only a man from Yamamah called al-Rahman teaches you this. By Allah, we will never believe in al-Rahman. We have made our excuse to you, O Muhammad. By Allah, we will not leave you and what you have conveyed to us until we destroy you or you destroy us." One of them said: "We worship the angels, and they are the daughters of Allah." Another said: "We will not believe you until you bring Allah and the angels before us as a tribe (qabilan)." When they said this to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he rose from them, and with him rose Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah ibn al-Mughirah ibn Abd Allah ibn Umar ibn Makhzum, who was his paternal aunt's son; his mother was Atikah bint Abd al-Muttalib. He said to him: "O Muhammad, your people offered you what they offered, and you did not accept it from them. Then they asked you for things for themselves, so that they might know by them your rank with Allah as you claim, and so that they might confirm you and follow you, but you did not do it. Then they asked you to take for yourself what they might know by which to recognize your favor over them and your rank with Allah, but you did not do it. Then they asked you to hasten for them some of what you warn them of of punishment, but you did not do it," or as he said to him. "By Allah, I will never believe in you until you take a ladder to the sky, climb up it while I look on, until you reach it, and then come with you a document with four angels who testify for you that you are as you say. By Allah, even if you did that, I would not think that I would confirm you." Then he turned away from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned to his family, grieved and saddened by what he had lost of what he hoped for from his people when they called him, and by what he saw of their distance from him. All of this is the wording of Ibn Ishaq.

Al-Wahidi related from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas: Then Allah revealed ﴿And they say, "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth"﴾.

"Yanbu'an" means springs, according to Mujahid. It is of the form fa'ul, from nabaa'a, yanba'u. Asim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "tafjura lana" with a light (unshaddahed) form. Abu Hatim preferred this because yanbu' is singular. They did not differ that the gushing of the rivers (tafajjur al-anhar) is with the doubled (shaddah) form. Abu Ubayd said: The first is like it. Abu Hatim said: It is not like it, because the first is followed by yanbu', which is singular, while the second is followed by al-anhar, which is plural, and doubling indicates multiplicity. It is answered that although yanbu' is singular, what is meant by it is plural, as Mujahid said: yanbu' is a spring of water, and its plural is yanabi'.

Qatadah read: ﴿Or there be for you a garden﴾.

(Khilalaha) means in its midst.

(Or you cause the sky to fall) is the reading of the majority. Mujahid read: ﴿Or the sky fall﴾, attributing the verb to the sky.

(Kisafan) means pieces, according to Ibn Abbas and others. Kasaf, with a fatha on the sin, is the plural of kisfah, and this is the reading of Nafi', Ibn Amir, and Asim. The rest read kasafan with a sukun on the sin. Al-Akhfash said: Whoever reads kisfan min al-sama' takes it as singular, and whoever reads kasafan takes it as plural. Al-Mahdawi said: Whoever reads the sin with a sukun may take it as the plural of kisfah, or as a verbal noun from kasaftu al-shay' when I covered it, as if they said: drop it upon us in a covering layer. Al-Jawhari said: The kisfah is a piece of a thing; one says: give me a kisfah of your garment, and its plural is kisaf and kisf. It is also said: kisfah is singular.

(Or you bring Allah and the angels as a tribe) means face to face (mu'ayanah), according to Qatadah and Ibn Jurayj. Al-Dahhak and Ibn Abbas said: as a guarantor (kafilan). Muqatil said: as a witness (shahidan). Mujahid said: it is the plural of qabilah, meaning with kinds of angels, tribe by tribe. It is also said: sureties who guarantee to us your coming with it.

(Or there be for you a house of gold) means of gold, according to Ibn Abbas and others. Its root meaning is adornment; al-muzakhraf is the adorned. The zakhaaruf of water are its currents. Mujahid said: I did not know what zukhruf was until I saw it in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "a house of gold." That is, we will not submit to you with this poverty that we see.

(Or you ascend into the sky) means you climb. One says: raqaytu fi al-sullam arqa ruqiyyan wa raqyan, idha sadadtu, and irtaqaytu is similar.

(And we will not believe in your ascent) means on account of your ascent. It is a verbal noun, like mada yamdi mudiyyan and hawa yahwi huwiyyan. Similarly raqia yarqa ruqiyyan.

(Until you send down upon us a book that we may read) means a book from Allah, the Exalted, to each man among us, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Nay, every man of them desires to be given scrolls spread out﴾ [74:52]. [See vol. 19, p. 88.]

When they said this to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he rose from them, and with him rose Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah ibn al-Mughirah ibn Abd Allah ibn Umar ibn Makhzum, who was his paternal aunt's son; his mother was Atikah bint Abd al-Muttalib. He said to him: "O Muhammad, your people offered you what they offered, and you did not accept it from them. Then they asked you for things for themselves, so that they might know by them your rank with Allah as you claim, and so that they might confirm you and follow you, but you did not do it. Then they asked you to take for yourself what they might know by which to recognize your favor over them and your rank with Allah, but you did not do it. Then they asked you to hasten for them some of what you warn them of of punishment, but you did not do it," or as he said to him. "By Allah, I will never believe in you until you take a ladder to the sky, climb up it while I look on, until you reach it, and then come with you a document with four angels who testify for you that you are as you say. By Allah, even if you did that, I would not think that I would confirm you." Then he turned away from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned to his family, grieved and saddened by what he had lost of what he hoped for from his people when they called him, and by what he saw of their distance from him. All of this is the wording of Ibn Ishaq.

Al-Wahidi related from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas: Then Allah revealed ﴿And they say, "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth"﴾.

"Yanbu'an" means springs, according to Mujahid. It is of the form fa'ul, from nabaa'a, yanba'u. Asim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "tafjura lana" with a light (unshaddahed) form. Abu Hatim preferred this because yanbu' is singular. They did not differ that the gushing of the rivers (tafajjur al-anhar) is with the doubled (shaddah) form. Abu Ubayd said: The first is like it. Abu Hatim said: It is not like it, because the first is followed by yanbu', which is singular, while the second is followed by al-anhar, which is plural, and doubling indicates multiplicity. It is answered that although yanbu' is singular, what is meant by it is plural, as Mujahid said: yanbu' is a spring of water, and its plural is yanabi'.

Qatadah read: ﴿Or there be for you a garden﴾.

(Khilalaha) means in its midst.

(Or you cause the sky to fall) is the reading of the majority. Mujahid read: ﴿Or the sky fall﴾, attributing the verb to the sky.

(Kisafan) means pieces, according to Ibn Abbas and others. Kasaf, with a fatha on the sin, is the plural of kisfah, and this is the reading of Nafi', Ibn Amir, and Asim. The rest read kasafan with a sukun on the sin. Al-Akhfash said: Whoever reads kisfan min al-sama' takes it as singular, and whoever reads kasafan takes it as plural. Al-Mahdawi said: Whoever reads the sin with a sukun may take it as the plural of kisfah, or as a verbal noun from kasaftu al-shay' when I covered it, as if they said: drop it upon us in a covering layer. Al-Jawhari said: The kisfah is a piece of a thing; one says: give me a kisfah of your garment, and its plural is kisaf and kisf. It is also said: kisfah is singular.

(Or you bring Allah and the angels as a tribe) means face to face (mu'ayanah), according to Qatadah and Ibn Jurayj. Al-Dahhak and Ibn Abbas said: as a guarantor (kafilan). Muqatil said: as a witness (shahidan). Mujahid said: it is the plural of qabilah, meaning with kinds of angels, tribe by tribe. It is also said: sureties who guarantee to us your coming with it.

(Or there be for you a house of gold) means of gold, according to Ibn Abbas and others. Its root meaning is adornment; al-muzakhraf is the adorned. The zakhaaruf of water are its currents. Mujahid said: I did not know what zukhruf was until I saw it in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "a house of gold." That is, we will not submit to you with this poverty that we see.

(Or you ascend into the sky) means you climb. One says: raqaytu fi al-sullam arqa ruqiyyan wa raqyan, idha sadadtu, and irtaqaytu is similar.

(And we will not believe in your ascent) means on account of your ascent. It is a verbal noun, like mada yamdi mudiyyan and hawa yahwi huwiyyan. Similarly raqia yarqa ruqiyyan.

(Until you send down upon us a book that we may read) means a book from Allah, the Exalted, to each man among us, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Nay, every man of them desires to be given scrolls spread out﴾ [74:52]. [See vol. 19, p. 88.]

(Say: Glory be to my Lord) The people of Mecca and Syria read "Qala Subhana Rabbi" (He said), meaning the Prophet (ﷺ), that is, he said this to glorify Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, above being unable to do anything, or being opposed in any action. It is also said: all of this is an expression of wonder at the extreme of their disbelief and their proposals. The rest read "Qul" as an imperative, meaning: Say to them, O Muhammad: ﴿Am I but a mortal messenger?﴾ That is, I am not, except that I follow what is revealed to me from my Lord, and Allah does what He wills of these things which are not within the power of a human being. Have you heard of any human who brought these signs? Some of the atheists said: This is not a convincing answer. They erred, because he answered them by saying: I am only a human; I am not able to do anything of what you ask me, and it is not for me to choose over my Lord. The messengers before me did not bring their peoples everything they desired and wanted, and my way is their way. They would limit themselves to what Allah gave them of His signs indicating the truth of their prophethood. When they established the proof against their people, it was not necessary for their people to propose other than these. If it were obligatory upon Allah to bring them everything they proposed of signs, it would be obligatory upon Him to bring them whatever messengers they chose, and it would be obligatory for every person to say: I will not believe until I am given a sign other than what another asked. This leads to the affair being left to people, whereas the disposition belongs only to Allah, the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 94:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And nothing prevented the people from believing when guidance came to them﴾, meaning the messengers and the books from Allah, by calling them to Him.

(Except that they said) out of ignorance.

(Has Allah sent a human as a messenger?) That is, Allah is too exalted for His messenger to be from among the humans. Allah, exalted is He, then clarified the extent of their obstinacy, for they said: "You are like us, so we are not obliged to submit," and they overlooked the miracle. The first "an" (أَنْ) is in the accusative position by the omission of the preposition. The second "an" (أَنْ) is in the nominative position as the subject of "manaʿa" (مَنَعَ), meaning: and nothing prevented the people from believing when guidance came to them except their saying, "Has Allah sent a human as a messenger?"

I know that Allah, may He be exalted, made clear that an angel is only sent to angels, because if He sent an angel to the children of Adam, they would not be able to see him in the form in which he was created. Rather, He enabled the prophets to do so and created in them what enables them to do it, so that this would be a sign and a miracle for them. A parallel to this verse has already been mentioned in "al-An'am", namely His saying: ﴿They say, "Why has an angel not been sent down to him?" Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided, and they would not be reprieved. And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾ [[See vol. 6, p. 393.]]. The discussion of it has already been given [[See vol. 6, p. 393.]].

It is narrated that the disbelievers of Quraysh, when they heard His saying, "Am I not but a human messenger?", said: "Who will testify for you that you are the Messenger of Allah?" So the following was revealed: "Say, 'Allah is sufficient as a witness between me and you. Indeed, He is ever, of His servants, Acquainted and Seeing.'"

He (the Exalted) said: ﴿Whomever Allah guides, he is the one who is guided﴾. That is, if Allah had guided them, they would have been guided.

(﴿And whomever He leads astray, you will not find for them protectors besides Him﴾). That is, no one will guide them.

(﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces﴾). There are two views on this. The first is that it is a figure of speech for driving them quickly toward Hell, from the Arabs' saying, "The people came upon their faces" when they hurried. The second is that they will be dragged on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces toward Hell, as is done in this world to one whose humiliation and punishment are intended to be extreme. This second view is the correct one, based on the hadith of Anas that a man said: "O Messenger of Allah, those who are gathered upon their faces, will the disbeliever be gathered upon his face?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Is not the One who made him walk on his two feet able to make him walk on his face on the Day of Resurrection?" Qatadah, when this reached him, said: "Yes, by the might of our Lord." Related by al-Bukhari and Muslim. That is sufficient for you.

(﴿Blind, dumb and deaf﴾). Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan said: That is, blind to what would please them, dumb from speaking with a proof, and deaf to what would benefit them. According to this view, their senses remain as they were. It has also been said that they will be gathered in the state in which Allah described them, so that this will increase their punishment; then that state will be created for them in the Fire, so they will see, based on His saying: "And the criminals will see the Fire and will be certain that they are going to fall into it" [see vol. 11 p. 3]; and they will speak, based on His saying: "There they will call out for destruction" [see vol. 13 p. 7]; and they will hear, based on His saying: "They will hear its raging and its roaring" [see vol. 13 p. 7]. Muqatil ibn Sulayman said: When it is said to them, "Begone into it, and do not speak to Me" [see vol. 12 p. 153], they become blind, not seeing; deaf, not hearing; dumb, not understanding. It has also been said: They became blind when they entered the Fire because of its intense blackness, and their speech ceased when it was said to them, "Begone into it, and do not speak to Me." The roaring and the wailing took away their hearing, so they heard nothing.

(﴿Their refuge is Hell﴾). That is, their place of settling and dwelling.

(﴿Whenever it dies down﴾). That is, it subsides, according to al-Dahhak and others. Mujahid said: it is extinguished. It is said: "The fire died down" (khabat al-nar, takhbu khaban), meaning it was extinguished, and "I caused it to die down" (akhbaytuha).

(﴿We increase them in blaze﴾). That is, a fire that flares. Its subsiding of flaming is not a lessening of their pain, nor an easing of their punishment. It has also been said: this refers to when it is about to die down, like His saying: "And when you recite the Qur'an" [see p. 269 of this part].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 98–99:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is their recompense, because they disbelieved in Our signs﴾. That is, that punishment is the recompense for their disbelief.

(And they said, "When we are bones and crumbled particles, shall we indeed be resurrected in a new creation?") That is, dust.

(Shall we indeed be resurrected in a new creation?) So they denied the Resurrection, and Allah, exalted is He, answered them, saying: (Have they not considered that Allah, who created the heavens and the earth, is able to create the likes of them? And He has appointed for them a term about which there is no doubt.) It is said: there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech, meaning: Have they not seen that Allah, who created the heavens and the earth, and who appointed for them a term about which there is no doubt, is able to create the likes of them? The term (ajal) is the duration of their existence in this world and then their death, and that is beyond doubt since it is witnessed. It is also said: it is the answer to their statement, "Or You cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claim." It is also said: it is the Day of Resurrection.

(But the wrongdoers refused everything except denial.) That is, the polytheists refused everything except rejection of that term and of the signs of Allah. It is also said: that term is the time of the Resurrection, and there should be no doubt about it.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 100:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: "Even if you possessed the treasuries of the mercy of my Lord"﴾, meaning the treasuries of provisions. It was also said: the treasuries of blessings, and this is more general.

(﴿Then you would surely withhold, out of fear of spending﴾) out of stinginess. This is the answer to their saying: "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth" (Qur'an 17:90), until we are granted abundance in livelihood. That is: even if you were to be granted abundance, you would still be stingy. It was also said: the meaning is that if one of the created beings possessed the treasuries of God, he would not give generously with them as God the Exalted gives generously, for two reasons. The first: he must necessarily keep back some of them for his own sustenance and for what returns to his benefit. The second: he fears poverty and dreads destitution, whereas God, exalted be He, is far above these two states in His generosity. "Spending" (infaq) in this verse means "poverty" (faqr), as related by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah. The lexicographers record that anfaqa, asrama, a'dama and aqtara are used when a person's wealth has become little.

(﴿And man has always been stingy﴾) meaning niggardly and constricting. One says: qatara 'ala 'iyalihi yaqturu wa yuqtiru qatran wa qutura, when he restricts his household in expenditure; likewise taqtir and iqtar, three dialects. The commentators differed regarding this verse on two views: the first is that it was revealed specifically concerning the polytheists, as related by al-Hasan. The second is that it is general, and this is the view of the majority, and it was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 101:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We gave Moses nine clear signs﴾. There is a difference of opinion regarding these signs. It was said: they are in the sense of the verses of the Book (āyāt al-kitāb), as al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i narrated from Safwan ibn 'Assal al-Muradi that two Jews said, one of them to his companion: "Come, let us go to this Prophet and ask him." The other said: "Do not call him a prophet, for if he hears us he will have four eyes." So they came to the Prophet ﷺ and asked him about the saying of Allah, exalted is He: "And We gave Moses nine clear signs." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not associate anything with Allah, do not commit adultery, do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, do not steal, do not practise sorcery, do not walk with a tale-bearer to the authority so that he kills him, do not consume usury, do not slander a chaste woman, and do not flee from the battlefield" – Shu'bah was uncertain – "and for you [O assembly of] Jews in particular: do not transgress on the Sabbath." They kissed his hands and feet and said: "We testify that you are a prophet." He said: "Then what prevents you two from becoming Muslim?" They said: "Dawud supplicated Allah that there should never cease to be a prophet among his descendants, and we fear that if we become Muslim the Jews will kill us." Abu 'Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: this is a hadith that is hasan sahih. It has already passed in al-Baqarah [see vol. 1, p. 439]. It was also said: the signs are in the sense of miracles and proofs. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: the nine signs are the staff, the hand, the tongue, the sea, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs and the blood, as distinct signs. Al-Hasan and al-Sha'bi said: the five mentioned in al-A'raf [see vol. 7, p. 267] – they mean the flood and what is joined to it, the hand, the staff, the years (of drought), and the shortfall in fruits. A similar account is narrated from al-Hasan, except that he makes the years and the shortfall in fruits one sign, and makes the ninth the swallowing of what they falsely showed by the staff. From Malik it is likewise, except that in place of the years and the shortfall in fruits he mentions the sea and the mountain. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: they are the five in [al-A'raf], and the sea, the staff, the stone, and the obliteration of their property. The explanation of these signs has already been given in full, and praise be to Allah.

(So ask the Children of Israel when he came to them) That is: ask them, O Muhammad, when Moses came to them with these signs, as its explanation has already passed in Yunus [see vol. 8, p. 373 onwards]. This is a question of inquiry, so that the Jews may know the truth of what Muhammad ﷺ says.

(Pharaoh said to him: "Indeed, I think you, O Moses, are bewitched.") That is, one bewitched by the strange nature of your deeds. This was said by al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubaydah. So the object is placed in the position of the subject, as you say: "this is ill-omened (mash'um) and blessed (maymun)," meaning "one who brings ill omen" (sha'im) and "one who brings blessing" (yamin). It was also said: "deceived" (makhdu'an). It was said: "overcome" (maghlu'an), as Muqatil said. Other meanings have also been given, and they have already been mentioned. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Nahik that they both read "fa-sa'ala Bani Isra'il" in the indicative, meaning that Moses asked Pharaoh to release the Children of Israel, let them go free, and send them away with him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 102:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said: "You certainly know that none has sent down these [signs] except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as clear evidences"﴾. That is, the nine signs. And "anzala" (sent down) here means "awjada" (brought into existence).

(﴿...as clear evidences﴾) That is, proofs by which His power and His oneness are inferred.

The recitation of the majority is "'alimta" (you know) with a fatha on the ta', addressed to Pharaoh. al-Kisa'i read it with a damma on the ta', and this is the recitation of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "By Allah, the enemy of Allah did not know it, but it was Musa who knew it." This reached Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "It is 'laqad 'alimta'," and he cited His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they denied them wrongfully and arrogantly, though their souls were convinced of them﴾. [See vol. 13, p. 156 onward.] And he attributed obstinacy to Pharaoh. Abu 'Ubayd said: "What we adopt is the fatha on the ta', and it is the more correct, due to the meaning which Ibn 'Abbas cited, and because Musa cannot be cited as saying 'I know'; he is the messenger and the one who calls. Even if, along with all this, the recitation were authentically transmitted from 'Ali, it would be a proof; but it is not established from him. It is only from Kulthum al-Muradi, who is unknown and unidentified, and we know of no one who recited it except al-Kisa'i." It was said: Musa attributed knowledge of these miracles to Pharaoh only because Pharaoh knew the extent of what the magicians could accomplish, and that what Musa did is not possible for a magician, and that no one can do it except one who creates bodies and owns the heavens and the earth. Mujahid said: Musa entered upon Pharaoh on a rainy day while he was wearing a woolen garment of his. Musa threw down his staff and it became a serpent, and Pharaoh saw it between the two sides of the house with its jaws, so he was frightened and defiled his garment. [Al-Fuqm, with a damma: the jaws (in the Nihayah: with a damma or fatha, the jaws). The full hadith is "and his legs, he enters Paradise," meaning one who guards his tongue and his private parts; and in the hadith, "whoever guards what is between his fuqmayn," i.e., what is between his jaws.]

(﴿And indeed, I think you, O Pharaoh, are doomed﴾) Here "zann" (thinking) means certainty. And "thubur" means destruction and perdition as well. al-Kumayt said:

"And Qudaa'ah saw, among the Ayyam, an opinion of one doomed and one who is ruined..."

That is, lost and ruined, in their claim of descent from Yemen. It was also said: cursed. This was narrated by al-Minhal from Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas. And Aban ibn Taghlib said, and recited:

"O our people, do not seek our war in folly... indeed folly and oppression are doomed."

That is, cursed. Maymun ibn Mihran said, from Ibn 'Abbas: "mathbur" means deficient in intellect. al-Ma'mun looked at a man and said to him: "O mathbur," so he asked about him, and [the report] says... Al-Rashid said: al-Mansur said to a man, "mathbur," so I asked him and he said: Maymun ibn Mihran narrated to me... and he mentioned it. Qatadah said: "halikan" (destroyed). And from him also, and al-Hasan and Mujahid: "muhlakan" (ruined). "Thubur" is destruction; it is said: "thabara Allah al-'aduwwa thuburan," meaning He destroyed the enemy. It was also said: prevented from good. The lexicographers relate: "ma thabaraka 'an kadha," meaning what prevented you from such-and-such. And "thabarahu Allah yuthbiruhu" [and "yathburuhu" are two dialects]. Ibn al-Zib'ara said:

"When I contend with Satan in the paths of error, and whoever inclines in his inclination is mathbur."

al-Dahhak: "mathburan" means "masharan" (bewitched). He returned to him the same as he had said to him, with a difference in wording. Ibn Zayd said: "mathburan" means deluded, having no intellect.

Qur'an 17:103–104 in al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So he wanted to drive them out of the land﴾. That is, Pharaoh wanted to expel Moses and the Children of Israel from the land of Egypt, [either [[in some copies: either by killing or by banishment.]]] by killing or by banishment, but Allah, Mighty and Majestic, destroyed him.

(And We said after him) That is, after his drowning.

(to the Children of Israel: Dwell in the land) That is, the land of Greater Syria (al-Sham) and Egypt.

(Then when the promise of the Hereafter comes) That is, the Resurrection.

(We will bring you forth in a mixed multitude) That is, from your graves, gathered from every place, mingled together, the believer mixed with the disbeliever, not recognizing one another, and none of you withdrawing to his own tribe and clan. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: "We will bring you all together from various directions." The meaning is the same. Al-Jawhari said: al-lafif is what gathers of people from various tribes; it is said: "The people came with their lafif and lafif (mixed multitude)," that is, with their mixed company. And His saying, Exalted is He, "We will bring you forth in a mixed multitude" means gathered and mingled together. A food is called lafif when it is mixed from two or more kinds. And "so-and-so is the lafif of so-and-so" means his friend. Al-Asma'i said: al-lafif is a plural noun with no singular, like al-jami'. The meaning: they will come out of the graves at the time of the gathering like scattered locusts, mingled, not recognizing one another.

Al-Kalbi said: "Then when the promise of the Hereafter comes" means the coming of 'Isa (peace be upon him) from the sky.

Qur'an 17:103–104 in al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So he wanted to drive them out of the land﴾. That is, Pharaoh wanted to expel Moses and the Children of Israel from the land of Egypt, [either [[in some copies: either by killing or by banishment.]]] by killing or by banishment, but Allah, Mighty and Majestic, destroyed him.

(And We said after him) That is, after his drowning.

The meaning: they will come out of the graves at the time of the gathering like scattered locusts, mingled, not recognizing one another.

Al-Kalbi said: "Then when the promise of the Hereafter comes" means the coming of 'Isa (peace be upon him) from the sky.

Qur'an 17:105: "And with the truth We sent it down, and with the truth it came down."

Al-Qurtubi said: The Almighty's words, ﴿And with the truth We sent it down, and with the truth it came down﴾, are connected to what preceded of the mention of the miracles and the Qur'an. The pronoun (al-kinaya) refers back to the Qur'an.

As for the repetition in His words "and with the truth it came down," it is possible that the meaning of the first is: We made its sending down obligatory with the truth. And the meaning of the second: "and it came down with the truth in it," like the saying "he went out with his garments," meaning "and his garments were upon him." It has also been said that the "bi" (ba') in the first "and with the truth" means "with" (ma'), i.e., "with the truth," like your saying "the commander rode with his sword," meaning "with his sword." "And with the truth it came down" means: upon Muhammad ﷺ, i.e., it came down upon him, just as you say "I alighted with Zayd," meaning I alighted at Zayd's place.

It has also been said: it is possible that the meaning is: "and with the truth We decreed that it should descend, and so it descended."

The Qur'an verse: ﴿We have divided it, so that you may recite it to the people at a measured pace﴾.

Sibawayh's view is that "Qur'anan" (ﷲ) is in the accusative because of an implied verb, which the apparent verb explains.

Most reciters read "farraqnahu" with a light *ra'*, and its meaning is that We made it clear and explained it, and that We distinguished within it between truth and falsehood. This is the view of al-Hasan. Ibn 'Abbas said: We detailed it.

Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Qatadah, Abu Raja' and al-Sha'bi read "farraqnahu" with a doubled *ra'* (*tashdid*), meaning: We sent it down piece by piece, not all at once. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy, however, it is "farraqnahu 'alayka" (We divided it upon you).

Scholars differed over how long the Qur'an was revealed. It was said: over twenty-five years. Ibn 'Abbas said: twenty-three years. Anas said: twenty years. This depends on the disagreement over the age of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). There is no disagreement that it descended to the lowest heaven all at once. This has already been discussed in al-Baqarah. [See vol. 2, p. 297.]

"'Ala mukth" means: over a lengthy period, piece by piece. According to the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, this Qur'an is coherent, meaning We sent it down verse by verse and surah by surah. According to the first view, "'ala mukth" means: with deliberate pace in recitation and proper articulation. This is the view of Mujahid, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jurayj. The reciter should give the recitation its due: reciting it measuredly, beautifying it, and making it pleasant with a good voice as far as possible, without melodizing or singing that would lead to changing the wording of the Qur'an by adding or omitting anything. That is forbidden, as was mentioned at the beginning of the book. [See vol. 1, p. 27.]

The readers agreed on pronouncing the *mim* of "mukth" with a *damma*, except Ibn Muhaysin, who read "makth" with a *fatha* on the *mim*. It is said that there are three dialectal forms: *makath*, *makt* and *mikth*. Malik said: "'ala mukth" means: with steadiness and deliberate pace.

The Almighty's words: ﴿And We sent it down in gradual revelation﴾ are an intensifier and an emphasis by means of the verbal noun, for the meaning already mentioned. That is, We sent it down star by star (*najman ba'da najm*) [meaning: verse by verse and surah by surah]. Had they been required to take on all the obligations at one time, they would have recoiled.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 17, verse 107:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: "Believe in it or do not believe."﴾ He means the Qur'an. This is from Allah, mighty and majestic, in the manner of rebuke and threat to them, not in the manner of giving them a choice.

(Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it) i.e., before the revelation of the Qur'an and the emergence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and they are the believers among the People of the Book, according to the saying of Ibn Jurayj and others. Ibn Jurayj said: the meaning of (when it is recited to them) is their Book. It was also said: the Qur'an.

(They fall down upon their faces in prostration) It was said: they are a people from the descendants of Isma'il who held fast to their religion until Allah, exalted is He, sent the Prophet (peace be upon him). Among them were Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl and Waraqah ibn Nawfal. According to this, He does not mean "those given the Scripture" but rather "those given the knowledge of the religion." Al-Hasan said: "Those who were given knowledge" are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). Mujahid said: they are people from among the Jews, and this is more apparent given His saying "before it." (When it is recited to them) means the Qur'an according to the saying of Mujahid. Whenever they heard what Allah, exalted is He, had revealed of the Qur'an, they would prostrate and say: ﴿Glory be to our Lord! Indeed the promise of our Lord has been fulfilled.﴾ It was also said: whenever they recited their Book and what had been revealed to him of the Qur'an, they would humble themselves, prostrate, and glorify Allah, and say: "This is the one mentioned in the Torah, and this is his description, and Allah's promise concerning him is certainly coming to pass," and they inclined toward Islam, so the verse was revealed concerning them. A group said: the intended meaning of "those who were given knowledge before it" is Muhammad (ﷺ), and the pronoun in "before it" refers to the Qur'an, in line with the pronoun in His saying "Believe in it." It was also said: both pronouns refer to Muhammad (ﷺ), and the mention of the Qur'an was resumed in His saying: "when it is recited to them."

This is evidence for the permissibility of glorifying God (tasbih) during prostration (sujud). In Sahih Muslim and elsewhere, it is narrated from ʿĀʾisha (may Allah be pleased with her) that she said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would often say in his prostration and his bowing (ruku')": "Glory be to You, O Allah, [our Lord [[from J, W, and Y.]]] and praise be to You, O Allah, forgive me."

**First issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they fall down upon their faces weeping﴾. This is an intensification in describing them and a praise of them. Anyone who bears the mark of knowledge and has acquired some of it should aspire to this rank, so that he humbles himself (*yakhsha'*), is lowly and submissive when the Qur'an is recited. In Musnad al-Darimi, Abu Muhammad narrates from al-Taymi, who said: "Whoever has been given knowledge but is not moved to weep by it is unlikely to have truly been given knowledge, for Allah, Exalted is He, described the scholars and then recited this verse." al-Tabari also mentioned it. *Al-adhqan* is the plural of *dhaqan*, which is the meeting point of the two jawbones (the chin). Al-Hasan said: "*Al-adhqan* refers to the beards, meaning they place them upon the ground during prostration, and this is the utmost humility." The *lam* in *lil-adhqan* carries the sense of *'ala* (upon), as one says: "He fell *lafihi*," meaning upon his mouth. Ibn Abbas said: "*Yakhirrun lil-adhqan sujjadan*" means "for the faces." The chin was singled out for mention because it is the part of a person's face closest to the ground. Ibn Khuwaiz Mindad said: "Prostrating upon the chin is not permissible, because the *dhaqan* here is an expression for the face. Something may be referred to by what is adjacent to it, and by a part of it for the whole. So one says, 'He fell prostrate on his face (*kharra li-wajhihi sajidan*),' even if he did not prostrate upon his cheek or his eye. Do you not see the saying: 'He fell prone upon his face and his hands'?"

**Second issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿weeping﴾ is evidence for the permissibility of weeping during prayer (*salah*, the ritual prayer) out of fear of Allah, Exalted is He, or out of regret for disobedience to Allah's religion, and that this does not invalidate the prayer or harm it. Ibn al-Mubarak narrated from Hammad ibn Salama, from Thabit al-Bunani, from Mutarrif ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Shikhkhir, from his father, who said: "I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was praying, and there was a sound in his chest like the boiling of a cauldron, from weeping." In the book of Abu Dawud it reads: "And there was a sound in his chest like the grinding of a millstone, from weeping."

**Third issue:** The jurists differed regarding groaning (*anin*). Malik said: "Groaning does not invalidate the prayer for one who is sick, but I dislike it for one who is healthy." al-Thawri also said this. Ibn al-Hakam narrated from Malik: "Clearing the throat, groaning and blowing do not invalidate the prayer." Ibn al-Qasim said: "It does invalidate it." al-Shafi'i said: "If it has letters that can be heard and understood, it invalidates the prayer." Abu Hanifa said: "If it is out of fear of Allah, it does not invalidate the prayer; if it is out of pain, it does." It is narrated from Abu Yusuf that his prayer in all of this is valid, "because no sick or weak person is free from groaning."

**Fourth issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And it increases them in humility﴾. The discussion of *khushu'* (humble submissiveness) has already been presented in Surat al-Baqarah, and it will come again.

**The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Say: "Call upon Allah, or call upon the Most Gracious; whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names."﴾** The occasion of revelation of this verse is that the polytheists heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ calling out, "O Allah, O Most Gracious," and they said: "Muhammad orders us to call upon one God, yet he calls upon two gods." This was related by Ibn 'Abbas. Makhul said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ performed the night prayer (tahajjud) one night and said in his supplication, "O Most Gracious, O Most Merciful." A man among the polytheists heard him. There was a man in Yamama named al-Rahman, so the listener said: "What is the matter with Muhammad, calling upon the Rahman of Yamama?" Then the verse was revealed, clarifying that they are two names for one named being: if you call upon Him as Allah, He is that, and if you call upon Him as al-Rahman, He is that. It was also said: They used to write at the head of their letters, "In Your name, O Allah," so the verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, it is from Solomon, and indeed it is: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.﴾ Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wrote, "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," and the polytheists said: "This Merciful (al-Rahim) we know, but what is the Gracious (al-Rahman)?" So the verse was revealed. It was also said: The Jews said: "Why do we not hear in the Qur'an a name that is much mentioned in the Torah?" meaning al-Rahman, so the verse was revealed. Talha ibn Musarrif recited: "Whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names," meaning the names that imply the best attributes and the noblest meanings. The goodness of the names pertains only to the goodness given by the Sharia, since they are unrestricted and explicitly stated. In addition to this, they imply good and noble meanings. Names are by divine stipulation (tawqif), so it is not valid to coin a name for Allah except by divine stipulation from the Qur'an, the Hadith, or ijma' (scholarly consensus) (ijma' here meaning consensus), as we have explained in (al-Kitab al-Asna fi Sharh Asma' Allah al-Husna).

**The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And do not raise your voice in your prayer, nor be silent in it.﴾** On this there are two issues.

**The first issue:** They differed concerning the occasion of its revelation, in five opinions.

The first: What Ibn 'Abbas related regarding His words: "Do not raise your voice in your prayer, nor be silent in it." He said: It was revealed while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was hiding in Makkah. When he led his companions in prayer, he would raise his voice with the Qur'an. When the polytheists heard that, they would revile the Qur'an, the one who revealed it, and the one who brought it. So Allah the Exalted said: "Do not raise your voice in your prayer," so that the polytheists would hear your recitation, "nor be silent in it," from your companions. Make them hear the Qur'an, but do not raise your voice that much.

"And seek between that a way" (17:110). He said: It means between loud and silent. This was narrated by al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and others, and the wording is that of Muslim. Al-mukhafatah (silence) means lowering the voice and being quiet. It is said of a dead person when he has grown cold: "khafata." The poet said:

"Nothing remained but a faint breath,
and an eye whose pupil has gone dull.
The mocker pitied it for what it had become;
woe to him whom the mocker pities!"

The second: What Muslim also related from 'A'isha regarding the words of the Mighty and Majestic: "Do not raise your voice in your prayer, nor be silent in it." She said: This was revealed concerning supplication (du'a').

The third: Ibn Sirin said: The Bedouins used to raise their voices in their tashahhud (testimony recitation in prayer), so the verse was revealed about that. I say: According to this, the verse includes the instruction to recite the tashahhud silently. Ibn Mas'ud said: "It is from the Sunnah that you recite the tashahhud silently." This was mentioned by Ibn al-Mundhir.

The fourth: It was also related from Ibn Sirin that Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) used to recite quietly, while 'Umar used to recite aloud. They were asked about this, and Abu Bakr said: "I am conversing with my Lord, and He knows my need of Him." 'Umar said: "I drive away Satan and wake the drowsy." When this verse was revealed, it was said to Abu Bakr: "Raise your voice a little," and it was said to 'Umar: "Lower your voice a little." This was mentioned by al-Tabari and others.

The fifth: It was also related from Ibn 'Abbas that its meaning is: "Do not raise your voice in the prayer of the day, nor be silent in the prayer of the night." This was mentioned by Yahya ibn Salam and al-Zuhrawi. Thus the verse included the rulings on loud and silent recitation in the voluntary (nafl) and obligatory (fard) prayers. As for voluntary prayers, the worshipper has the choice between loud and silent recitation by night and by day, and it is likewise related from the Prophet ﷺ that he did both. As for obligatory prayers, their ruling regarding recitation is known: loud at night and silent by day.

The sixth: Al-Hasan said: Allah says, "Do not show off with your prayer, beautifying it in public and neglecting it in private." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Do not pray showing off to people, and do not abandon it out of fear of people."

**The second issue:** The Exalted used the word "prayer" here to mean recitation, just as He used "recitation" to mean prayer in His words: "And the recitation of dawn; indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed" (17:78). This is because each of the two is linked to the other, since the prayer includes recitation, bowing and prostration, so recitation is one of its parts. Thus He used the part to refer to the whole and the whole to refer to the part, in accordance with the Arabic custom in figurative speech, which is abundant. Among this is the sound hadith: "I have divided the prayer between Me and My servant," meaning the recitation of al-Fatiha, as previously explained.

The Qur'an says: ﴿Say: "Praise be to God, who has not taken a son."﴾ This verse refutes the Jews, the Christians, and the Arabs in their saying, afdhadhan: "'Uzayr, 'Isa, and the angels are the offspring (dhurriyyah) of God. Exalted is God above what they say!" (And He has no partner in the dominion) because He is One, with no partner in His dominion or in His worship.

(And He has no ally out of weakness) Mujahid said: The meaning is that He does not form alliances with anyone, nor does He seek the help of anyone, that is, He has no helper who would protect Him from weakness so that He would need defense. Al-Kalbi said: He has no ally from among the Jews and Christians, because they are the most abased of people, in reply to their statement: "We are the sons of God and His beloved." Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: "And He has no ally out of weakness" means that He is not abased, so as to need an ally or a helper, owing to His might and His majesty.

(And magnify Him with full magnification) That is, exalt Him with complete exaltation. It is said: the most eloquent expression in the Arabic language for glorifying and honouring is "Allahu akbar" (God is greater), meaning a description of Him as greater than everything. A poet said:

"I have seen God as greater than everything,
Though its contenders are many, and its hosts more numerous."

When the Prophet (ﷺ) began the prayer, he would say, "Allahu akbar." This has already been mentioned at the beginning of the book (see vol. 1, p. 175). 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: The servant's saying "Allahu akbar" is better than the world and whatever is in it. This verse is the conclusion of the Torah. Mutarrif narrated from 'Abdullah ibn Ka'b, who said: The Torah began with the opening of Surat al-An'am and ended with the conclusion of this surah. In a report it is said that this is the verse of might (ayat al-'izz), narrated by Mu'adh ibn Jabal from the Prophet (ﷺ). 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb narrated from his father, from his grandfather, who said: When a boy of the Banu 'Abd al-Muttalib became eloquent, the Prophet (ﷺ) would teach him "Say: Praise be to God who..." (the verse). 'Abd al-Hamid ibn Wasil said: I heard from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever recites 'Say: Praise be to God...' (the verse), God will write for him a reward like the earth and the mountain, because God, exalted is He, says of whoever claims that God has a son: 'The heavens are almost rent asunder from it, and the earth is split open, and the mountains fall down in ruin.'"

It is also reported in a narration that a man complained to the Prophet (ﷺ) about his debt, and he instructed him to recite "Say: Call upon God or call upon the Most Gracious..." up to the end of the surah, and then say, "I place my trust in the Living One who does not die," three times.

The Surah of al-Isra' is complete. All praise is due to God alone, and blessings and peace be upon the one after whom there is no prophet.
